design.landing-page.question: I can't code and need a landing page live this week. Which builder won't trap my site or slow it down?

method.how: Ordered by how fast a non-coder gets a live, light one-pager, then penalised for what leaving costs. Export and hosting portability were weighted above visual polish, because a landing page you cannot move is a landing page you rebuild every time a price changes. Free tiers were judged on two things only: can you point your own domain at it, and is there a forced badge. Price per site, per editor and per AI credit was read off each vendor's own page on 29 August 2026.
method.tested_on: Nothing was built, shipped or measured. No Lighthouse runs, no Core Web Vitals, no A/B tests, no conversion data, no support tickets, no billing disputes. Prices and feature limits come from each vendor's own pricing and help pages, read on 29 August 2026; the ordering is judgement on top of published documentation, not evidence.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No blind benchmark exists for this category, and nobody is running one. Every comparison you will find, including this one, is somebody reading marketing pages. So judge on the two things you can verify yourself after signing up: how heavy the published page is (view source, check the payload), and whether you can get the site out. Both matter more than which editor looks nicer in a demo video.

ranked.name: Carrd
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest fast one-pager on the internet. Genuinely still the default.
ranked.use_it_when: You want a single page live tonight, with a form, and you do not want a monthly bill.
ranked.cost: Free for three sites with a footer badge; Pro Standard $19/year adds custom domains.
ranked.pricing_detail: All Carrd plans are annual. Pro Lite $9/yr (3 sites, no branding, NO custom domains), Pro Lite 10 $14/yr, Pro Lite 25 $29/yr. Pro Standard $19/yr (10 sites, custom domains, no branding), then 25 sites $39/yr, 50 $69/yr, 100 $119/yr, 250 $249/yr, 500 $399/yr, 1000 $599/yr. Pro Plus $49/yr (25 sites) up to $999/yr for 1000. Free plan: 3 sites, carrd.co subdomain, 'Made with Carrd' footer.
ranked.good_at: Weight. Pages are small and static, so they load fast on bad mobile connections with no tuning from you. Nothing else gets a working one-pager with a form up for the price of a sandwich.
ranked.the_catch: There is no export. None. No HTML download, no self-hosting, no migration path: if you leave Carrd you rebuild the page somewhere else from scratch. Day three you also discover the cheap tier is a trap for the thing you actually wanted, because Pro Lite at $9/yr does not do custom domains at all, so the real entry price is $19/yr. And Carrd is genuinely one page. The moment you need a second page, a blog, or a pricing table that updates itself, you have outgrown it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone building a site rather than a page, or anyone who needs the markup back later. Go to Webflow.

ranked.name: Framer
ranked.one_liner: Best-looking result without CSS. You will never get it out.
ranked.use_it_when: The page has to look designed, you have a day, and you are happy to stay on Framer's hosting indefinitely.
ranked.cost: Free on a Framer subdomain with a badge; Basic $10/mo, Pro $30/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Framer's pricing page lists Free ($0, 500 AI credits, 1GB bandwidth, no custom domain), Basic $10/mo (1,000 AI credits, custom domain, 50GB bandwidth), Pro $30/mo (3,000 AI credits, staging, branching, 100GB bandwidth), Enterprise custom. Prices shown are per month with a yearly toggle; the page states prices are billed by the cycle chosen at checkout, so check the total before paying. These are Site plans, bought against a published site, and extra editors are $20/mo each on top. Add-ons: $20 per extra locale, $50 per 500,000 Convert events.
ranked.good_at: Getting a modern, animated, responsive page out of someone who cannot write CSS. The template library is the best in this list, and the editor does not fight you on layout the way Webflow does.
ranked.the_catch: Total lock-in, stated by Framer in writing: 'Framer does not offer HTML export for self-hosting.' The site runs on their rendering, image resizing and CDN, so leaving means rebuilding the page elsewhere. Then the bill grows sideways rather than up. Plans attach to sites, extra editors are $20/mo each, AI credits are metered, and the free tier cannot use your own domain at all, so the free plan is a demo, not a launch. Day three is usually the day you add a second site and realise you are paying twice.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who expects to move hosts, or an agency shipping many client pages on thin margins. Carrd for cheap, Webflow if you need the code.

ranked.name: Webflow
ranked.one_liner: The escape hatch. Real HTML out, if you pay for it.
ranked.use_it_when: The landing page is the start of a real site, and you want the option of taking the markup with you.
ranked.cost: Free Starter (2 pages, webflow.io, badge); Basic site plan $15/mo billed yearly, $18 monthly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Site plans: Starter free (2 static pages, 1GB bandwidth, 50 form submissions, webflow.io subdomain, 'Made in Webflow' badge), Basic $15/mo billed yearly or $18/mo monthly (10GB bandwidth, custom domain), Premium $25/mo yearly or $30 monthly. Ecommerce: Standard $29/$35, Plus $74/$89, Advanced $212/$255. Code export is a Workspace feature, not a site plan: it starts on Core, listed at $39/mo per full seat or $15/mo per limited seat, billed yearly.
ranked.good_at: Portability. It is the only tool here that exports clean semantic HTML and CSS you can host on any static host, which is the whole ballgame if you distrust platforms. Also the only one that scales from one page to a real site without a migration.
ranked.the_catch: The escape hatch is behind a second subscription. Export needs a Core Workspace seat on top of your site plan, and the export drops CMS items and CMS pages, so anything dynamic does not come with you. Meanwhile the free Starter tier is two static pages on a webflow.io address with a badge, which is a preview, not a launch. And the real cost is day three: Webflow makes you learn the box model, positioning and flexbox in a visual wrapper. You have not avoided coding, you have avoided typing.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants a page done in an hour and will never touch it again. Carrd or Framer.

ranked.name: Lovable
ranked.one_liner: Describe the page, get code you actually own via Git.
ranked.use_it_when: You want the page and the source, and you have somewhere to host it if you walk away.
ranked.cost: Free tier with 5 build credits a day (30/month cap); Pro from $25/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Lovable's docs list Free (no monthly credits, 5 daily build credits capped at 30/month, Git sync included, no code editing, no custom domain, badge cannot be removed), Pro from $25/mo for 100 monthly credits and scaling to roughly $2,250/mo at 10,000 credits, Business from $50/mo on the same credit ladder plus roles and internal publishing, Enterprise custom. Custom domains, code editing and badge removal all start at Pro. Annual billing is discounted around 16%.
ranked.good_at: You leave with the source. Git sync is on every tier including free, so the code lands in your own repository and can be hosted anywhere. No other tool here gives a non-coder both the page and the escape route.
ranked.the_catch: It builds you an app, not a page. The output is a JavaScript front end rendered in the browser, which is heavier and slower than the static HTML that Carrd or an exported Webflow page produces, and that is the wrong shape for a page whose only job is to load fast and rank. Then the money: credits burn on every 'actually, make the hero bigger' loop, and the free tier's 30 messages a month will not finish a page. Day three you are on Pro at $25/mo because you cannot connect your domain or remove the 'Edit with Lovable' badge without it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who just wants a marketing page that loads instantly and does nothing clever. Carrd, or Webflow with export.

ranked.name: Canva Websites
ranked.one_liner: Two clicks if the design already lives in Canva. Otherwise no.
ranked.use_it_when: The artwork is already a Canva design and the page is a short-lived event, launch or link page.
ranked.cost: Free with a 'Designed with Canva' footer; Pro $180/year to use your own domain.
ranked.pricing_detail: Canva's pricing page lists Free $0, Pro $180/year for one person, Teams/Business $250/year per person, Enterprise custom. Websites are included on Free: up to five live sites on a free canva.site address (canva.link for mobile and Link in Bio templates), with a 'Designed with Canva' footer that only paid plans remove. Canva's help pages state a custom domain requires Canva Pro, Teams, Business or Education.
ranked.good_at: Zero new tool. If the visual is already made in Canva, publishing it as a page takes minutes and looks exactly like the design, which no other route guarantees.
ranked.the_catch: It is a picture of a website. There is no HTML export and no self-hosting, so leaving means rebuilding, and you have very little control over the underlying markup, which is a bad starting point for anything you want Google to rank. The free tier is not a launch tier either: your own domain needs Pro at $180/year, and until then you carry a Canva footer on a canva.site address. Day three is when the SEO person asks for structured headings and you find there is nothing to hand them.
ranked.wrong_for: Anything meant to rank, convert paid traffic, or last a year. Carrd for speed, Webflow for control.

also_considered.name: Wix
also_considered.why_not: Capable, but plans start at $17.77/mo on yearly billing, the free tier has no custom domain, and there is no code export.

also_considered.name: Squarespace
also_considered.why_not: No free plan at all, just a 14-day trial, and it is priced for a whole site rather than one page.

also_considered.name: Softr
also_considered.why_not: Built for data-backed internal tools and portals; overkill and overweight for a static one-pager.

also_considered.name: Hostinger Horizons
also_considered.why_not: Cheap AI builder bundled with hosting, but the same SPA-bloat problem as Lovable without the Git escape route.

also_considered.name: Durable
also_considered.why_not: Fast AI generation aimed at local service businesses; templated output and no export.

also_considered.name: Notion plus Super
also_considered.why_not: Fine for docs-shaped pages, wrong shape for a conversion page, and adds a second subscription.

watch_list: Framer shipping any form of HTML export would move it to rank 1 immediately, and its written policy is the only thing holding it back.
Webflow moving code export off the Core Workspace tier, or raising the seat price, changes rank 3 completely, because export is the entire reason it is here.
Carrd is maintained by one person. A quiet acquisition or a stalled changelog is the risk you accept for $19/year, and it would drop the rank.
AI builders shipping static, server-rendered output instead of client-side SPAs. If Lovable or a rival does that, it beats Framer on both speed and portability.
Credit-metered pricing spreading. Framer already meters AI credits and Lovable meters everything; if Webflow or Carrd follow, the flat annual price advantage disappears.
Canva adding real HTML export or SEO controls, which would make the free tier a genuine launch option.

sources.label: Framer: no HTML export or self-hosting
Framer: removing the Made in Framer badge
Webflow pricing: site plans, Workspace plans and code export
Canva: custom domains require a paid plan
Canva: free publishing, canva.site and the footer

writing.blog.question: I can write. I just need help drafting faster. Which tool won't make my posts sound like everyone else's?

method.how: Ranked on how much each tool helps a person who is actually writing, not on how fast it fills a page. Three things moved the order: whether it can hold your existing voice from samples, whether it grounds claims in something real rather than plausible-sounding filler, and whether it makes you edit. Tools that produce a finished-looking article from a keyword were pushed down, because that output is exactly what reads as AI. Prices were read at each vendor's own pricing page on 29 August 2026.
method.tested_on: Nothing was tested. I did not write a post with any of these, did not run drafts past a human panel, and did not measure anyone's traffic or rankings. I read the vendors' pricing and product pages and reasoned about the workflow. There is no bench here and I am not pretending otherwise.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no blind-vote benchmark for writing quality. Nothing like a head-to-head arena exists for 'does this read as human', because the judgement is subjective, reader-specific and unfalsifiable at scale. So treat this ordering as argued, not measured. Worse: search results in this category are almost entirely SEO content produced by the tools themselves, or by affiliates paid on signup. The 'best AI writing tools 2026' listicles are the product demonstrating itself, and they mostly rank whoever pays the highest commission. Read vendor pricing pages directly and distrust every comparison table you did not build.

ranked.name: Claude
ranked.one_liner: Best prose judgement; treat it as an editor, not a ghostwriter.
ranked.use_it_when: You have a rough draft, a transcript or a pile of notes and you want a hard structural edit, or you want to paste in six of your published posts and have it flag where the new one drifts off your voice.
ranked.cost: $20/mo Pro, or $17/mo billed annually ($200 upfront).
ranked.pricing_detail: Free tier available. Pro $20/mo, or $17/mo on annual billing charged $200 upfront. Max from $100/mo for 5x Pro usage, with a 20x tier above it. Team $25/seat/mo, $20/seat annually; premium seats $125/$100. Anthropic states Pro gives 'at least 5x the usage compared to our free service' and 'at least 45 messages every 5 hours' — a floor, not a promise.
ranked.good_at: Following a long, fussy instruction about register and keeping it for the whole draft. Give it real samples of your writing and it matches sentence rhythm and vocabulary better than anything else here. It is also the best of these at telling you a paragraph is weak instead of politishing it.
ranked.the_catch: It agrees with you. Ask 'is this good?' and you will be told it is sharp and compelling, which is worthless. You have to actively instruct it to attack the draft. And its own unprompted default register — measured, balanced, fond of three-part lists and 'it's not just X, it's Y' — is one of the most recognisable AI voices in existence. Left alone it will quietly sand your writing back toward that. Usage limits also bite mid-edit on Pro if you are working through a long piece.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants to type a headline and get a publishable post. It will produce one and it will read as AI. If that is genuinely what you need, you have a content-volume problem, not a writing problem, and no tool here solves it honestly.

ranked.name: ChatGPT
ranked.one_liner: Unmatched for research grounding. Its default voice is the giveaway.
ranked.use_it_when: The post needs facts, figures, sources or a survey of what has already been said, and you want citations you can open and check before you write a word.
ranked.cost: $20/mo Plus; Pro at $100 and $200/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free tier. A cheaper 'Go' tier sits below Plus — its price would not render on OpenAI's own pricing page when I read it, so check it at signup. Plus is $20/month billed monthly, confirmed in OpenAI's help documentation. Pro comes in two tiers, $100/mo for roughly 5x Plus usage and $200/mo for roughly 20x. Business and Enterprise plans exist at unlisted prices.
ranked.good_at: Deep research. Point it at a question and it will come back with a sourced briefing, and the specifics it digs up — the actual number, the actual quote, the contrarian paper — are what stop a post reading as generic. Genericness is the real AI tell, more than any turn of phrase.
ranked.the_catch: The prose. This is the voice the entire internet has been trained to recognise, because it wrote a large fraction of the internet since 2023. Em dashes, 'delve', 'in today's fast-paced landscape', a tricolon every third paragraph, and an unshakeable habit of restating your point as a conclusion. You can suppress it with a long style prompt, but it reverts within a few hundred words and you will not notice it happening. Use it for the research, write the prose elsewhere.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone hoping the drafting is the part that gets solved. Also wrong if your topic is niche enough that the research comes back confidently wrong — you still have to verify every claim, and it will not tell you which ones it invented.

ranked.name: Descript
ranked.one_liner: Talk the post out loud, then edit the transcript.
ranked.use_it_when: You know the subject cold and explain it well in conversation, but freeze at a blank page. Record fifteen minutes of yourself talking, then cut the transcript into a post.
ranked.cost: $24/seat/mo, or $16 billed annually. Free tier: 60 min/month.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 60 transcription minutes/month, 100 one-off AI credits. Hobbyist $24/seat/mo monthly, $16/seat/mo on annual billing, 600 transcription minutes and 400 AI credits per month. Creator $35 monthly, $24 annual, 1,800 minutes, 800 credits. Business $65 monthly, $50 annual, 2,400 minutes, 1,500 credits. Enterprise custom. Descript advertises 'up to 35%' off for paying annually.
ranked.good_at: This is the only entry that attacks the problem at its root. A transcript of you talking is your voice by definition — your hesitations, your analogies, the aside you would never have thought to type. Edit that down and no detector, and no reader, will call it machine-written, because it isn't. Descript's text-based editing makes the cutting genuinely fast.
ranked.the_catch: Speech is not prose, and the gap is bigger than people expect. A raw transcript is repetitive, badly ordered and full of sentences that die halfway through. Turning it into a post is real editing work — often more than writing from scratch would have been, for the first few attempts. Descript is also built for video and podcast production, so you are paying for and navigating a timeline editor to do a job a text editor could do. The AI credits are a metered currency that runs out quietly.
ranked.wrong_for: People who write better than they speak, and anyone who just wants a transcript. If transcription is all you need, a plain transcription tool costs far less and Descript's editor is dead weight.

ranked.name: Lex
ranked.one_liner: A writing app that critiques instead of writing for you.
ranked.use_it_when: You want the AI held at arm's length — a clean editor where you do the typing, and ask for feedback on a finished draft rather than autocompletion while you think.
ranked.cost: check current pricing — the tiers would not render at source.
ranked.pricing_detail: Lex has a free tier and a paid Lex Pro tier, with a Lex Teams add-on for collaboration. I could not read the actual figures: lex.page/pricing renders its price cards client-side and they did not appear in the fetched page. Rather than repeat a number from a third-party review — and this category's reviews are unreliable, see the note above — I am telling you to read the price at signup.
ranked.good_at: Its design choice. Most tools default to generating text; Lex defaults to you writing and the AI commenting. Ask for feedback and it responds like a sceptical editor rather than filling the page. That difference in default matters more over a year than any feature list, because the tool that writes for you is the tool that erodes your voice.
ranked.the_catch: On day three you notice it is a text editor with a chat sidebar, and you are doing all the work. That is the point, and it is also why people quit — the value is discipline, and discipline is easy to get for free by simply not opening the other tab. You are paying a subscription for a constraint. And the unverifiable price means you may be signing up to a figure you have not seen; check it before you enter a card.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs research, citations or heavy factual grounding — go to ChatGPT for that. Also wrong if you already draft happily in Google Docs or Obsidian; adding a tool will not add sentences.

ranked.name: ProWritingAid
ranked.one_liner: Fixes the flat rhythm that makes prose read as machine.
ranked.use_it_when: The draft is done and you want a mechanical pass over sentence-length variation, pacing and repeated openings before you publish.
ranked.cost: $30/mo, $120/year, or $399 one-off lifetime.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free tier capped at 500 words, 2 report runs each per day, 10 rephrases a day. Premium $30/month, $120/year, or $399 lifetime one-off: unlimited word count, unlimited report runs, 25+ analysis reports, custom style guide. Premium Pro $36/month, $144/year, $699 lifetime, adding higher daily limits on its AI features plus workshops and community extras aimed at fiction authors.
ranked.good_at: The reports nobody else runs. Sentence-length variation, sentence-opener repetition, pacing, sticky sentences. Uniform rhythm is the single most reliable tell of machine-written prose, and this is the only tool here that shows it to you as a chart. It diagnoses rather than rewrites, which keeps your hands on the text.
ranked.the_catch: It is slow and it nags. Twenty-five reports on a 2,000-word post produces hundreds of suggestions, most of which you should ignore, and separating signal from pedantry takes judgement you may not have yet. Accept its recommendations uncritically and you will smooth your prose into exactly the flat, correct, characterless register you were trying to escape. The lifetime licence is only a bargain if the company is still here in four years, and its recent feature push is aimed at novelists rather than bloggers.
ranked.wrong_for: Drafting — it does none. And anyone whose problem is thin thinking rather than clumsy sentences; no editor, human or machine, fixes having nothing to say.

also_considered.name: Jasper
also_considered.why_not: $69/mo per seat monthly, $59 annual — marketing-team pricing for a job a $20 chat subscription does better.

also_considered.name: Sudowrite
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely good at voice, but tuned for fiction; and the credits ($10/225k, $22/1M, $44/2M monthly) are a quota dressed as abundance.

also_considered.name: Grammarly
also_considered.why_not: Its suggestions push prose toward flat correctness — the exact quality that makes writing read as AI.

also_considered.name: Surfer SEO / Frase
also_considered.why_not: Optimise for keyword-density patterns that Google's own spam policy now treats as scaled content abuse.

also_considered.name: Koala / Byword and similar one-click article generators
also_considered.why_not: Bulk publishing at the precise thing Google says it demotes. Volume is the risk, not the fix.

also_considered.name: Undetectable AI, StealthGPT and other 'humanisers'
also_considered.why_not: They paraphrase against detectors that are themselves unreliable. You get mangled prose and a false sense of safety.

also_considered.name: Originality.ai and AI detectors generally
also_considered.why_not: False positives on human writing are well documented. Never let one be the judge of your own work.

also_considered.name: iA Writer
also_considered.why_not: Its Authorship feature marking pasted AI text is smart and honest, but it offers no research or editing support.

also_considered.name: Notion AI
also_considered.why_not: Fine if you already live in Notion. Nothing about it is aimed at voice.

also_considered.name: Perplexity
also_considered.why_not: Good sourced research, but ChatGPT's deep research covers the same slot in a tool you likely already pay for.

watch_list: Lex publishing readable prices, or any of these putting real numbers behind a client-rendered paywall — opaque pricing is a mark against a tool.
Anthropic or OpenAI shipping durable per-user voice profiles trained on your archive, rather than style prompts that decay after a few hundred words.
Google acting on scaled content abuse in a way that visibly hits sites publishing unedited AI drafts — that would reorder the SEO entries downward, hard.
Any credible blind study on whether readers can distinguish edited-AI from human prose. There is none now; one would change this whole ranking.
Descript's AI credit allowances shrinking, or a lighter dictate-and-edit tool appearing that does the same job without the video timeline.
ProWritingAid's lifetime licence disappearing, which usually signals a company moving to pure subscription.

sources.label: Lex pricing page — figures did not render
Google spam policies: scaled content abuse

writing.summarise.question: I've got a 200-page report and an hour. Which tool gives me a summary I can actually trust?

method.how: Ranked on one axis above all others: can you check the summary against the source without re-reading the document. Tools that cite back to a specific passage rank above tools that emit fluent prose with no trail, because a summary you cannot verify is one you must trust blindly. Second axis: how much of the document actually survives ingestion — the real context on the plan you would actually buy, not the headline token number. Third: whether the document can stay on your own infrastructure.
method.tested_on: Nothing. I did not upload a single document, did not run a summary, did not compare outputs, and did not measure what any of these drop. This is desk research: vendor pricing pages, official support documentation and published limits, read on 29 August 2026. Treat every quality claim as inference from documented architecture and limits, not from testing.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: Benchmarks exist and none measure the thing that matters here. Vectara's HHEM leaderboard scores hallucination when summarising documents from 50 to 24,000 words, but it catches invented content, not omitted content — and its current leaders are nano-class models, because a summary that says almost nothing hallucinates almost nothing. RULER, LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack test retrieval of a planted fact, a far easier task than judging what mattered. SummHay (Salesforce, EMNLP 2024) is the closest thing to a coverage benchmark and is not run against current consumer products. So there is no trustworthy public benchmark for 'did this summary drop the clause that mattered'. Citations are the only practical defence, which is why they drive this ranking.

ranked.name: Gemini Notebook
ranked.one_liner: Every claim footnoted to your source. The paranoid reader's default.
ranked.use_it_when: You have between five and fifty documents and must be able to prove where each claim came from — board papers, a case bundle, a literature pile, a due-diligence room.
ranked.cost: Free tier is genuinely usable; Google AI Pro at $19.99/month raises the caps.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 100 notebooks, up to 50 sources each, 500,000 words per source, 200MB per uploaded file, 50 chat queries and 3 audio generations per day. Google AI Plus $4.99/month. Google AI Pro $19.99/month: 500 notebooks, 300 sources per notebook, 500 chat queries/day, 20 audio generations/day. Google AI Ultra from $99.99/month: 500 sources per notebook and 2,500 queries/day, rising to 600 sources and 5,000 queries/day on the $199.99 tier.
ranked.good_at: Inline citations on essentially every claim, clickable straight through to the source passage. It refuses to answer from outside your uploads, which is the entire point. At 500,000 words per source it has the most generous per-document ceiling here. Renamed from NotebookLM on 16 July 2026 — same product, now with native code execution for data analysis grounded in your sources.
ranked.the_catch: It is grounded, not clever. It will not tell you what the document failed to say, and it will not push back on the author's framing — ask for the risks and you get the risks the author chose to list. Citations point at a chunk, not always the exact clause, and Google's own documentation admits that on short sources it references the whole document with no cited passage at all. On the free tier, 50 chat queries a day vanishes fast and tends to run out mid-argument.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs the summary to reason beyond the text or draft something new from it — go to Claude. Anyone whose documents cannot go to Google — go to AnythingLLM.

ranked.name: Claude
ranked.one_liner: Reads the whole thing at once. Make it quote.
ranked.use_it_when: One very long document — a 400-page filing, a full contract, a technical standard — where the argument runs across the whole text and chunking would sever it.
ranked.cost: Free tier exists; Pro is $17/month billed annually or $20/month billed monthly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0. Pro: $17/month annual, $20/month monthly. Max: from $100/month, with 5x or 20x Pro usage. Team: $20/seat/month annual or $25 monthly; Premium seats $100/$125. Uploads on claude.ai: 500MB per file, up to 20 files per chat, PDFs capped at 1,000 pages. Current models default to a 1M-token context window on paid plans; free plans get less, and Anthropic's support docs note the window varies by model (1M, 500K or 200K).
ranked.good_at: Holding a genuinely long document whole rather than retrieving fragments of it, so cross-references and 'notwithstanding clause 14' actually survive. The 1M-token window is the default on current models, not a beta flag. Best here at nuance, and the most responsive to being told 'quote the exact wording before you characterise it'.
ranked.the_catch: No inline citation UI. It produces a fluent, confident summary with nothing linking back to the page, and you will not spot the dropped clause unless you explicitly demand verbatim quotes — which you must remember to do every single time, on every follow-up. Pro usage limits also bite hard mid-document: one long PDF plus a few rounds of questions can end your session for hours.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs auditable citations by default, or a shared team notebook — Gemini Notebook. Anyone pushing 200 PDFs a month on a tight budget — Humata.

ranked.name: ChatGPT
ranked.one_liner: Best prose, smallest context. The truncation happens quietly.
ranked.use_it_when: Short-to-medium documents, or when you want the summary immediately rewritten into a memo, an email or speaker notes.
ranked.cost: Free $0; Go $8/month; Plus $20/month; Pro from $100/month.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free $0: 27K context on the instant model, limited file uploads and limited deep research. Go $8/month: 54K instant, 256K reasoning. Plus $20/month: 54K instant, 256K reasoning, full deep research. Pro: $100/month for 5x Plus usage, $200/month for 20x, with 128K instant and 400K reasoning. Note that chatgpt.com/pricing renders its dollar figures in-browser and they do not appear in the page source; the Go figure comes from OpenAI's own launch announcement and the Plus and Pro figures from OpenAI's help centre.
ranked.good_at: Turning a summary into something usable — the writing is the best of the five — and Deep Research is strong when the job is many documents rather than one long one. Widest ecosystem, most integrations, most people already have it.
ranked.the_catch: The context windows are small and plan-dependent, and this is precisely where confident omission is manufactured. On Free you get 27K tokens on the instant model, which a long PDF blows past with no warning; even Plus is 54K on the instant model. The system quietly retrieves fragments and summarises those, and the result reads exactly as complete as one that read everything. Citations into your own uploaded files are inconsistent and cannot be relied on.
ranked.wrong_for: Long single documents where completeness matters, and anything you must later audit. Claude for the first, Gemini Notebook for the second.

ranked.name: Humata
ranked.one_liner: Purpose-built PDF Q&A with real citations. Metered by the page.
ranked.use_it_when: A steady diet of PDFs where you repeatedly need to jump to the exact paragraph that justifies an answer, and scanned documents that general assistants mangle.
ranked.cost: Free for 60 pages; Expert $9.99/month for 500 pages, then $0.02 per page.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, 1 user, 60 pages. Expert: $9.99/month, 3 users, 500 pages/month, additional pages $0.02 each. Team: $49/user/month, 10 users, 5,000 pages/month, additional pages $0.01 each, adds OCR, folder and department permissions, response personalisation and enterprise support. Enterprise: custom pricing, adds SOC-2 certificate, uptime SLA and early feature access.
ranked.good_at: Citations are the product rather than a feature — every answer cites the relevant sections of your uploaded file and links back into it, which is the same defence Gemini Notebook offers but in a tool built purely around documents. OCR on the Team tier handles scanned and photographed pages properly.
ranked.the_catch: Pages are the currency and long documents devour them. Sixty free pages is one report, not a trial. Expert's 500 pages a month sounds ample until you upload three annual reports and start paying $0.02 a page for the privilege of re-reading your own files. Underneath, the summarisation is a wrapper on a frontier model you could use directly — you are paying for the citation interface, not for better comprehension.
ranked.wrong_for: Occasional users, who get more from the free tiers of Gemini Notebook or Claude, and anyone whose material is not PDFs.

ranked.name: AnythingLLM
ranked.one_liner: Runs on your own kit. Free, MIT-licensed, citations included.
ranked.use_it_when: The document legally cannot leave your infrastructure — patient records, privileged material, unreleased financials, anything under a data-residency clause.
ranked.cost: Self-host with Docker: free, MIT licence. Managed cloud from $50/month.
ranked.pricing_detail: Self-hosted via Docker or the desktop app: free under the MIT licence, with no page or document metering. Managed cloud: Basic $50/month, Pro $99/month, Enterprise custom with on-premise deployment. Model costs are separate, and are zero if you point it at a local model through Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp; it also connects to Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, Mistral and others if you would rather mix.
ranked.good_at: Nothing leaves your network when paired with a local model, and it still shows source citations in the chat interface — rare among self-hosted options. Provider-agnostic, so one interface can run a local model for sensitive documents and a frontier API for everything else.
ranked.the_catch: Summary quality is your model's quality, and a locally-run open-weight model is materially worse on long documents than anything else on this list — this is where confident omission is at its very worst, and you have no benchmark to warn you. It is also chunked retrieval by default: ask it to summarise a whole document and it summarises the chunks it retrieved, not the document. Plus you own the upgrades, the vector store and the 3am failures.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone without someone to run it, and anyone whose documents are not genuinely confidential — you are accepting a large quality penalty for privacy you may not need. Gemini Notebook or Claude instead.

also_considered.name: Gemini app / Google AI Studio
also_considered.why_not: Huge context and free, but no notebook structure and no grounded citations — Gemini Notebook is the same models with the receipts attached.

also_considered.name: Elicit
also_considered.why_not: Excellent across academic literature, but $49/month for Pro and built for systematic review across many papers, not for boiling down one long document.

also_considered.name: ChatPDF
also_considered.why_not: Free plan is two documents a day, and it is thinner and less audit-friendly than Humata at a comparable price.

also_considered.name: Open WebUI
also_considered.why_not: Strong self-hosted chat front end, but document citation and knowledge-base handling are weaker than AnythingLLM's for this specific job.

also_considered.name: Microsoft 365 Copilot
also_considered.why_not: Sensible if your documents already live in SharePoint and you are paying anyway; poor value if they don't.

watch_list: Whether ChatGPT lifts Plus above its 54K instant-model context. That single number is the largest quality gap in this list.
Whether Claude adds inline, clickable source citations to the consumer interface. It would take rank 1 immediately.
How the NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook rename settles — deeper Gemini app and Search integration could change what it is actually grounded on.
Any benchmark that scores omission and coverage rather than hallucination. That is the metric this job needs and it barely exists.
Long-context recall in open-weight models. If local models close that gap, AnythingLLM climbs several places.
Humata's page metering. A shift to token or per-document pricing would change its value sharply in either direction.

audio.voice-clone.question: I want a synthetic copy of my own voice I can legally ship. Who does it best now?

method.how: Five things drove the order. First, the route to fidelity: a fine-tune on 30+ minutes of your audio still beats a 10-second zero-shot clone for anything longer than an advert, so tools with a real professional-clone path rank above pure instant-cloners. Second, whether consent is actually verified rather than asserted in a checkbox — this job is you cloning you, but the platform's controls are what stop someone else cloning you on the same platform. Third, machine-readable marking of output, because EU AI Act Article 50(2) has applied since 2 August 2026 and puts that duty on the provider, not on you. Fourth, whether the price is readable at the tier where cloning actually unlocks, which is usually one or two tiers above the headline. Fifth, an exit: Play.ht's users lost every clone they had built when Meta shut it down, so a self-hostable option is in the list on purpose.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No audio was generated, no clone was trained, no similarity scoring was run. Prices, tier gates and cloning limits were read from each vendor's own pricing, docs and legal pages on 2026-08-29. Latency, language counts and quality claims are the vendors' own unless attributed to the benchmark below.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: One genuinely independent benchmark exists and it is unusually well suited to this job: Artificial Analysis's Controlled Voice Arena, which compares TTS models on the same eight cloned voices (four US, four UK) in blind head-to-head Elo voting. On 2026-08-29 it read Cartesia Sonic 3.6 first (1,119), Sonic 3.5 second (1,096), Inworld Realtime TTS-2 Flash third (1,075), ElevenLabs Eleven v3 fourth (1,062). Read it for what it is: a crowd preference vote on how good the speech sounds, not a measurement of how closely the clone resembles the person it was cloned from — which is the thing you actually care about here, and which nobody publishes. Beyond that, search results in this category are close to worthless: the first two pages are vendor blogs ranking themselves and affiliate roundups reprinting each other's tables.

ranked.name: ElevenLabs Professional Voice Cloning
ranked.one_liner: Still the deepest clone of your own voice, and now watermarked
ranked.use_it_when: You have 30 minutes to three hours of clean recordings of yourself and you want one durable voice you will use for months — narration, audiobooks, course modules, a newsletter read-aloud — not a one-off demo.
ranked.cost: Free tier, no commercial rights. Paid $6-$990/mo. The good clone starts at $22/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read from elevenlabs.io/pricing on 2026-08-29: Free $0 (10k credits/mo), Starter $6 (30k), Creator $22 regular with first month half price at $11 (121k), Pro $99 (600k), Scale $299 (1.8M), Business $990 (6M), Enterprise custom. The commercial licence begins at Starter — the free tier does not carry one. Instant Voice Cloning unlocks at Starter; Professional Voice Cloning (PVC) needs Creator or above and gives 1 slot on Creator and Pro, 3 on Scale, 10 on Business. A yearly-billing toggle exists on the page but the discount percentage is not stated there. Unused credits roll over up to twice your monthly quota, capped at three times quota in total.
ranked.good_at: The fine-tune path. PVC wants a 30-minute minimum and recommends two to three hours, then takes roughly 3-6 hours to train — that is a genuinely different product from a ten-second zero-shot clone, and it is why long-form output holds up. It is also the only tool here that does the consent and provenance work end to end: cloning runs through a voice-captcha in which you record a spoken phrase on the spot, and since 25 June 2026 ElevenLabs has been embedding Google's SynthID watermark in generated audio, starting with free-tier text-to-speech and rolling out to all generations, detectable through its own free Audio Detector and claimed to survive compression, trimming, speed changes and format conversion. That is the closest thing on this list to an Article 50(2) answer you do not have to build yourself.
ranked.the_catch: Your voice is collateral for the subscription. Cancel or downgrade below Creator and the PVC is not deleted but you cannot use it until you upgrade back — and any unused credits, including everything you rolled over, are wiped at the end of that billing cycle. The $11 Creator price splashed on the pricing page is a first-month promotion; the real number is $22. And ElevenLabs' own docs admit the voice-captcha 'cannot guarantee that the provided recording truly belongs to the requester, only that the requester was present' — so treat it as friction, not as protection of your likeness.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants sub-100ms speech in a live agent — use Cartesia. Anyone whose audio cannot leave their own infrastructure, or who refuses to rent access to their own voice — self-host Chatterbox.

ranked.name: Cartesia Sonic 3.6
ranked.one_liner: Top of the blind arena, ten-second clone, five dollars
ranked.use_it_when: You are building something that speaks in your voice in real time — a phone agent, an assistant, an interactive demo — and latency matters more than a two-hour fine-tune.
ranked.cost: Free tier (~27 min). Paid $5-$299/mo. Professional clone needs the $49 tier.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read from cartesia.ai/pricing on 2026-08-29: Free $0 (20k credits, roughly 27 minutes of TTS), Pro $5/mo (100k, ~133 min), Startup $49/mo (1.25M, ~1,667 min), Scale $299/mo (8M, ~10,667 min), Enterprise custom. Commercial use licence begins at Pro. Instant voice cloning from Pro up; Professional Voice Cloning from Startup (2 clones), 4 on Scale. Sonic 3.6 went generally available on 27 August 2026.
ranked.good_at: Sounding good and arriving fast at a price nothing else matches. Sonic 3.6 and 3.5 hold the top two places on Artificial Analysis's Controlled Voice Arena — the one blind test built specifically on cloned voices — and Cartesia's instant clone needs about ten seconds of you. Cartesia claims sub-90ms latency and 44 languages; those are the vendor's numbers, not measured here. At $5/mo for a commercially licensed instant clone it is the cheapest credible entry point on this list.
ranked.the_catch: No watermarking. There is no mention of watermarking, SynthID or content provenance anywhere in Cartesia's terms of service or its 2026 changelog. Under Article 50(2), marking synthetic audio in a machine-readable format is the provider's obligation, so if you publish Cartesia audio into the EU you are relying on your own audible disclosure with nothing embedded underneath it. Consent is equally thin: the terms require 'express permission' from the voice owner and a representation that you hold the necessary rights, but describe no verification step — it is an attestation, enforced after the fact. Also note the gate: the real clone lives on the $49 Startup tier, not the $5 one, and the old voice-embedding endpoints were removed on 1 June 2026, so older integration code will not work.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone shipping to EU audiences who needs the provider-side marking done for them — use ElevenLabs. Anyone who wants one high-fidelity narration voice rather than a low-latency API — also ElevenLabs.

ranked.name: Chatterbox
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed, watermarked by default, and nobody can revoke it
ranked.use_it_when: Your voice recordings cannot leave your infrastructure, or you have watched a vendor take a voice product offline and want the weights on your own disk this time.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT licence, weights included. You pay for the GPU.
ranked.pricing_detail: No pricing. Code and weights are MIT on GitHub and Hugging Face, which permits commercial use. Your cost is hardware: Multilingual V3 is a 0.5B model on a Llama backbone, Turbo is 350M, and Nano is 110M, which Resemble claims runs on CPU at about 3x realtime on eight cores. The 23+ language multilingual model is the one to start with.
ranked.good_at: Being the only pick here that cannot be taken away from you, and the only free one with a real commercial licence. It is also, quietly, the most Article-50-shaped option: every file Chatterbox generates carries Resemble's PerTh perceptual watermark by default, so machine-readable marking is on out of the box rather than being a roadmap item. MIT on both code and weights means no field-of-use clause to argue about with a client's lawyer — which is more than can be said for most 'open' TTS.
ranked.the_catch: You become the provider, and Article 50(2) attaches to providers. Self-hosting means you own the marking duty, the disclosure duty and the consent process — and there is no consent process, because there is no platform: nothing stops anyone with a GPU cloning anyone. The PerTh watermarker ships in an MIT repo, so it can be removed by anyone who reads the code; it is provenance for your own honest output, not evidence against anyone else's. Practically, expect to spend a day on inference plumbing, and expect zero-shot output from a short reference clip to be less consistent across a long script than a paid fine-tune.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who does not want to run inference — use Cartesia at $5/mo. Anyone who needs a platform-side consent record to show a client or a broadcaster — use ElevenLabs or Descript.

ranked.name: Descript AI Speech (Overdub)
ranked.one_liner: The only one built to patch your own recorded audio
ranked.use_it_when: You record yourself for a living — podcast, course, YouTube — and mostly want to fix the four words you fluffed without redoing the take.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $16-$50/mo billed annually ($24-$65 month-to-month).
ranked.pricing_detail: Read from descript.com/pricing on 2026-08-29: Free $0 (60 min media/mo, 100 one-time AI credits, watermarked exports, limited AI Speech), Hobbyist $16/mo annual or $24 month-to-month (10 h media, 400 AI credits/mo, 1080p exports), Creator $24 annual or $35 monthly (30 h, 800 credits, 4K, 3 seats), Business $50 annual or $65 monthly (40 h, 1,500 credits, 5 seats), Enterprise custom. Custom voice clones are on all paid tiers; the free plan is a limited trial.
ranked.good_at: The workflow, not the voice. Cloning takes about 90 seconds of reading a script, and the clone lands inside a transcript editor where changing a word in the text changes the audio — which is the actual job for most people who want their own voice cloned. Its consent handling is the strictest here and the most literal: you record a spoken authorisation on the spot, beginning 'I want Descript to create an artificial version of my voice', and it will not train without it.
ranked.the_catch: Two meters, not one. Media hours and AI credits are separate quotas, and heavy editing burns credits fast on the 400/month Hobbyist allowance — the tier most solo podcasters land on. The consent statement must be read in English even if you intend to generate in another language, which is an odd blocker for non-English creators. The clone is tuned for short corrective patches in your own recordings, not for narrating a whole audiobook from scratch, and it shows over long passages. And the pricing table's headline numbers are the annual-billing rates: month-to-month is 30-35% more.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants a voice as an API for another product — use Cartesia or Inworld. Anyone narrating long-form from a script — use ElevenLabs.

ranked.name: Inworld Realtime TTS-2
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest per character at volume; cloning itself costs nothing
ranked.use_it_when: You are generating a lot of speech in your voice programmatically and the per-character rate, not the monthly subscription, is what decides the bill.
ranked.cost: Free 70 min. $15-$25 per million characters; plans $25-$1,500/mo cut the rate.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read from inworld.ai on 2026-08-29: free on-demand tier includes up to 70 minutes of TTS and 100 custom voices, at $25 per million characters for Realtime TTS-2 and $15/M for TTS-2 Flash. Paid plans are effectively prepaid credit at a lower rate: Creator $25/mo ($25 credit, $20/M and $10/M, 500 voices), Builder $100/mo ($17.50/M and $9/M, 3,000 voices), Developer $300/mo ($15/M and $8/M, 10,000 voices), Growth $1,500/mo ($12.50/M and $7/M, 30,000 voices), Enterprise as low as $5/M. Instant cloning needs 5-15 seconds of audio and is included on every tier — Inworld states voice cloning itself is free and you pay only for synthesis.
ranked.good_at: Unit economics and headroom. Nothing else here gives you 500 to 30,000 custom voices and free clone creation — you pay only when you synthesise. It also holds up on quality: Realtime TTS-2 Flash sits third on the Controlled Voice Arena, above ElevenLabs v3, at the cheaper of its two rates. For a product that speaks in many voices including yours, this is the cost structure that survives contact with scale.
ranked.the_catch: The tier that matters is behind a sales call. Professional cloning — the 30+ minute fine-tune that makes your voice actually sound like you over long output — is arranged through Inworld's sales team and appears as an add-on from the $300/mo Developer plan; the self-serve product is 5-15 second instant cloning only. And the compliance story is blank: the TTS pages state no consent verification step and no watermarking or provenance scheme, so as with Cartesia you carry the Article 50 disclosure yourself with nothing machine-readable embedded. Note too that the cheap per-million rates are attached to monthly prepaid credit, not to on-demand use — the free/on-demand rate is the most expensive one on the sheet.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone cloning exactly one voice — their own — for their own content: the volume pricing buys you nothing, so use Cartesia at $5 or ElevenLabs at $22. Anyone who needs a verified consent record — use Descript or ElevenLabs.

also_considered.name: Play.ht / PlayAI
also_considered.why_not: Discontinued. Meta acquired PlayAI in July 2025 and the service was terminated on 31 December 2025 — accounts, audio libraries and every user voice clone deleted, with no migration path. The cautionary tale behind rank 3.

also_considered.name: Resemble AI (hosted platform)
also_considered.why_not: The company has pivoted to deepfake detection — Detect, Meetings, Watermarker, Identity — and its pricing page now sells detection seconds, not cloning minutes, with speech generation demoted to 'Voice AI Research'. Its consent workflow and PerTh watermarking are the best in the category; the risk is that the product carrying them is no longer the business. Use its open model, Chatterbox, instead.

also_considered.name: Hume Octave
also_considered.why_not: Cheap and permissive — the pricing page lists unlimited voice cloning on every tier including Free ($0, 10k characters), with Starter $3 and Creator $14 — and cloning explicitly requires user consent. But it does not appear in the Controlled Voice Arena top ten, and its real differentiator is prompt-driven emotional delivery, not fidelity to your specific voice.

also_considered.name: Coqui XTTS-v2
also_considered.why_not: Licence trap. The weights are under the Coqui Public Model License, which is non-commercial, and Coqui shut down in January 2024 — so there is nobody left to sell you a commercial licence. Free to download, not free to use in a business. Chatterbox is MIT and does the same job.

also_considered.name: Speechify
also_considered.why_not: Voice cloning exists in Speechify Studio but is absent from the public pricing page, which sells a $29/mo Premium listening product. If the tier that includes cloning is not on the pricing page, check current pricing before committing.

also_considered.name: MiniMax Speech 2.8 HD
also_considered.why_not: Ninth on the Controlled Voice Arena, so the model is competitive. Its cloning terms, consent handling and pricing were not readable from the vendor's own audio page on 2026-08-29, so it is not ranked.

watch_list: Whether Cartesia and Inworld ship machine-readable marking. Article 50(2) has applied since 2 August 2026, with a grace period to 2 December 2026 for systems already on the market. If either adds provenance marking, it moves up; if neither has by December, ElevenLabs' SynthID lead becomes decisive for anyone publishing into the EU.

Whether ElevenLabs completes the SynthID rollout. It started on 25 June 2026 with free-tier text-to-speech and was said to be expanding to all generations 'over the coming weeks'. Confirm your own paid output is actually marked before you rely on it.
Cartesia moving Professional Voice Cloning down from the $49 Startup tier to $5 Pro. That would make rank 2 the default answer for most individuals.
A Chatterbox model larger than 0.5B, or any licence change away from MIT. The MIT grant on both code and weights is the whole argument for rank 3.

Movement at the top of Artificial Analysis's Controlled Voice Arena, and — more usefully — anyone publishing a speaker-similarity benchmark rather than a preference vote. Nothing currently measures how much a clone sounds like the person it copied.

More consolidation. PlayAI went from acquisition to total shutdown, with all user clones deleted, in under six months. Any acquisition of a voice vendor is a reason to re-check where your clone actually lives.

design.social-graphics.question: I need dozens of on-brand social graphics a week. What actually makes them at volume without me designing each one?

method.how: Ranked on three things only: does it hold a real brand kit, can it generate many graphics from a spreadsheet or a data source without hand-editing each one, and can code drive it. Entry-tier reality checked too — export multipliers, transparent PNG, and watermark rules decide whether a free tier is usable or a demo. Be honest about the trade the whole category hides: the tools that generate fastest (Canva, Express, Bannerbear) all produce recognisably templated output, and a graphic that reads as 'made from a template' is scrolled past — the picks with real typographic control (Affinity, and Figma below) are precisely the ones with the weakest automation. Nobody has solved both ends at once.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No graphics generated, no API called, no feed performance measured. Prices, quotas and limits read from vendors' own pricing pages and docs on 2026-08-29. Where a vendor did not show a number — Placid's plan prices, Adobe Firefly Services API pricing, Canva's month-to-month rate — that is stated rather than guessed.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark exists for template-based image generation — nobody publishes render-quality or throughput comparisons. Worse, search for this category and the first page is almost entirely 'best Bannerbear alternatives' listicles published by rival image APIs ranking themselves first. Treat every comparison table you find, including tables on vendor sites, as marketing.

ranked.name: Canva
ranked.one_liner: Brand kits, spreadsheet bulk create, and everyone already knows it
ranked.use_it_when: A marketing team of non-designers has to ship a steady stream of on-brand posts, and the data lives in a spreadsheet someone maintains by hand.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro US$180/yr for one person; Business US$250/yr per person.
ranked.pricing_detail: The pricing page shows Free (US$0/yr, one person, 1 brand kit limited to 3 colours), Pro (US$180/yr, one person, 5 brand kits), Business (US$250/yr per person, 100 brand kits) and Enterprise (quote, page states 150+ contracted seats, 1000 brand kits). A monthly toggle exists and the page advertises 16% saving on yearly, but no month-to-month dollar figure was visible when checked — check current pricing before assuming the monthly rate.
ranked.good_at: Bulk Create pulls a sheet into a template and spits out one design per row with the brand kit already applied, and someone non-technical can run it unsupervised. Template and stock breadth is unmatched. Connect API can create, autofill and export designs, so it can sit in a pipeline rather than only in a browser tab.
ranked.the_catch: The automation you were sold is fenced. The Bulk Create app caps at 300 rows and 60 columns, is desktop-only, and won't take direct image URLs — images must already be uploaded to Canva. The Connect API's autofill endpoint requires the connected user to be a member of a Canva Enterprise organisation (paid-plan users get only limited trial access during development) and is rate limited to 60 requests per minute per user, so 'Canva has an API' quietly means 'buy Enterprise'. On free, exports are 1x only — no size multiplier, no transparent PNG, no SVG — and any premium element leaves criss-cross watermarks until you buy it. And everything comes out looking like Canva.
ranked.wrong_for: Developers who want one HTTP call per image without an Enterprise contract — use Bannerbear. Anyone whose brand dies if the graphic looks templated — use Affinity.

ranked.name: Bannerbear
ranked.one_liner: One API call, one on-brand image; built for pipelines
ranked.use_it_when: Images have to be generated by code — from a CMS, a webhook, a nightly job — with no human in the loop.
ranked.cost: No free tier; 30-credit trial. Automate $49/mo (1,000 images), Scale $149/mo, Enterprise $299/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Automate $49/mo for 1,000 credits; Scale $149/mo for 10,000, with tiers up to 40,000; Enterprise $299/mo for 50,000, with tiers up to 2,000,000. Unlimited templates on every plan. Automate excludes Simple URLs, Signed URLs, team members and team roles; Scale excludes bring-your-own-storage. No annual pricing shown on the page. Free trial is 30 API credits, no card.
ranked.good_at: Template-plus-JSON rendering that actually holds up in production: images, multi-file PDFs, video and title animations from the same template model, plus a Figma plugin to convert designs into templates and an MCP server. The August 2026 v5 release added scoped API keys with origin allowlists — the changelog shows monthly shipping through 2026, which is not true of every tool in this category.
ranked.the_catch: You rent a bucket of credits every month and the pricing page says nothing about rollover — assume unused credits die on renewal, which makes bursty workloads expensive. At $49 for 1,000 that is about 5 cents an image, far above what a self-hosted renderer costs, and the entry plan is a solo plan: no team members, no signed URLs. The built-in template editor is not a design tool, so in practice a designer builds in Figma and imports, adding a handoff step every time the brand changes.
ranked.wrong_for: Marketers with no developer — use Canva. Low, irregular volume — the monthly floor of $49 is dead money; use Canva Bulk Create or Affinity.

ranked.name: Adobe Express
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest branded team seats, with a hard 99-variation ceiling
ranked.use_it_when: A small team is already inside Adobe's ecosystem, needs brand-locked templates and per-seat governance, and batches are small.
ranked.cost: Free tier (watermarked with premium content). Premium $9.99/mo. Teams $4.99/user/mo first year, then $7.99.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free $0 (5GB storage, 1 social account, no brand kit). Premium $9.99/mo adds brand kits, 250 monthly generative credits, transparent-PNG and 4K export, 100GB. Firefly Pro $19.99/mo adds 4,000 credits and Photoshop on web. Teams $4.99/month per licence is a first-year promo — the page states it is regularly $7.99, two-seat minimum — so budget for the year-two step up. Enterprise is quote-only. Firefly Services API pricing is not published anywhere we could read; contact sales.
ranked.good_at: Brand management and asset-sharing controls at a price per seat that undercuts Canva Business heavily, plus Adobe Stock breadth and one-click resize across platform formats. The Firefly generative credits are included rather than metered separately at the entry tier.
ranked.the_catch: Bulk Create tops out at 99 design variations per run — a third of Canva's already-modest 300 rows — and Adobe's own feature comparison table does not list Bulk Create at all, so you cannot tell from the pricing page which plan you need until you are inside. The free tier stamps a watermark on any export containing premium content, and caps stock use at 200 premium images per day; transparent PNG and 4K are paid-only. Programmatic generation means Firefly Services, whose price Adobe does not publish.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone generating hundreds of variations per run — Canva's 300 rows or Bannerbear's API. Anyone who needs a quoted API price up front — Bannerbear.

ranked.name: Affinity
ranked.one_liner: Free, no watermark, real typography, genuine data merge
ranked.use_it_when: The graphics have to look designed rather than assembled, and you can accept a human pressing the button on a laptop.
ranked.cost: Free. Requires a free Canva account to download and activate.
ranked.pricing_detail: The vendor states: 'Yes, Affinity really is free... You can use every tool in the Pixel, Vector, and Layout studios, plus all of the customization and export features, as much as you want, with no restrictions or payment needed.' Optional Canva AI tools inside the app require a Canva premium plan. Enterprise licensing is quote-only. The separately-sold Affinity Designer/Photo/Publisher v2 apps have been replaced by this single free app.
ranked.good_at: The only pick here with proper layout and typographic control, so the output does not read as templated. Layout studio does data merge — 'flow spreadsheet or database content directly into your designs' — which covers the batch case without a subscription. No watermarks, no export multiplier gate, no per-image fee, no resolution tier.
ranked.the_catch: No API, no webhooks, no scheduling: data merge is a manual step on one machine, so it does not fit a pipeline and it does not scale past what a person will sit through. Windows and macOS only, iPadOS still 'coming soon', no Linux. Activation requires a Canva account and an internet connection, and the paid perpetual licences are gone — the price of 'free' is that Canva now controls whether it stays free and which features get gated behind a Canva premium plan. Brand assets live on the designer's machine, not in a governed shared kit.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone automating from a CMS or a queue — Bannerbear or Satori. Teams needing enforced brand governance across many non-designers — Canva Business or Express Teams.

ranked.name: Satori
ranked.one_liner: Self-hosted HTML-to-image renderer; unlimited output, zero per-image cost
ranked.use_it_when: Volume is high enough that per-image API pricing hurts, or the data cannot leave your infrastructure, and you have a developer.
ranked.cost: Free, open source (MPL-2.0). You pay in engineering time and hosting.
ranked.pricing_detail: No licence fee, no quota, no seat count. MPL-2.0 is a file-level copyleft: commercial use is fine, but modifications to Satori's own source files must be published. Real costs are developer time to build the templates and a renderer to run them — Satori emits SVG, so you need something like resvg to produce PNG.
ranked.good_at: Unlimited renders at any resolution on your own infrastructure with no watermark, no credit bucket and no vendor. Templates are HTML/CSS in version control, so brand changes go through code review and diff like anything else, and output is deterministic. This is the answer for tens of thousands of images a month, and the only pick that keeps customer data entirely in-house.
ranked.the_catch: It is a library, not a design tool: no brand kit UI, no template gallery, nothing a marketer can touch. It implements its own layout engine, so as the docs warn, output 'may not 100% match browser-rendered HTML' — and the unsupported list is long: no z-index, no calc(), no 3D transforms, no RTL text, limited OpenType features, no external stylesheets or scripts. Fonts must be supplied as TTF/OTF/WOFF. Expect to debug typography by eye against a headless-browser render, then own that pipeline forever.
ranked.wrong_for: Any team without a developer to maintain it — Canva. Anyone who wants complex layouts to render exactly as in a browser — use a Playwright screenshot pipeline, or pay Bannerbear.

also_considered.name: Figma
also_considered.why_not: Best control of anything here, but bulk generation is third-party plugins only; the pricing page we opened showed just '$12 per month paid annually, $15 per month when paid monthly' per editor and '$45 per month paid annually' for Organization, with no seat types listed — verify seat types before buying.

also_considered.name: Placid
also_considered.why_not: Does Bannerbear's job with a nicer editor and 500-100,000 monthly credits by tier, but no dollar prices were visible on its pricing page when checked — we will not quote a number we cannot read.

also_considered.name: Templated.io
also_considered.why_not: Cheaper on paper — $29/mo for 1,000 render credits, $79 for 5,000, $179 for 25,000, 50 free trial credits — but every price is billed annually, and the page is silent on watermarks.

also_considered.name: Penpot
also_considered.why_not: Open-source and self-hostable with a free fully-featured cloud tier ($7/user/mo Unlimited, capped at $175/mo), but it is a design tool with REST API and webhooks, not a data-merge or batch image generator.

also_considered.name: Corel Vector
also_considered.why_not: Excluded: Corel discontinued it on 31 August 2025, and stored files went with it.

also_considered.name: Adobe Firefly Services
also_considered.why_not: The genuine programmatic route into Adobe's stack, but no pricing is published and access looks enterprise-gated — unquotable.

watch_list: Canva opening the Connect API autofill endpoint below Enterprise. That single change would make it the clear pick for developers as well as marketers.
Whether Adobe raises the 99-variation Bulk Create ceiling and publishes Firefly Services API pricing.
Whether Canva starts gating Affinity's export or data-merge features behind a paid Canva plan — the free app's whole case rests on that not happening.
Bannerbear credit rollover, or any rival (Placid, Templated) publishing readable per-image pricing that undercuts 5 cents an image.
Satori gaining grid, z-index and RTL support, which would close most of the gap with a headless-browser renderer and make self-hosting the default for volume.
Any platform or audience signal that visibly penalises obviously templated creative — it would push the ranking towards Affinity and Figma and away from one-click bulk.
