marketing.aeo.question: Do ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity mention my brand when people ask — and can anything actually prove it?

method.how: Be honest first: this category is immature and most of it is selling certainty it cannot have. Every tool here does the same thing — it writes some prompts, sends them to a few models on a schedule, and counts how often your name appears. That is a sample, not 'your visibility'. Independent research by SparkToro and Gumshoe.ai (2,961 runs, Nov-Dec 2025) found under a 1-in-100 chance that two ChatGPT or Google AI answers to the same question list the same brands, and roughly 1-in-1,000 for the same order — so a tool that runs each prompt once a day per model (Peec's own FAQ says exactly that) is charting noise at the prompt level, and only an aggregate share over hundreds of runs means anything. None of these vendors can see what real users actually type; 'AI search volume' products are modelled from undisclosed panels. So the ranking is driven by how much of the method the vendor will show you, which engines you genuinely get at the advertised price, and cost per prompt tracked — not by dashboard polish.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No prompts were run through any platform and no vendor's accuracy was checked. Prices, prompt quotas and engine lists were read from each vendor's own pricing page on 2026-08-29. Peec AI's pricing page rendered its tiers but no numbers, so no Peec price is quoted here.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark of these tools' accuracy exists — nobody has published a controlled test of whether Profound, Peec, Otterly or anyone else reports the same brand share as a careful manual run. The nearest independent work is SparkToro's study with Gumshoe.ai (600 volunteers, 12 prompts, 2,961 runs across ChatGPT, Claude and Google AI, Nov-Dec 2025), which measures how unstable the underlying answers are, not how good the tools are; its authors concluded visibility percentage over many runs is defensible while rank-position tracking is not. Search is worse than useless here: page one for 'best AI visibility tools' is vendors ranking themselves — Profound's own blog ranks for it — plus a long tail of unfamiliar sites publishing comparison posts about products they sell against.

ranked.name: Otterly.AI
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest transparent read on four engines; add-ons bite
ranked.use_it_when: You want a defensible answer within a week, on a monthly rolling plan, without a sales call or an annual commitment — and you can live with a small set of prompts.
ranked.cost: $29-$489/mo monthly. Annual saves 15%. Enterprise from $1,000/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Monthly: Lite $29 (15 prompts, 1 workspace), Standard $189 (100 prompts), Premium $489 (400 prompts). Annual: $25 / $160 / $422 per month. Enterprise custom, stated as starting at $1,000/mo. Base engines on every tier: ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, tracked daily, with unlimited team members. Add-ons per month by tier: Claude $29 / $109 / $439; Google AI Mode and Gemini $9 / $59 / $149. Free trial offered; the page states all subscriptions are monthly and cancellable anytime.
ranked.good_at: Honesty about what is in the box. It states which engines the base price covers, prices the rest as add-ons instead of hiding them behind 'contact sales', gives unlimited seats even on the $29 plan, and bills monthly so you can quit after a bad month.
ranked.the_catch: The Claude add-on on the Lite plan costs $29/mo — the same as the plan itself — and Gemini plus Google AI Mode is another $9. So the four-model picture most people actually want is $67/mo, not the advertised $29. And 15 prompts is a keyhole: with answers as unstable as they are, 15 prompts sampled once a day is far too small a sample to read week-to-week movement into. The next step up is $189.
ranked.wrong_for: Agencies reporting on many clients — use Scrunch or Peec. Anyone who needs to see AI crawler and referral traffic on their own site as well as mentions — use Profound.

ranked.name: Profound
ranked.one_liner: Deepest data; the advertised $99 tier watches ChatGPT only
ranked.use_it_when: You have to report AI visibility to people who will challenge the number, and you want mention-sampling sitting next to actual agent and referral traffic hitting your own site.
ranked.cost: $99/mo Starter, $399/mo Growth — both billed yearly. Enterprise on quote.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter $99/mo billed yearly (2 months free): ChatGPT tracking only, 50 prompts, 1 seat, 100 agent credits/month, email support, no Agent Analytics. Growth $399/mo billed yearly: 3 answer engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews), 100 prompts, 3 seats, 400 agent credits/month, Agent Analytics with unlimited domains. Enterprise: quote only, up to 9 answer engines including Google AI Mode, Gemini, Copilot, Grok, DeepSeek and Claude. No monthly-billing price is shown for any tier.
ranked.good_at: Agent Analytics is the one number here that is measured rather than sampled — AI crawler and referral traffic arriving at your own site. Widest engine list of any vendor with a public rate card, and the most developed research output.
ranked.the_catch: The prices are annual-billed, and the headline $99 tier is thinner than it looks: one model, one seat, 50 prompts, and no Agent Analytics — the feature that is the actual reason to buy Profound. Claude and Gemini tracking is Enterprise-only, so 'up to 9 answer engines' means a sales call. Separately, treat Prompt Volumes with care: the launch post claims 'billions of near real-time data signals' and refers to a 'panel' whose size it never discloses, and the feature shipped as a closed beta. Vendor-modelled estimates, not measured search volume.
ranked.wrong_for: Solo founders and small teams checking whether they exist at all — that is $1,188 a year to watch one model. Start with Otterly or self-hosted Elmo.

ranked.name: Scrunch
ranked.one_liner: Most prompts per pound, and Claude without an Enterprise call
ranked.use_it_when: You are past experimenting, need a few hundred of your own prompts across six engines including Claude and Meta, and want a proper trial before paying.
ranked.cost: Starter $300/mo monthly, $250/mo annual. Growth $500/$417. 7-day trial, no card.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter $300/mo monthly or $250/mo billed annually (17% discount): 3 user licences, 350 custom prompts, 1,000 industry prompts, 3 personas, 5 page audits. Growth $500/mo monthly or $417/mo annual: 5 licences, 700 custom prompts, 2,500 industry prompts, 5 personas, 10 page audits. Enterprise: custom, adds SAML/OIDC and an Enterprise Data API. Extra seats $25/mo each, or $75/mo for up to 5 extra seats on Starter. All tiers monitor ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, and Meta.
ranked.good_at: Engine coverage at the entry price. Claude and Meta AI are included on the cheapest tier, where Profound puts Claude behind Enterprise and Otterly charges for it. 350 custom prompts is a large enough sample to average meaningfully.
ranked.the_catch: There is no cheap tier — the floor is $250/mo annual, $300 monthly, so the real trial period is seven days. The big number on the page, 1,000 industry prompts, is Scrunch's pre-built set, not yours; the one that matters is the 350 you write. Seats are per user beyond three, at $25/mo each, which is per-seat pricing sitting under a plan price that reads per-account.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone testing whether this whole category is worth anything — that decision costs $300 here. Use Otterly or Elmo first.

ranked.name: Elmo
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed, self-hostable, and you can audit the sampling
ranked.use_it_when: Your data cannot leave your infrastructure, or you want to see exactly how many runs per prompt produced the number before you believe it.
ranked.cost: Free self-hosted (MIT). Hosted $29-$649/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Self-hosted: free forever, no licence fee, no per-seat charge; you pay your own infrastructure and your own AI provider API keys. MIT licence, so commercial use is permitted. Hosted: Starter $29/mo ($290/yr) 50 prompts, ChatGPT only, 1x daily scraping; Basic $99/mo ($990/yr) 50 prompts, choice of 4 platforms, 4x daily; Pro $299/mo ($2,990/yr) 150 prompts, 2 brands, premium LLM APIs included; Business $649/mo ($6,490/yr) 350 prompts, 5 brands; Custom on contract. Repo: github.com/elmohq/elmo.
ranked.good_at: The only option on this list where the method is inspectable. You can read how prompts are dispatched, how many samples are taken and how mentions are matched, instead of trusting a vendor's word for it — and the MIT licence means commercial use with no strings.
ranked.the_catch: 201 GitHub stars on 2026-08-29 — a young project, not an ecosystem, with no SLA and no support. Self-hosting shifts the cost to you: you pay per API call for the models with APIs, and for the surfaces with none (ChatGPT web, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode) it scrapes — scraping breaks, and you own the breakage and whatever the terms of service say about it. The hosted Starter is ChatGPT-only at one run per day, the same too-small sample as everyone else's entry tier.
ranked.wrong_for: Teams with no engineer to run it, and agencies who need client-ready reporting out of the box — use Peec or Scrunch.

ranked.name: Peec AI
ranked.one_liner: Broad model coverage, daily runs, and no published price
ranked.use_it_when: You are an agency tracking several brands across many models and are willing to go through a trial and a quote to find out what it costs.
ranked.cost: Check current pricing — no numbers rendered on peec.ai/pricing on 2026-08-29. Free trial available.
ranked.pricing_detail: Tier contents are published, prices are not. Starter: 50 prompts, choice of 3 models, 1 project. Pro: 150 prompts, 3 models, 2 projects. Advanced: 350 prompts, 3 models, 5 projects, multi-country, Looker Studio. Enterprise: unlimited prompts, all 11 models, API access, SSO, daily or weekly frequency. All listed as annual billing, with a stated 15% discount for annual. Unlimited users on every tier. Agency plans are sold as annual credits — Essential 10,000 (about 111 prompts daily, 3 brands), Growth 25,000 (about 277 daily, 10 brands), Scale 65,000 (about 722 daily, 25 brands, adding Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-5 Search, DeepSeek, Qwen and Mistral), Comprehensive unlimited. No EUR or USD figure appears on either the standard or agency pricing page.
ranked.good_at: Model breadth per project once you are on the higher agency tiers, unlimited seats on every plan, and daily execution against every model you select. Widely used by European SEO agencies, and the client reporting is the part people rate.
ranked.the_catch: We could not read a single price on their own pricing page — the tiers render, the numbers do not — so you cannot compare Peec against anything without booking a trial and talking to them. The plans are quoted as annual billing, and credits are sold as an annual allowance, so an agency plan is a year-long commitment with a usage cap. Their own FAQ states each prompt runs 'once every 24 hours on every AI model you've selected': one sample per model per day, which given how unstable these answers are means day-to-day wobble in your chart is mostly noise, not movement. Everything below Enterprise is capped at three models.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs a price before a sales conversation, or who is buying for one brand rather than a portfolio — use Otterly or Scrunch.

also_considered.name: Ahrefs Brand Radar
also_considered.why_not: The free AI Visibility Checker (no signup, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and AI Overviews, limited to the top 5 results per section) is the best zero-cost sanity check going — but tracked prompts are 5/day on the $129/mo Lite plan and full Brand Radar AI is $199/mo on top of a subscription you may not want.

also_considered.name: Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit
also_considered.why_not: $99/mo per domain billed annually buys only 25 custom prompts across ChatGPT, Google AI, Gemini and Perplexity. Adobe completed its acquisition of Semrush on 28 April 2026 and says it will fold the product into Experience Manager and Experience Platform; nothing here is announced as discontinued, but do not sign a long annual deal into a product mid-integration.

also_considered.name: Evertune
also_considered.why_not: Methodologically the most serious of the lot — the vendor claims it samples each prompt up to 100 times per model across 11 models, which is the right way to do this — but there is no public pricing whatsoever, only a demo request, so it cannot be compared on cost.

also_considered.name: Cloudflare AI Crawl Control
also_considered.why_not: Free and available on all Cloudflare plans, and it shows which AI services are actually fetching your pages. It measures crawler access, not whether an assistant names you in an answer. A complement to the tools above, never a substitute.

also_considered.name: Rolling your own (provider APIs plus a cron job)
also_considered.why_not: Cheapest way to run 50 prompts 100 times each and compute your own confidence intervals — but the surfaces that matter most for consumer queries (ChatGPT's web app, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode) have no API, so a DIY harness sees a systematically different world from the one your customers use.

watch_list: Any vendor publishing runs-per-prompt and confidence intervals by default. Evertune's 100-samples-per-prompt approach becoming table stakes would reorder this list on method alone.
Whether OpenAI or Google ever release real prompt-frequency data. Until they do, every 'AI search volume' figure sold in this category is a modelled estimate from an undisclosed panel.
Cleaner referral attribution from AI assistants in analytics. If log-based measurement gets reliable, the tools with real agent analytics beat the prompt-samplers outright.
Adobe's repackaging of Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit — pricing and availability could change materially now the acquisition has closed.
Peec AI publishing prices on its pricing page. It would move up this list the day it does.
Elmo gaining contributors, releases and a maintenance track record — a credible open-source option changes the economics of this whole category.

Ahrefs pricing — tracked AI prompts per plan

social.schedule.question: Which scheduler actually auto-publishes to Instagram, TikTok and LinkedIn, and what does it really cost per account?

method.how: Ranked on two things a scheduler either does or does not do: how many networks it publishes to without a human touching a phone, and what the bill looks like at ten accounts rather than one. Every publishing claim was checked against the vendor's own help centre and then against the platform API doc behind it - Meta's Instagram content-publishing reference, TikTok's Content Posting API, LinkedIn's Posts API - because the API decides whether a post fires, not the marketing page. Price per connected account at scale broke ties. Nothing here auto-publishes everything: Instagram Stories carrying links or stickers, Reels with off-catalogue music, Facebook Groups and TikTok effects are reminder-only across all five, and a tool claiming otherwise is describing a reminder.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No post was scheduled or published through any of these tools. Prices and publishing-capability claims were read from the vendors' own pricing and help pages, and from Meta, TikTok and LinkedIn developer documentation, on 2026-08-29.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark exists for social schedulers. There is no neutral body testing whether a given tool's scheduled post actually lands, so nobody can tell you a failure rate. Search results here are dominated by vendors ranking themselves - Buffer, Hootsuite, Sprout Social and SocialBee all publish 'best scheduling tools' listicles that place themselves at or near the top. Everything above traces to a vendor's own documentation or a platform's API reference, which are self-interested in opposite directions: vendors overstate coverage, platforms understate what they will let third parties do.

ranked.name: Buffer
ranked.one_liner: Per-channel pricing and the most honest publishing docs here.
ranked.use_it_when: You run roughly eight channels or fewer and want to know, before you pay, exactly which posts fire on their own and which ping your phone.
ranked.cost: Free for 3 channels. Paid from $5/channel/mo (Essentials) or $10/channel/mo (Team).
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 3 channels, 10 scheduled posts per channel, 1 user, 30-day analytics history, 100 ideas. Essentials $5 per channel per month: unlimited scheduled posts, 1 user, advanced analytics, first-comment scheduling. Team $10 per channel per month: unlimited team members, approval workflows, permissions, branded reports. 20 percent off on annual billing - $60 per channel per year on Essentials. No minimum channel count; you can buy one. A channel is one social account, so one Instagram profile, one Facebook page and one LinkedIn page are three channels and three charges.
ranked.good_at: It publishes a plain table of what is direct versus what is a notification, instead of burying it. Direct publish covers Facebook Pages, Instagram business and creator accounts, X, LinkedIn company pages AND personal profiles, Pinterest, TikTok, Google Business Profile, YouTube Shorts, Threads, Bluesky and Mastodon. Notification publishing is reserved for the four cases the APIs genuinely block: Facebook Groups, Instagram personal accounts, adding music to Reels or TikToks, and images outside Instagram's accepted aspect-ratio range.
ranked.the_catch: 'Every channel' is exactly where per-channel billing bites. Twelve accounts on Team is $120 a month - more than Hootsuite Standard, which bundles ten. Buffer's own supported-channels page marks TikTok, Threads, Bluesky, Mastodon and YouTube Shorts as available on 'new plans only', so anyone still on a legacy Buffer subscription cannot connect them without migrating plan. And the free tier's 10 scheduled posts per channel is a queue-depth cap, not a monthly allowance - it demos, it does not run anything.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone past about ten accounts: the per-channel maths turns against you, so take Metricool or Publer. Also wrong if you plan Instagram visually first and captions second - Later is built for that.

ranked.name: Metricool
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest way to run many networks, provided you skip X.
ranked.use_it_when: You manage several distinct brands or clients, each with one account per network, and you want analytics worth actually reading alongside the calendar.
ranked.cost: Free for 1 brand, 20 posts/mo. Starter $20/mo annual ($25 monthly). Advanced $53/mo annual ($67 monthly).
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 1 brand you cannot delete, 20 planner posts per month, 30 days of analytics with a watermark, 5 competitors, 5 AI credits - and no LinkedIn and no X. Starter: up to 10 brands, 'unlimited' publishing under an unpublished fair-use limit, $20/month billed annually or $25 month-to-month. Advanced: up to 50 brands, team management, post approval, full X analytics, API access, $53/month annually or $67 month-to-month. Custom: unlimited brands, white label, quote only. Critically, the billing unit is a BRAND, not a channel: one brand holds one profile per social network, so Instagram plus Facebook plus TikTok plus YouTube plus Pinterest for the same business is a single brand. Two Instagram accounts, however, is two brands.
ranked.good_at: Cost per connected account once you pass a handful, by a wide margin - ten networks under one brand cost the same as one. Its help pages are also the most specific of any vendor here about what the APIs refuse: Instagram Stories carrying links, mentions or stickers drop to manual publishing, carousels with video over 60 seconds do the same, and TikTok auto-publish cannot use effects or any music outside TikTok's trending Top 100 and strips line breaks entirely.
ranked.the_catch: X/Twitter is a paid add-on at $10 per month per account on top of the plan, and it is absent from the free tier altogether - five brands with an X presence adds $50/month to a $20/month plan, more than tripling it. 'Unlimited publishing' is qualified by a fair-use limit Metricool does not publish. Advanced Analytics and the Looker Studio connector are further add-ons, so the headline number is rarely the invoice.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone needing two accounts on the same network for one client - each extra one consumes a whole brand slot. Use Publer, which charges per account. Skip it too if X is central to your posting; Buffer includes X in its flat per-channel price.

ranked.name: Publer
ranked.one_liner: Lowest marginal cost per extra account; covers the odd networks.
ranked.use_it_when: You add accounts one at a time and want the next one to cost a few dollars rather than force a plan upgrade.
ranked.cost: Free for 3 accounts (no X). Professional from $5/mo + $4 per extra account. Business from $10/mo + $7 per extra.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 3 social accounts excluding X, 1 user, 1 workspace, 10 pending scheduled posts per account, 25 drafts, 24-hour post history. Professional: from $5/month for the first account, $4/month per additional account, $2/month per extra member; adds X support, unlimited scheduling and drafts, permanent post history, bulk scheduling, unbranded link-in-bio. Business: from $10/month for the first account, $7/month per additional, $3/month per member; adds analytics reports, AI Assist, best-time-to-post, hashtag suggestions and post recycling. Enterprise by quote. Every 10th social account and every 10th member is free. Yearly billing gives two months free.
ranked.good_at: Networks the others ignore - Telegram, Mastodon, WordPress, Google Business Profile, Bluesky and Threads sit alongside the usual six - and the cheapest marginal account of any hosted tool listed. Post recycling and evergreen queues arrive on Business rather than being reserved for a top agency tier.
ranked.the_catch: The free plan's '10 pending scheduled posts per account' is a queue-depth cap, so three weeks of daily posts will not fit and the tier only ever demos. X is excluded from free entirely. And the advertised '$5/month' buys one account: the real number is $5 plus $4 for every account after it, and analytics are not on Professional at all - they need Business at $10 plus $7 each, double the headline.
ranked.wrong_for: Teams needing polished client-facing approvals and reporting - Buffer Team or SocialBee do that properly. Anyone who wants deep native analytics should take Metricool instead.

ranked.name: SocialBee
ranked.one_liner: Evergreen category queues, plus an unusually candid publishing table.
ranked.use_it_when: You want a repeating calendar that refills itself from content categories rather than scheduling every single post by hand.
ranked.cost: No free plan. $29/mo (5 profiles) to $99/mo (25 profiles). Agency tiers $179-$449/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Bootstrap $29/month, or $24.92/month billed annually ($290/year): 5 social profiles, 1 user, 1 workspace. Accelerate $49/month, or $40.83/month annually ($490/year): 10 profiles. Pro $99/month, or $82.50/month annually ($990/year): 25 profiles, 3 users, 5 workspaces. Agency tiers: Pro50 $179/month for 50 profiles, Pro100 $329/month for 100, Pro150 $449/month for 150. 14-day trial, 30-day money-back guarantee, no free plan of any kind.
ranked.good_at: Content categories with automatic recycling: you define buckets, set a weekly slot pattern, and the queue refills itself indefinitely - nothing else on this list does evergreen as its core model. Its help centre also spells out direct versus reminder per network, including the awkward ones: Facebook profiles and groups and Instagram personal accounts are reminder-only, LinkedIn personal profiles and company pages are both direct, and TikTok is direct for one video with up to twelve more per day via reminders.
ranked.the_catch: If you bought a lifetime deal, X posting is reminders-only unless you buy a $10/month direct-posting add-on - SocialBee's own docs say so. Profiles are counted flat, so an agency with fifteen clients on three networks each is 45 profiles and lands on Pro50 at $179/month, not Pro at $99. And there is no free tier at all: 14 days is the only way to find out whether the recycling engine suits you.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone scheduling a fixed calendar who will never recycle a post - you are paying for an engine you do not use, and Buffer or Publer cost less. Skip it entirely if you need a permanent free tier.

ranked.name: Postiz
ranked.one_liner: The only credible self-hosted option; TikTok will fight you.
ranked.use_it_when: Your data or your clients' tokens cannot sit on someone else's SaaS, and you have an engineer willing to run a Docker stack and chase platform app reviews.
ranked.cost: Self-host free under AGPL-3.0. Hosted $29/mo (5 channels) to $99/mo (100 channels).
ranked.pricing_detail: Source is AGPL-3.0 on GitHub: free to self-host and free to use commercially, with the AGPL condition that modifications you serve over a network must be published under the same licence. Hosted plans: Standard $29/month for 5 channels, Team $39/month for 10, Pro $49/month for 30, Ultimate $99/month for 100, all with unlimited posts and a 7-day trial. Self-hosting imposes no channel limit, but the platform developer apps are yours to register and get approved. Postiz sells optional 'apps approval' assistance as a paid add-on, which tells you how hard that step is.
ranked.good_at: Genuinely open source and genuinely runs on your own hardware, covering X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, Threads, Pinterest, Reddit, Discord, Bluesky and Mastodon. Ten of those - Bluesky, Mastodon-likes, WordPress, Dev.to, Hashnode, Medium, Listmonk, Nostr, Lemmy and Skool - need no developer app at all: you paste your own credentials and they work the same day.
ranked.the_catch: Self-hosting means you register the developer apps, and that is precisely where the auto-publish promise dies. Postiz's own docs state that until your TikTok app passes TikTok's audit, privacy_level is forced to SELF_ONLY so every post is private, only 5 users can post per 24 hours, and the target account must itself be private. Instagram and LinkedIn need your own Meta and LinkedIn app review on top. Media must be reachable over public HTTPS, so localhost deployments fail; and unconfigured platforms still appear in the connect list and simply error when clicked.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone without an engineer, and anyone self-hosting purely to save money - three weeks in TikTok's review queue costs more than Buffer at $5 a channel. Take Postiz's own hosted plan, or Buffer, unless the data-residency requirement is real.

also_considered.name: Later
also_considered.why_not: No free plan. $18.75/month billed yearly buys one 'social set' of 8 profiles and caps you at 30 posts per profile per month on Starter - a hard ceiling nobody expects from a scheduler.

also_considered.name: Hootsuite
also_considered.why_not: $99 per user per month billed annually for 10 accounts, and it is priced per seat: a three-person team is $297/month before a single extra account. The free plan was withdrawn years ago.

also_considered.name: Sprout Social
also_considered.why_not: $99-$399 per seat per month, and you stay capped at 5 social profiles until the $299 Professional tier. Superb reporting, indefensible price if what you want is scheduling.

also_considered.name: Mixpost
also_considered.why_not: Self-hosted like Postiz, but the free open-source Lite edition only connects Facebook Pages, X and Mastodon. Everything else needs the $299 one-off Pro licence, which explicitly forbids building a commercial SaaS on it.

also_considered.name: Meta Business Suite
also_considered.why_not: Free, and it absorbed the now-retired Creator Studio, but it schedules Facebook and Instagram only. A useful second tool, not an answer to 'every channel'.

watch_list: TikTok audit status at each vendor. An unaudited Content Posting API client has its posts forced to private viewing - if a tool's audit lapses, your scheduled TikToks go out invisible and nothing in the UI will say so. Spot-check that a posted video is actually public.
X/Twitter API terms. They are why Metricool and SocialBee bill X separately at $10/month. Another change would move per-channel pricing at Buffer and Publer too.

Meta's Instagram content-publishing limits: currently 100 API posts per rolling 24 hours per account, no filters, no shopping or branded-content tags, JPEG only. Loosen or tighten those and every Instagram-heavy pick reorders.

LinkedIn organic carousels remain sponsored-only in the Posts API - document posts are the workaround everyone uses. If LinkedIn opens organic carousels, all five gain the feature at once and it stops being a differentiator.
Buffer's per-channel model versus Metricool's per-brand model. If Buffer adds a bundle price above roughly eight channels, it takes first place outright for larger accounts.
Postiz shipping shared app credentials for self-hosters. Removing the Meta, TikTok and LinkedIn app-review burden would move it up several places immediately.

writing.my-voice.question: I want AI to rewrite my drafts and still sound like me. Which tool actually learns my voice?

method.how: Ranked by mechanism, not marketing. For each tool I asked one question: what does it still know about your writing when you open it tomorrow morning? Be clear-eyed about the answer — nothing mainstream trains on your prose. Claude, ChatGPT, Grammarly and Jasper all condition a general model on your samples, or on a short description derived from them, and feed that back in as context. Only a local LoRA changes any weights. So the order follows three things: how much of your actual writing stays in front of the model, how reliably it gets applied without you re-asking, and whether the prose that comes out is worth editing. On that test the category is weak — every option here is prompt engineering with a nicer cover, and the best of them still drifts back to house style over a long document.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No side-by-side generation runs, no stylometry, no blind rating. Feature mechanics, tier gates and prices read from vendors' own pages and help centres on 2026-08-29. ChatGPT Go and Pro prices were not visible on OpenAI's own pricing page and are not quoted here.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for voice fidelity in this category — nothing peer-reviewed, nothing reproducible, no stylometric leaderboard. Search results are almost entirely vendor blogs and affiliate listicles ranking themselves; the one page that presents itself as a 2026 study of which tools preserve your voice is published on a writing app's own blog and hangs a Berkeley researcher's name on it. Treat every 'trained on your writing' claim as marketing until the vendor tells you where the weights live.

ranked.name: Claude (Projects + Skills)
ranked.one_liner: Best prose, holds the most of your writing, free to start
ranked.use_it_when: You have 5,000-30,000 words of your own published writing and want a persistent workspace that keeps those samples in front of the model every session.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro $20/mo ($17/mo billed annually, $200 up front). Max from $100/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 5 projects. Pro $20/mo monthly, or $17/mo on the annual plan billed as $200 up front. Max starts at $100/mo in 5x and 20x usage tiers. Team $25/seat monthly, $20/seat annually; premium seats $125 monthly, $100 annually.
ranked.good_at: How you teach it: paste your best pieces into a Project as knowledge, then write the voice rules into the project instructions. Both persist for every chat in that project, and Claude's large context means you can keep several thousand words of genuine samples in play rather than a paragraph describing them. The generated prose needs the least de-slopping of anything here. Skills, available even on the free plan, let you package the voice rules once and reuse them across projects.
ranked.the_catch: Styles — the feature where you uploaded samples and Claude derived a reusable style profile — is gone. Anthropic's own personalisation help page no longer lists it, and it was reported retired around June 2026, folded into Skills. Skills are not the same thing: Claude decides when a skill is relevant, so your voice skill fires on some turns and not others. Tone drifts mid-document and you only catch it on re-read. Sample documents in project knowledge also consume the context window you were counting on for the actual draft.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants the voice applied automatically to everything they type anywhere, including email and Slack — that is Grammarly. Also wrong if you need a shared brand voice several colleagues apply identically; Jasper is built for that.

ranked.name: ChatGPT (Projects + custom instructions)
ranked.one_liner: Same trick as Claude, tighter caps, better everywhere-else integration
ranked.use_it_when: You already live in ChatGPT and want a per-project voice that overrides your global instructions, without paying for a second subscription.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Plus $20/mo. Go and Pro: check current pricing.
ranked.pricing_detail: Projects work on every tier including Free. File limits per project: Free 5, Go and Plus 25, Pro/Business/Enterprise/Edu 40. Custom instructions cap at 1,500 characters on Free and Go, 5,000 on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu. Plus is $20/mo per OpenAI's help centre; Go and Pro prices were not shown on the pricing page when checked, so confirm them at checkout.
ranked.good_at: Project instructions override your global custom instructions inside that project, which is the cleanest way to keep a work voice and a personal voice apart. Uploaded samples act as project knowledge. Memory carries preferences between chats without you restating them, and Characteristics give you persistent dials for warmth, enthusiasm, headers and emoji.
ranked.the_catch: The persistence is thinner than it looks. Characteristics are four sliders, not your voice. Memory accumulates its own summaries of how you write and will quietly reassert the house register — the tricolon, the 'it's not X, it's Y' construction — so you end up correcting the same tics for months. On Free you get 1,500 characters of custom instructions and 5 project files, which is not enough room for a real style brief plus samples.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose main complaint is that AI prose sounds like AI prose — start with Claude. If your writing has to stay on your own infrastructure, this is the wrong shape entirely; fine-tune locally.

ranked.name: Grammarly Pro
ranked.one_liner: The only one that builds the profile without you doing anything
ranked.use_it_when: You want your voice applied to everything you type across the web — email, docs, Slack — rather than in one chat window.
ranked.cost: Free tier (no voice features). Pro $12/mo billed monthly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Voice features are included in Pro, Plus, Business and Enterprise; the Free plan does not get them. Pro is $12/mo on monthly billing. The annual per-month rate was not displayed on the pricing page when checked. Enterprise is contact-sales only.
ranked.good_at: It is the only tool here that derives a voice profile from your writing automatically and keeps updating it as you write, with separate profiles for documents and for messages. You can inspect the profile, set role and dialect, and strip out style elements you do not want it to keep. No pasting samples, no prompt to maintain, and it follows you into every text box in the browser.
ranked.the_catch: It learns the voice you use inside Grammarly, which for most people is email and Slack — so it captures your quick-reply register, not the considered essay voice you actually want cloned. It is a rewriter, not a drafter: it will smooth a paragraph you wrote, it will not produce 1,200 words in your voice from a brief. And the voice features are entirely absent from the free plan, so you cannot evaluate the thing you are buying without paying.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs long-form generation in their voice rather than sentence-level rewriting — use Claude or ChatGPT. Anyone unwilling to let a third party continuously analyse everything they type.

ranked.name: Jasper (Brand Voice)
ranked.one_liner: Explicit saved voice profile, priced for marketing teams
ranked.use_it_when: Several people need to produce copy in one identical voice, and someone has to be able to point at where that voice is defined.
ranked.cost: No free tier. Pro $69/mo per seat ($59/mo billed annually). Business: custom.
ranked.pricing_detail: Pro is $69/mo per seat monthly, $59/mo per seat on annual billing, and includes one seat, 2 Brand Voices, 5 knowledge assets and 3 audiences. Business is custom-priced with unlimited brand voices, unlimited knowledge, style guides, visual guidelines, custom agents and API access.
ranked.good_at: The most explicit mechanism on this list: you give it up to 8 items — pasted text, .txt/.pdf/.docx files, or URLs it crawls — and it analyses them into a named, saved voice you then apply across chat, the document editor and agents. Because it is a stored object rather than a prompt you retype, everyone on the team applies the identical voice, and you can audit what it was built from.
ranked.the_catch: Eight examples is a hard ceiling on how much of you it ever sees, and there is no way to buy more depth. Style guides — the rules layer that handles Oxford commas, banned words and terminology — are Business-only, so the tier you can actually see a price for cannot enforce your rules; you get a vibe, not a spec. Pro is one seat at $69/mo, more than three times Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus, for worse prose.
ranked.wrong_for: Solo writers cloning their personal voice — you are paying a marketing-team price for a marketing-team feature. Use Claude or ChatGPT. Anyone who needs enforceable house rules should assume Business pricing and get a quote before committing.

ranked.name: Unsloth + Ollama (local LoRA fine-tune)
ranked.one_liner: The only option that actually trains on your writing
ranked.use_it_when: Your drafts cannot leave your machine, or you have years of your own writing and want a model that has genuinely absorbed it rather than been shown eight samples.
ranked.cost: Free and open source. You pay only for GPU time or your own hardware.
ranked.pricing_detail: Unsloth core is Apache 2.0; the Unsloth Studio UI is AGPL-3.0. Free Colab notebooks are published for Qwen, Gemma and Llama family models. No paid tier is advertised. Your real costs are GPU rental or hardware, and your own time.
ranked.good_at: This is the only entry where the phrase 'trained on your writing' is literally true — LoRA and QLoRA adapters change weights, and the result runs offline through Ollama with nothing leaving your machine. It supports LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tuning and preference methods across Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek and Llama families, on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, macOS and multi-GPU. Unsloth claims roughly 2x faster training with 70% less VRAM than a standard setup; that is the vendor's own number, unverified here.
ranked.the_catch: Fine-tuning teaches surface style — cadence, sentence length, favourite constructions — far more readily than judgement, and it can degrade instruction-following, so you gain a model that sounds like you and argues worse. You also need a real corpus: OpenAI's own supervised fine-tuning guidance calls 10 examples the minimum and 50 a starting point, and voice work wants far more than that. Then check the base model licence before you sell anything written with it — Llama ships under Meta's community licence with conditions, not an OSI-approved open licence; Qwen and Mistral releases are commonly Apache 2.0. A wasted weekend is the normal first outcome.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants to be writing by this afternoon, or who does not have a GPU and a few hundred pieces of their own prose. Use Claude. Also wrong if you need current facts — your fine-tune inherits the base model's cutoff and none of the retrieval you get in a chat app.

also_considered.name: OpenAI fine-tuning platform
also_considered.why_not: Excluded: OpenAI's own docs say the fine-tuning platform is winding down and is closed to new users, with existing users able to run training jobs for a few more months.

also_considered.name: Claude Styles
also_considered.why_not: Excluded: the sample-upload style profile was retired around June 2026 and folded into Skills, which Claude invokes at its own discretion.

also_considered.name: Anyword
also_considered.why_not: The only mainstream tool advertising custom-built models, but they are gated to Business and Enterprise at custom pricing; the $49/mo Starter and $99/mo Data-Driven plans get one brand voice and no custom model.

also_considered.name: Sudowrite
also_considered.why_not: Its Match My Style feature is real and works, but the whole product is built around novels and screenplays — $10 to $44/mo on credits, and only the $44 Max plan rolls unused credits over.

also_considered.name: Writer
also_considered.why_not: Brand and personality profiles on both tiers, but no price is shown for the self-serve Starter plan without starting a trial, and Starter gives you one team personality profile, not a personal voice.

also_considered.name: Lex
also_considered.why_not: A genuinely good editor with useful AI feedback, but it markets nothing that learns or stores your voice — and its pricing page would not render prices when checked.

watch_list: Whether Anthropic gives Claude a deterministic always-on style mechanism again, or leaves voice to Skills that the model chooses whether to run.
OpenAI's fine-tuning wind-down completing — once it closes, local LoRA is the only realistic route to weights that have actually seen your writing.
Whether Grammarly extends its automatic voice profile from rewriting into long-form drafting, which would make $12/mo very hard to beat.
Jasper unbundling style guides from the Business tier, or bringing back a solo plan under $30/mo.
Any independent, reproducible stylometric benchmark of voice fidelity appearing — right now there is nothing to cite and vendors know it.
Context windows and cached prompts getting cheap enough that pasting 50,000 words of your own writing into every request stops being a cost decision.

writing.repurpose.question: I have one podcast, video or long post. What turns it into ten platform-native pieces without just chopping it up?

method.how: Ranked on three things a buyer only cares about later. First, does it restructure per platform or just slice and truncate — a tool that cuts a 40-minute video into vertical clips is not writing you a LinkedIn post. Second, does it ingest video and audio, or only text you paste in. Third, is posting bundled or a second subscription. Castmagic wins because it genuinely rewrites one recording into structurally different assets; Opus Clip is ranked for what it actually is, a clipper with a scheduler bolted on; Buffer and Postiz are here because they publish and cost nothing to start.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No files were processed and no output quality was compared. Prices, limits and feature gates were read from vendors' own pricing and help pages on 2026-08-29.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark of repurposing quality exists for this category. Search results are dominated by vendors ranking themselves and each other — Klap publishes an Opus Clip pricing review, quso.ai publishes a Blaze review, sendshort.ai reviews Munch. Treat every ranking here, this one included, as opinion rather than measurement.

ranked.name: Castmagic
ranked.one_liner: One recording in, genuinely different assets out. No publishing.
ranked.use_it_when: Your source is audio or video — a podcast, webinar, sales call, YouTube upload — and you want a transcript, article, newsletter, LinkedIn post, thread, quote cards and show notes that each read like they were written for that place.
ranked.cost: No free plan. Hobby $19/mo, Starter $48/mo, Team $139/mo (all billed annually). Business from $699/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Prices on the table are per-month equivalents billed annually: Hobby $239/yr for 30 transcribed hours, Starter $579/yr for 100 hours, Team $1,669/yr for 400 hours and 5 seats. Extra Team seats +$159/yr (+$19/mo). The monthly-billing rate is not shown on the pricing table, and the page advertises 30% annual savings, so paying monthly costs meaningfully more. Extra transcription hours can be bought on any plan.
ranked.good_at: Restructuring rather than trimming. Output templates produce a long-form article, an email, a LinkedIn post and a thread that are different pieces of writing, not the same paragraph at four lengths. Imports from 12+ sources including YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, TikTok, Loom, Wistia and RSS, plus direct upload up to 1GB.
ranked.the_catch: It does not post anything. You export and paste, or pay separately for Buffer, Postiz or similar — so the real bill is Castmagic plus a scheduler. Transcription hours are the meter and the pricing page does not state whether unused hours roll over, so budget as if they vanish. There is no free plan to test the output quality on your own material before committing to a year.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose source is text — a blog post or newsletter — since Castmagic is built around media. Use Blaze or Buffer for that. If you only want vertical clips, Opus Clip is cheaper and better at it.

ranked.name: Opus Clip
ranked.one_liner: Best video clipper here; a clipper, not a rewriter.
ranked.use_it_when: You have long video and the ten formats you want are mostly vertical clips for Shorts, Reels and TikTok, with captions and auto-reframe, scheduled straight out of the same tool.
ranked.cost: Free tier (60 credits/mo, watermarked). Starter $15/mo. Pro $29/mo or $14.50/mo billed yearly ($174/yr). Business custom.
ranked.pricing_detail: 1 credit = 1 minute of imported video; sub-minute videos round up, partial minutes round down. Free gives 60 credits/mo with watermarks, 9:16 only, a 3-day export window and no editing. Starter is 150 credits/mo, one brand template, no scheduler, no API. Pro is 3,600 credits per year on the annual plan, adds the social scheduler, a 2-seat workspace, 2 brand templates and limited API. Posting to X costs 1 extra credit per clip.
ranked.good_at: Turning one long video into many usable short ones with captions, reframing and speaker tracking, then scheduling them to YouTube Shorts, TikTok, Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook and X without leaving the tool.
ranked.the_catch: The scheduler is Pro-only — the advertised cheap tiers cannot post at all. The $14.50 headline is the annual plan, and annual plans drop all 12 months of credits in at once: burn 3,600 credits in February and you wait until renewal. Monthly credits expire after 60 days, and if you cancel, remaining credits die on their original date. And it slices video; it will not write you a newsletter.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants written formats out of a recording — that is Castmagic. Anyone starting from a blog post has nothing to feed it.

ranked.name: Blaze
ranked.one_liner: Reshapes text, video or audio and publishes it. Expensive.
ranked.use_it_when: You want one subscription that takes a blog post, video or audio file, produces social posts, emails, blog articles, landing page and ad copy in a fixed brand voice, and pushes them to the calendar automatically.
ranked.cost: No free tier; 7-day trial, no card. Starter $79/mo, Growth $149/mo, All-In-One $2,499/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter $79/mo: 3 posting accounts, 600 generation credits/mo, 1 user. Growth $149/mo: 10 posting accounts, 1,500 credits/mo, unlimited users. Credits are consumed per output: 1 for a static social post, 3 for an email, 3 for a blog post, 15 for an AI video. All-In-One at $2,499/mo is a managed marketing service, not a bigger version of the tool.
ranked.good_at: Being the whole chain in one place. It has explicit video-to-content and audio-to-content wizards as well as text input, writes to a brand kit built from your existing site and content, and publishes automatically across connected channels — no second scheduling subscription.
ranked.the_catch: $79/mo is the floor and it buys one user and three posting accounts, which is fewer channels than most people repurposing to ten formats actually have. Credits meter output rather than input, so anything video-shaped drains them fast at 15 a go. Seven days is not long enough to judge brand-voice quality, and there is no free tier to fall back to.
ranked.wrong_for: Solo creators watching cost — Buffer free or Postiz self-hosted does the publishing half for nothing. Podcasters wanting deep written assets from one recording will get more from Castmagic.

ranked.name: Buffer
ranked.one_liner: Free, publishes everywhere, but its AI only rewrites what you paste.
ranked.use_it_when: You already have the ideas written down and want them adapted per channel and scheduled, at zero or near-zero cost, without another tool in the stack.
ranked.cost: Free plan (3 channels, 10 queued posts per channel). Essentials from $5 per channel per month, $60/yr per channel.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: up to 3 channels, 10 scheduled posts per channel refilled as they publish, 100 ideas, one user, AI Assistant with unlimited credits, 1 API key at 3,000 requests/month. Essentials $5/channel/mo, Team $10/channel/mo; annual billing is stated as $60/yr per channel with a 20% discount over monthly. Volume discount kicks in above 10 channels.
ranked.good_at: The publishing half, for free, on more platforms than most, plus per-channel tailoring of a post you already have. The AI Assistant carries unlimited credits even on the free plan, which no other tool here matches.
ranked.the_catch: This is the truncation end of the market. The AI Assistant refines and reshapes a post you paste; it does not ingest a podcast, video or 3,000-word article and build you a content pack — Buffer's own pricing page says nothing about accepting media files for repurposing. And per-channel pricing compounds: six channels on Essentials is six times $5, not $5.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose source material is a recording. Use Castmagic or Blaze to generate, and keep Buffer only as the publishing layer.

ranked.name: Postiz
ranked.one_liner: The only credible self-hosted option. Publishing strong, repurposing thin.
ranked.use_it_when: Your content or client data cannot sit on a vendor's servers, and you would rather run a container and point it at your own LLM key than sign another SaaS contract.
ranked.cost: Self-hosted free (AGPL-3.0). Cloud $29/mo Standard, $39 Team, $49 Pro, $99 Ultimate.
ranked.pricing_detail: Cloud tiers are priced by channels: Standard $29/mo for 5 channels and 3 AI videos/mo with no team members; Team $39/mo for 10 channels, 10 AI videos and 100 AI images; Pro $49/mo for 30 channels; Ultimate $99/mo for 100 channels, 60 AI videos and 500 AI images. Posts are unlimited on all tiers. Self-hosting has no licence fee — AGPL-3.0 permits commercial use, with the usual condition that modifications you distribute stay under the same licence.
ranked.good_at: Scheduling to 15+ platforms including X, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, Discord, Bluesky and Mastodon, with OAuth rather than stored API keys, an API for n8n/Make/Zapier, and 34.7k GitHub stars behind it. Self-hosting means your drafts never leave your infrastructure.
ranked.the_catch: The AI is a copilot that rewrites a post, not a pipeline that turns a recording into ten assets — so on this specific job it does the distribution and you still supply the reshaping. Self-hosting means you run Postgres and Redis, and you register and renew every platform's OAuth app yourself, which is the genuinely painful part. AI features need your own OPENAI_API_KEY (plus optional ElevenLabs and Fal keys), so 'free' still carries a token bill.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants the reshaping done for them, or who does not want to operate a service. Buffer free covers the same publishing job with no ops; Castmagic or Blaze covers the generation.

also_considered.name: Descript
also_considered.why_not: Editor first. Underlord makes clips and show notes from video/audio, but there is no publishing anywhere in the product and it is metered in media hours per seat — $16/seat/mo billed annually, $24 monthly, 10 hours/mo on Hobbyist.

also_considered.name: Repurpose.io
also_considered.why_not: Distribution, not reshaping — it moves the same video between platforms on autopilot. $35/mo Starter to $179/mo Agency, and its pricing page makes no AI transformation claims. Buy it as plumbing, never as a repurposing tool.

also_considered.name: Podsqueeze
also_considered.why_not: Cheapest real option at $8.99/mo, but podcast-only and metered tightly: 120 minutes and 8 clips a month on Starter, jumping to $49/mo for 320 minutes. No scheduling listed.

also_considered.name: Vizard
also_considered.why_not: The pricing page rendered every paid tier as $0 when checked, so there is no price here we are willing to quote. Free tier is 60 credits/mo, watermarked, 720p, 3-day storage — check current pricing before buying.

also_considered.name: Lately.ai
also_considered.why_not: No public pricing at all, and the site says an all-new version with a chat agent is still on a waitlist. Skip a product mid-replacement.

also_considered.name: Klap
also_considered.why_not: Priced by clip count — $14/mo Basic, $39 Pro, $94 Pro+, all billed yearly — with no free tier and no scheduling documented on the pricing page. Opus Clip does the same job with a free tier to test on.

watch_list: Opus Clip moving the social scheduler down to Starter, or granting annual-plan credits monthly instead of all at once.
Castmagic adding native publishing — that would collapse two subscriptions into one and move it further clear of the field.
Buffer's AI Assistant accepting audio and video uploads; free per-channel repurposing from media would reorder this list immediately.
Blaze offering a free tier or dropping below $79/mo, which is the only thing keeping it off the top spot for text-first work.
Postiz shipping a real source-to-many-formats pipeline rather than a per-post copilot.
Any independent, reproducible benchmark of reshaping quality appearing — right now nobody is measuring this, only selling.

Blaze help — turn video into content

automation.browser-agent.question: I want an AI to click through websites for me. Which one actually works, and where does it break?

method.how: Start from the honest position: nothing in this category is reliable enough to leave running unwatched. The only benchmark with human-verified scoring, Online-Mind2Web, put frontier agents at 56-61% task success — vendors were claiming near-90% on an easier benchmark at the same time. So ranking was driven by four things: published success rates and who did the judging, whether the tool touches your real logged-in session or a throwaway cloud one, how it handles credentials and two-factor, and whether you have an escape hatch when it fails (source you can run, or a takeover button). Products that have been renamed or killed inside the last year were pushed down regardless of capability.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No tasks were run against any of these tools. Prices read from vendors' own pages on 2026-08-29; where a vendor's pricing page did not render its numbers, that is stated in the entry. Every success rate quoted is attributed to whoever produced it, and most were produced by the vendor being measured.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: The one genuinely independent source is Online-Mind2Web (Xue et al., Ohio State University and UC Berkeley, arXiv:2504.01382, 'An Illusion of Progress?'). Using human evaluation it scored OpenAI Operator at 61.3%, Claude Computer Use 3.7 at 56.3%, and Browser Use with GPT-4o at 30.0% — and showed WebVoyager's near-90% figures were inflated by shortcut tasks and an unreliable auto-judge. The public leaderboard at leaderboard.steel.dev now carries scores up to 97%, but it marks most of them self-reported and notes evaluators differ (human, WebJudge, and vendors' own agentic judges), so those numbers rank within themselves and nothing more. Beyond that, searching this category returns almost nothing but vendors ranking themselves and each other's 'alternatives' pages. Treat any listicle here as marketing until you find the methodology.

ranked.name: Browser Use
ranked.one_liner: Top of the leaderboard, MIT-licensed, and you can self-host it.
ranked.use_it_when: You write Python, you need the same browser task run repeatedly, and you want the option to pull it in-house if the vendor changes terms.
ranked.cost: Free tier: 10 agent tasks/mo. Cloud $29-$999/mo. Library free (MIT).
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, 10 agent tasks/month, 3 concurrent browsers, 1 team member. Pay-as-you-go: no subscription, credits from $5 to $500 (custom up to $100,000), removes the monthly task cap, 3 concurrent rising to 10 after first top-up. Dev: $29/mo grants $29 credits, 25 concurrent, bring-your-own model key and scheduled jobs; annual $290/yr grants $360 credits up front. Business: $299/mo grants $299 credits, 200 concurrent; annual $2,990 grants $3,600. Scaleup: $999/mo grants $999 credits, 500 concurrent; annual $9,990 grants $12,000. Browser sessions billed at $0.02/browser-hour. The library on GitHub is MIT and free for commercial use.
ranked.good_at: It holds the top published Online-Mind2Web score — 97% for Browser Use Cloud on bu-max, March 2026 — and the library underneath is MIT, so you can lift the agent loop out and run it on your own infrastructure with your own model key. Nothing else here gives you both the frontier score and a permissive licence.
ranked.the_catch: The 97% is their own number, produced by a judge they built themselves on the Claude Agent SDK, replacing the benchmark's original judge. The same benchmark's human-evaluated paper scored Browser Use at 30.0%. It is also two different products: the 97% belongs to bu-max, their proprietary hosted model, not to the MIT library you self-host. And their own docs say CAPTCHA handling needs better fingerprinting and proxies, and point you at Cloud for it. On money: monthly plan credits renew rather than roll over, so an unused month is gone; only separately purchased top-up credits never expire.
ranked.wrong_for: Non-programmers, and anyone who wants the agent working inside the browser they are already logged into — use Claude in Chrome. If you need a copyleft-free self-host with credential vaults for business forms, Skyvern.

ranked.name: Claude in Chrome
ranked.one_liner: Drives the Chrome you are already logged into. Refuses risky work.
ranked.use_it_when: You want a supervised agent doing chores in your own session — no re-login, no cloud browser, you watching the tab.
ranked.cost: Included with paid Claude plans. Pro $20/mo ($17/mo billed annually). Max from $100/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: No separate charge for the extension; it consumes your plan's normal usage. Anthropic's pricing page on 2026-08-29: Free $0. Pro $20/mo monthly, or $17/mo billed $200 annually. Max from $100/mo, sold as 5x or 20x Pro usage. Team standard seat $25/seat/mo monthly or $20 annual; premium seat $125 monthly or $100 annual. Enterprise $20/seat plus usage at API rates, billed annually. Anthropic's help centre states the extension is available on all paid plans (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) and does not publish a separate quota for it.
ranked.good_at: It uses your existing cookies and sessions, so there is no sign-in dance and no credential to hand over. With the 1Password integration Anthropic states passwords and one-time codes never enter Claude's context. Team and Enterprise admins get allowlists and blocklists. It is the least bad answer to the credentials problem short of not automating at all.
ranked.the_catch: Anthropic's own red-teaming put prompt injection success at 23.6% with no mitigations and 11.2% with them at launch; the help pages now claim under 0.08% on internal testing. All of those are vendor numbers, unaudited, and Anthropic still writes 'the risk is not zero.' The refusals are broad: it will not bypass CAPTCHAs, will not do stock trading, blocks adult and pirated sites, asks before financial sites, and Anthropic explicitly tells you not to use it for financial, legal, medical or sensitive work accounts — which removes most of the boring admin you wanted it for. Chrome only; no other Chromium browser, no mobile. And it draws on your normal plan usage, so a long browsing session eats the quota you wanted for coding.
ranked.wrong_for: Anything unattended, scheduled or high-volume — the whole design assumes you are watching. Use Browser Use for that, or Skyvern for repeatable business forms.

ranked.name: Cloud browser in ChatGPT
ranked.one_liner: Best credential design here. Also the most renamed product in the category.
ranked.use_it_when: You already pay for ChatGPT and want signed-in web chores done without typing a password into a chat box.
ranked.cost: Included with paid ChatGPT plans. Plus $20/mo, Pro $100 or $200/mo. Free and Go excluded.
ranked.pricing_detail: OpenAI's pricing page did not render its numbers when read on 2026-08-29 — the tiers were listed with blank prices. The figures here come from OpenAI's own help centre articles instead: Plus $20/month; Pro at $100 (5x Plus usage) or $200 (20x). The cloud browser article states it runs on paid plans in supported regions, excluding Free and Go, and that availability depends on rollout and workspace permissions. No task or message quota is published for it — check current pricing before sizing any workload on this.
ranked.good_at: The sign-in handling is the strongest here: when a site needs a login, ChatGPT pauses and presents a secure form, and OpenAI states the username and password entered there are not visible to the model and are not stored. The authenticated session then persists for later tasks, so you sign in once rather than every run.
ranked.the_catch: Churn, and it will cost you rebuild work. Operator became ChatGPT agent; ChatGPT agent was retired in August 2026 and the help page now reads 'ChatGPT agent is no longer available'; the standalone Atlas browser stops working on 9 August 2026 with nothing migrating automatically — you export your own bookmarks. Scheduled tasks built on agent mode had to be rebuilt by hand. Assume the same happens again. Separately, there is no published usage quota, and OpenAI states plainly that some sites block automated browser agents and that you may have to take over and finish the last step yourself.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs a stable API surface to build on, or whose data cannot leave their infrastructure. Use Playwright MCP locally, or Skyvern self-hosted.

ranked.name: Playwright MCP
ranked.one_liner: Free, local, Apache-2.0. Nothing about your session leaves the machine.
ranked.use_it_when: Your data cannot go to a vendor's cloud, or you already have Playwright in your test suite and want your coding agent driving the same browser.
ranked.cost: Free. Apache-2.0, commercial use permitted. You pay only your model's tokens.
ranked.pricing_detail: No tiers, no accounts, no metering. Apache-2.0 is permissive: commercial use and closed derivatives are both fine, unlike Skyvern's AGPL-3.0. Your only cost is whatever your MCP client charges for the model doing the reasoning, which for long browsing sessions is not trivial.
ranked.good_at: It drives pages through Playwright's accessibility tree rather than pixels, so no vision model is needed and the actions are deterministic rather than guessed from a screenshot — cheaper and steadier for structured pages. Via the Playwright extension it can attach to a running Chrome or Edge and use your logged-in state. It is the honest fallback when the polished agents flail.
ranked.the_catch: It is not an agent. It is a tool surface, and all the reliability is your model's — which is why no one publishes an Online-Mind2Web score for it, there is nothing to score. Microsoft's README states outright that Playwright MCP 'is not a security boundary' and that its allowed/blocked origin lists do not affect redirects, so do not treat it as a sandbox. A persistent profile can only be driven by one browser instance at a time, so two MCP clients sharing a workspace will conflict. And there is no stealth layer, no proxy pool and no CAPTCHA handling: sites with bot detection will block it, and nothing in the box helps.
ranked.wrong_for: Non-developers, and anyone scraping at volume behind bot walls — Browser Use Cloud or Browserbase have the fingerprinting and proxies for that.

ranked.name: Skyvern
ranked.one_liner: Credential vaults and 2FA done properly. The AGPL licence will bite.
ranked.use_it_when: Repeatable business form workflows — portals, applications, invoices — where logins and one-time codes are the actual hard part, and you may need to self-host.
ranked.cost: Free: 5,000 one-off credits. Hobby $29/mo, Pro $149/mo. Self-host free under AGPL-3.0.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, 5,000 credits once (not monthly), roughly 170 actions; stored credentials, 2FA, advanced CAPTCHA, residential proxy and team workspaces all excluded. Hobby $29/mo: 30,000 credits/month, roughly 1,200 actions; still no 2FA/TOTP, no 1Password, no residential proxy, no team workspaces. Pro $149/mo: 150,000 credits/month, roughly 6,200 actions, adds 2FA and password-manager integration; Azure Key Vault, Bitwarden, custom code blocks, human-in-the-loop and HIPAA remain gated. Enterprise custom, adds SOC-2 and HIPAA. Self-hosting the repo is free but AGPL-3.0.
ranked.good_at: Authentication is a first-class feature rather than an afterthought: TOTP, email and SMS codes, password-manager integrations, and a no-code workflow builder for people who will not write Python. It combines vision models with the DOM instead of relying on brittle selectors, and it is the one here you can run entirely on your own hardware with credential handling included.
ranked.the_catch: Two, and both land after you have built something. The licence is AGPL-3.0, not MIT — if you modify Skyvern and run it as a service, you owe your users the modified source, which is a legal problem for most commercial products and the reason to check with someone before you start. And the feature you came for is not where you think: stored credentials and 2FA are excluded from Free, and TOTP plus 1Password only appear at Pro, $149/mo. The repo also states the anti-bot measures are held back for the managed cloud, so the self-hosted build gets detected more than the demo did.
ranked.wrong_for: One-off personal chores — Claude in Chrome is quicker and free with a plan you probably have. If you need a permissive licence for a commercial product, Browser Use is MIT and Playwright MCP is Apache-2.0.

also_considered.name: ChatGPT Atlas and ChatGPT agent mode
also_considered.why_not: Both discontinued: Atlas stops working 9 August 2026 with no automatic migration, and OpenAI's help centre now states 'ChatGPT agent is no longer available.' Browsing moved into ChatGPT's cloud browser, ranked above.

also_considered.name: Browserbase (with Stagehand)
also_considered.why_not: Strong plumbing rather than an agent — Free gives 1 browser-hour and 3 agent runs, Developer $20/mo, Startup $99/mo, then $0.10-$0.12/browser-hour and $10-$12/GB of proxy; Stagehand's SDK is MIT but you still bring the agent.

also_considered.name: Chrome auto browse (Gemini)
also_considered.why_not: US preview only and restricted to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers; Google's own AI plans page did not render its prices on 2026-08-29, so check current pricing.

also_considered.name: Perplexity Comet
also_considered.why_not: Free, but Brave's security researchers demonstrated indirect prompt injection against it twice, including instructions hidden as faint text that only the screenshot pipeline could read.

also_considered.name: Gemini 2.5 Computer Use
also_considered.why_not: Scored 69% on Online-Mind2Web under Yutori's human evaluation — the best non-self-reported number on that board — but it is a model, not a product; you build and pay for the whole harness.

watch_list: Whether Online-Mind2Web settles on one trusted judge. Today the leaderboard mixes human evaluation, WebJudge and vendors' own agentic judges, so a 97% and a 61% are not the same measurement and cannot be compared.
Anyone publishing success rates on sites that actually fight back — bot detection, CAPTCHAs, SMS two-factor. Every score quoted here comes from tasks on sites that permit agents.

WebMCP. Chrome 149 opens an origin trial for sites to expose structured tools to agents directly. If publishers adopt it, screenshot-driving becomes the slow legacy path and this list reorders completely.
Browser Use's licence and the gap between the MIT library and the hosted bu-max model that earns the headline score. If that gap widens, the self-host argument for the number one pick weakens.
OpenAI's next rename. Operator to agent to cloud browser inside two years; a fourth would push it out of the ranked five on churn alone.
A prompt-injection audit from someone who is not the vendor. Anthropic's 0.08%, its earlier 11.2%, and every rival's equivalent are all self-reported.
