automation.connect-apps.question: Two apps I use every day don't talk to each other. What connects them without a bill that quietly triples?

method.how: Ranked on three things, in order: does the connector for YOUR two apps actually exist, what one automation run costs you in billing units, and whether the feature you need is one tier above the price you were shown. Billing unit is the whole game here — Zapier bills every successful action step, Make bills every module that runs (so one run over 50 rows is 50+ units), n8n and Activepieces bill one unit per whole workflow run regardless of steps. That difference is 10-50x on the same automation, and it is why Make and the run-priced tools outrank Zapier despite Zapier's much larger app catalogue. Coverage still trumps price: check the vendor's own app directory for both of your apps before you read another word of pricing.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No automations were built or benchmarked. Prices, allowances and billing-unit definitions were read from each vendor's own pricing and help pages on 2026-08-29. Pipedream's pricing page renders client-side and returned an empty document, so no Pipedream price is quoted anywhere in this entry.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark exists for this category — nobody publishes neutral throughput, reliability or connector-quality tests for iPaaS tools. Search results for 'Zapier alternatives' and 'best automation tool 2026' are overwhelmingly vendor comparison pages and affiliate listicles, including pages the vendors write about themselves. App counts (9,000+, 3,000+, 700+) are all vendor self-reported and count wildly different things; Activepieces claims 700+ integrations on its pricing page while its own GitHub README says 280+ pieces. Treat every one of those numbers as marketing until you find your specific app in the directory.

ranked.name: Make
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest real automation per run, if your apps are in it
ranked.use_it_when: Both apps appear in Make's directory and your automation loops over rows, records or emails in bulk — where Zapier's per-step billing would bankrupt you.
ranked.cost: Free tier (1,000 credits/mo). Paid $12-$38/mo billed annually.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read on Make's pricing page 2026-08-29: Free $0 with 1,000 credits/month, 2 active scenarios, 15-minute minimum interval, 5-minute max execution, 5MB files. Core $12/mo (about $10.20 with 15% annual discount) with 10,000 credits/month, unlimited active scenarios, 1-minute interval, 40-minute execution, 100MB files. Pro $21/mo adds custom variables, log search, high-priority execution, 250MB files. Teams $38/mo adds roles and team management, 500MB files. Enterprise is custom. All tiers get the same 3,000+ standard apps; custom and enterprise apps are gated higher. Note the base credit allowance is 10,000/month on Core, Pro AND Teams — you pay more for features, not volume.
ranked.good_at: Price per unit of work, and branching. Routers and error-handler modules are explicitly not billed, so conditional logic is free. The visual scenario canvas handles multi-branch flows, retries and iteration far better than Zapier's linear step list, and the 1-minute polling interval on paid tiers is genuinely fast.
ranked.the_catch: A 'credit' (Make's newer name for what it called an operation) is one module action, not one automation run. Fetch 50 rows and update each one and you have burned 50+ credits from a single trigger — the pricing page states data transformation and iteration count too. 10,000 credits/month sounds enormous and evaporates the first time you point a scenario at a real spreadsheet. The free tier is also capped at 2 active scenarios and a 15-minute polling interval, so it demos rather than runs anything.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose app isn't in the 3,000 — go to Zapier. Anyone who wants to build the thing in ten minutes and never look at it again; Make's canvas, data-structure mapping and array handling have a real learning curve. Zapier is faster to a first working connection.

ranked.name: Zapier
ranked.one_liner: Widest app catalogue, most expensive per unit of work
ranked.use_it_when: One of your two apps is obscure and only Zapier has a connector for it — which, with 9,000+ apps claimed, is often the deciding fact.
ranked.cost: Free tier (100 tasks/mo, 2 steps). Paid from $19.99/mo billed annually.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read on zapier.com/pricing 2026-08-29: Free $0, 100 tasks/month, two-step workflows only. Professional $19.99/mo at the page's default annual view (33% claimed saving, so monthly billing costs more), 750 tasks/month at the default slider — multi-step workflows, webhooks, paths and premium apps all start here. Team $69/mo billed annually, 2,000 tasks/month shared across 25 seats, adds SAML SSO and shared workflows. Enterprise is quote-only with annual task limits. Task allowances scale with a slider, so the headline price is the floor, not the price.
ranked.good_at: Connector coverage and time-to-working. If a SaaS product has an API and any users, Zapier probably has a maintained connector, and the setup flow gets a two-app connection live in minutes with no data-mapping theory required. Its billing definition is also the fairest of the paid SaaS tools: per its own help docs, triggers, filters, paths and any step that errors or is skipped cost you nothing — only successful action steps count.
ranked.the_catch: Webhooks and multi-step Zaps are gated behind Professional, so the free tier connects two apps in the most literal and least useful sense and nothing more. Worse, when you hit your task limit Zapier switches you to pay-per-task billing automatically, at a higher rate than your subscription tasks — you have to actively disable that to get a hard stop instead of a surprise invoice. Tasks do not roll over.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone doing volume or bulk loops — every action step is billed and 750 tasks disappears fast; use Make or n8n. Anyone whose data can't sit on a US SaaS platform; use n8n or Activepieces self-hosted.

ranked.name: n8n
ranked.one_liner: One price per workflow run, however many steps it has
ranked.use_it_when: Your automation is long, loops a lot, or calls an LLM — and you want the billing unit to be the run, not the step. Or you need it on your own infrastructure.
ranked.cost: Free self-hosted (Sustainable Use Licence, not OSI open source). Cloud from EUR20/mo billed annually.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read on n8n.io/pricing 2026-08-29: Starter EUR20/mo billed annually, 2,500 workflow executions, 5 concurrent, 1 shared project, 2,300 AI credits/month. Pro EUR50/mo billed annually, 10,000 executions, 20 concurrent, 3 shared projects, up to 13,700 AI credits, 7-day insights. Business EUR667/mo billed annually, 40,000 executions, 6 projects, SSO/SAML/LDAP, self-hosted option, 30-day insights. Enterprise is quote-only. Active workflows are unlimited on every tier. The vendor's own definition: 'An execution is a single run of your entire workflow. It doesn't matter how many steps are in the workflow or how much data it processes.' Self-hosted Community Edition is free from GitHub; self-hosted Business/Enterprise licences ping a licence server daily to validate.
ranked.good_at: Billing honesty and escape hatches. A 40-step workflow chewing through 500 records is one execution, which is the single biggest cost difference in this list. It also drops to raw JavaScript or Python in a node when the visual builder runs out, and the self-hosted Community Edition removes the metering entirely — you pay in servers instead.
ranked.the_catch: Two traps. First, the cloud pricing cliff: Pro is EUR50/mo and the very next tier, Business, is EUR667/mo — if you need SSO, more concurrency, or 40,000 executions, there is nothing in between and the jump is 13x. Second, the licence: the Sustainable Use Licence is not OSI-approved open source. Per the licence text it permits internal business use and non-commercial use, but you may only distribute it to others free of charge for non-commercial purposes, which rules out hosting it as a service for customers or white-labelling it in a product. Self-hosted Community also lacks SSO, RBAC and the governance features, which live in the paid tiers.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants to run it as a service for clients — the licence forbids it; use Activepieces (MIT). Non-technical users: self-hosting means Docker, a database, backups and queue mode, and even n8n Cloud assumes you can read JSON. Use Zapier or Make.

ranked.name: Activepieces
ranked.one_liner: Genuinely MIT-licensed, self-host it free forever
ranked.use_it_when: The data cannot leave your infrastructure, or a licence review will actually be run on whatever you pick, and you need a real OSI-approved licence rather than a source-available one.
ranked.cost: Free self-hosted (MIT, community edition). Cloud free 100 credits/day; paid $16-$166/mo billed yearly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read on activepieces.com/pricing 2026-08-29: Free $0 with 100 credits a day. Plus $16/month billed yearly, 10,000 credits/month. Team $166/month billed yearly, 50,000 credits/month. Ultimate is custom, pooled yearly. Billing unit is one full flow run = 1 credit regardless of step count; AI actions cost more (fast model 2 credits, smart model 10, frontier model 20, or 1 credit if you bring your own AI key). The vendor states the Community Edition is 'open source, free forever, with no cap on runs, users, or flows'.
ranked.good_at: The licence, checked at source: the GitHub repo states the Community Edition is released under the MIT licence, with enterprise features under a separate Commercial Licence. MIT means you can genuinely embed it, resell it, or run it for clients — the thing n8n's licence forbids. Run-based billing, TypeScript pieces you can write yourself, and no run cap at all when self-hosted.
ranked.the_catch: The dual licence means the repo you clone is not all MIT — SSO, SCIM, custom roles, audit logs, event streaming, private pieces, branding and Git sync sit under the Commercial Licence and behind the Team/Ultimate tiers, so a self-hosted deployment for a real organisation still ends up paying or going without governance. And the integration count is soft: the pricing page advertises 700+ integrations while the project's own README says 280+ pieces. Assume the smaller number and check your two apps by name before committing.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone connecting a long tail of niche SaaS — the catalogue is a fraction of Zapier's and you will end up writing pieces or HTTP calls yourself. Anyone without somewhere to run Docker; the cloud free tier's 100 credits/day is a demo. Use Make.

ranked.name: Power Automate
ranked.one_liner: Already in your Microsoft 365 tenant, with the useful half locked
ranked.use_it_when: Both apps are Microsoft — SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, Dataverse — and the automation has to run inside your tenant under existing compliance and identity controls.
ranked.cost: 30-day free trial (standard connectors only). Premium $15/user/mo paid yearly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read on Microsoft's pricing page 2026-08-29: Power Automate Free Trial, 30 days, comparison table states 'Standard connectors only'. Power Automate Premium $15.00 per user/month paid yearly — standard, premium AND custom connectors. Power Automate Process $150.00 per bot/month paid yearly. Power Automate Hosted Process $215.00 per bot/month paid yearly. Note the unit: per user or per bot, never per flow. Microsoft's page does not define which connectors count as premium, so check the connector reference for your specific two apps before buying.
ranked.good_at: Living inside the tenant you already pay for. Identity, DLP policies, audit and data residency are the same ones your IT team already administers, which is the argument no standalone iPaaS can make. Depth on Microsoft's own surfaces — SharePoint lists, Outlook, Teams, Excel Online, Dataverse — is better than anything else on this list.
ranked.the_catch: The connector tiering is where this hurts. Standard connectors are the Microsoft ones; the connectors you actually want for connecting two apps that don't talk — third-party SaaS, SQL, and generic HTTP — are classed premium, and Microsoft's own comparison confirms premium and custom connectors require the paid Premium plan. That is $15 per user per month, priced per person rather than per automation, so one shared flow can pull a whole team into licences. Microsoft's pricing page does not publish the premium-connector list, so you cannot confirm the cost of your specific integration from the pricing page alone.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone outside Microsoft 365 — there is no reason to be here; use Make or Zapier. Anyone who wants to hand a working automation to a colleague without a licensing conversation.

also_considered.name: Pipedream
also_considered.why_not: Code-first with a generous free tier and credits billed by compute (its docs state one credit per 30 seconds at 256MB, and testing is free), but the pricing page renders client-side and returned an empty document on 2026-08-29 — we will not quote a price we could not read. Check current pricing at pipedream.com/pricing.

also_considered.name: IFTTT
also_considered.why_not: Cheapest paid tier here at $2.99/mo Pro or $8.99/mo Pro+, but the free plan is 2 applets and the paid plans buy 20 or unlimited — and webhooks, multi-action applets, filter code and multiple accounts per service are all withheld from free. Consumer-grade; fine for phone-and-smart-home, not for business data.

also_considered.name: Node-RED
also_considered.why_not: Self-hosted and free, but you wire raw HTTP calls and OAuth token refresh yourself. It has no managed SaaS connector library, which is the entire hard part of this job.

also_considered.name: Workato
also_considered.why_not: Quote-only enterprise pricing with no public number, and typically a five-figure annual floor. Nothing to verify, nothing to recommend to someone connecting two apps.

also_considered.name: Tray.ai
also_considered.why_not: Same problem — enterprise sales motion, no published price, and a platform sized for an integration team rather than one broken connection.

also_considered.name: Zapier Starter plan
also_considered.why_not: No longer listed on Zapier's pricing page as of 2026-08-29 — the tiers now read Free, Professional, Team, Enterprise. If you are on an old Starter plan, assume it is being retired and price the move to Professional at $19.99/mo.

watch_list: Make renaming operations to credits: the pricing page now says 'credits' and AI actions may be priced at multiple credits each. If AI-step multipliers land in the standard tiers, Make's price advantage over Zapier narrows sharply.
n8n's EUR50-to-EUR667 gap between Pro and Business. If a mid tier appears, or SSO drops into Pro, n8n takes first place outright.
Whether Activepieces' MIT community edition keeps its scope. Every additional feature moved into the Commercial Licence weakens the only genuinely open-source pick here.
Zapier's automatic pay-per-task overage. If it becomes opt-in rather than opt-out, the single worst billing trap on this list disappears and Zapier's ranking improves.

MCP and agent-driven connectors. Activepieces already exposes its pieces as MCP servers; if generic MCP tool-calling becomes reliable enough to replace hand-built connectors, the app-count advantage that keeps Zapier at number two stops mattering.
Pipedream publishing a server-rendered pricing page. It is a credible pick that is unrankable while its prices cannot be read at source.

code.app-from-prompt.question: I describe an app and get a working one. Which builder actually hands over the code and a backend I can trust?

method.how: Three things drove the order, in this sequence. First, can you get the source out and run it somewhere else — and on which tier, because two of these gate code download behind a paid plan. Second, what the generated backend and auth actually are: a managed Postgres with AI-written row-level security is not the same promise as a proprietary black box, and buyers have shipped apps with wide-open databases because the security config was never shown to them. Third, how fast credits burn on real iteration, where you re-prompt the same screen eight times. Raw first-shot polish came last, which is why the tool most people name first is not first here.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No apps were built, no credit burn was measured, no generated code was audited. Every price, credit allowance and feature gate was read from the vendor's own pricing page or docs on 2026-08-29, and is quoted as the vendor states it.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent, reproducible benchmark that ranks these products against each other. Nothing like it exists for this category. The one independent work used here is security research: Wiz Research's study of misconfigurations in vibe-coded apps, and CVE-2025-48757, the disclosed Lovable row-level-security flaw. Be warned that search results for 'best AI app builder' are dominated by vendors ranking themselves — Lovable's own guide to the best AI app builders ranked second in the searches run for this entry, and several 'review' sites in the results are owned by competing builders.

ranked.name: Bolt.new
ranked.one_liner: Best ownership terms: download the code from day one
ranked.use_it_when: You want a real Vite/React codebase you can pull into your own editor, repo and host, and you are happy to wire the backend deliberately rather than have it appear.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $25/mo, ~$18/mo billed yearly. Teams $30/member/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 1M tokens/month with a 300K daily cap, public or private projects, Bolt branding, 10MB uploads. Pro: from $25/mo monthly or roughly $18/mo on annual billing (vendor states 28% saving), from 10M tokens/month, no daily cap, no branding, custom domains, 100MB uploads. Teams: $30 per member/month — Bolt states tokens are not shared between team members. Enterprise: quote. Since 1 July 2025 paid-plan tokens roll over one extra month, so two months' validity total.
ranked.good_at: Getting out. Download-as-ZIP and GitHub sync are documented as ordinary project features in Bolt's help centre, with no plan restriction stated — unlike Lovable and Base44, where code download sits behind a paid tier. What you get is a conventional Node project: unzip, npm install, npm run dev, deploy anywhere. Backend is your choice — the native Bolt Database, or a Supabase connection you own, with Netlify for hosting.
ranked.the_catch: Tokens vanish faster than you expect, and iteration is what eats them. A long debugging loop on one stubborn component can consume a meaningful slice of the free tier's 1M monthly allowance in an afternoon, and the 300K daily cap means you stop mid-thought. Also: your app runs in a browser WebContainer, so anything needing a non-JavaScript runtime is out. And Bolt does not document what the native Bolt Database is built on — if you care about knowing your own data layer, connect Supabase explicitly instead of taking the default.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants the prettiest possible app from one sentence with no follow-up work — Lovable does that better. Anyone who wants hosting, database and login provisioned for them in one place — use Replit.

ranked.name: Lovable
ranked.one_liner: Best first draft, worst free tier, real security history
ranked.use_it_when: You need something that looks and behaves like a finished product from a single prompt, you will pay from day one, and you will personally check the database policies before anyone else touches it.
ranked.cost: Free tier (5 credits/day, 30/mo cap). Pro from $25/mo. Business from $50/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 5 daily build credits capped at 30 per month, plus a 20-credit monthly Cloud grant and 4-credit AI grant. Per Lovable's docs the Free plan has no code editing, no code download, no custom domains and no private projects. Pro: tiers from $25/mo (100 credits) up to $2,250/mo (10,000 credits); annual $250–$22,500/yr. Business: $50/mo to $4,300/mo, annual $500–$43,000/yr, adds SSO and security features. Top-ups: Pro $15 per 50 credits ($0.30/credit), Business $30 per 50 ($0.60/credit). Unused subscription credits roll over while you stay subscribed but expire two months after issue; the daily and grant credits never roll over.
ranked.good_at: One-shot completeness. It produces a full-stack app with database, auth, storage, edge functions and scheduled jobs via Lovable Cloud, which the docs describe as built on Supabase's open-source foundation. Fewer follow-up prompts to something demo-ready than anything else here.
ranked.the_catch: Two things. First, the free tier is a demo, not a trial — you cannot download your code, edit it, or attach a domain, so anything you build there is stuck until you pay at least $25/mo. Second, the security record: CVE-2025-48757 was a row-level-security failure in Lovable-generated Supabase apps, reported as exposing data across 170+ projects, and Wiz Research documented client-side-only authentication, hardcoded API keys and disabled RLS in vibe-coded apps including one that leaked users' PII. Lovable has since shipped a pre-publish Security Scan and an AI Security Reviewer, and states plainly it cannot guarantee your app is secure. Treat every generated RLS policy as unreviewed until you have read it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone evaluating on a zero budget — the free tier will not let you keep what you make; use Bolt or Dyad. Anyone handling regulated or personal data without someone who can read a Postgres policy.

ranked.name: Replit
ranked.one_liner: Whole stack hosted for you; billing has two meters
ranked.use_it_when: You want the app built, given a Postgres database, given login, and left running on a URL, without touching a deploy pipeline.
ranked.cost: Free Starter. Core $20/mo ($204/yr). Pro $100/mo. Hosting billed separately.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter: free, daily agent allowance, one published project. Core: $20/mo, or $204/yr; includes $20/mo of credits, 2 parallel agents. Pro: $100/mo (vendor lists $95/mo on annual), $100/mo of credits, 10 parallel agents, 28-day database rollback. Agent work uses effort-based pricing — Replit replaced the old flat $0.25-per-checkpoint model so simple requests cost under $0.25 and complex ones more. Publishing is billed from the same credits: Autoscale $2/mo base plus $0.60/million compute units and $0.40/million requests; Scheduled $2/mo base; Reserved VM $15/mo shared 0.5 vCPU, $35/mo for 1 vCPU/4GB, $50/mo for 2 vCPU/8GB, $130/mo for 4 vCPU/16GB; Static hosting free plus $0.05/GB transfer. Production Postgres is Neon, billed on usage and idling after five minutes.
ranked.good_at: Being the only one where 'built' and 'running in production with a database and users logging in' are the same step. Replit Auth gives you Google, GitHub, X, Apple and email sign-in without an integration, and dev databases are included free with every app.
ranked.the_catch: Your subscription is not a build budget — it is a shared pot that agent work and hosting both drain, so a chatty debugging session and a live Reserved VM compete for the same $20. On Core, unused credits do not roll over at all (only Pro carries them for two months). And effort-based pricing means you cannot predict a request's cost before you send it. Worst on exit: Replit Auth is documented for replit.dev, replit.app and custom domains on Replit's own infrastructure — export the code and your entire login system needs rebuilding.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose plan is to move the app to their own AWS or Vercel account later — the auth and hosting coupling makes that a rewrite; start with Bolt or v0 instead.

ranked.name: v0
ranked.one_liner: Next.js output you would have written; thin on backend
ranked.use_it_when: Your destination is already Next.js, Tailwind and shadcn/ui on Vercel, and you want generated code that drops into an existing repo as a pull request.
ranked.cost: Free ($5 credits/mo, 7 messages/day). Plus $30/user/mo. Business $100/user/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, $5 of included monthly credits, 7 messages per day, deploys to Vercel, Design Mode and GitHub sync included. Plus: $30/user/mo with $30 of included credits per user plus $2 of free daily credits on login. Business: $100/user/mo but still $30 of included credits per user plus the same $2 daily — you are paying for training opt-out, SSO-adjacent features and team controls, not more usage. Enterprise: custom. Credits are spent at per-token model rates across v0 Mini, Pro, Max and Max Fast, listed from $0.20 to $10 per million input tokens. Extra credits can be bought on Plus and Business.
ranked.good_at: Code quality and fit. The output is idiomatic Next.js/Tailwind/shadcn that a competent React developer will recognise and want to keep, and the ship path is a Vercel deploy or a pull request rather than a copy-paste. Best of these five if a human developer is going to inherit the codebase.
ranked.the_catch: Read the Business tier carefully: at $100/user/mo you get the same $30 of monthly credits as the $30 Plus plan. The extra $70 buys governance, not capacity — a per-seat charge that looks like a usage upgrade. Separately, credits are consumed at raw model token rates, so picking a Max model burns your allowance an order of magnitude faster than Mini for the same prompt, and the $5 free tier plus 7-messages-a-day cap is a taster, not a build budget.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants the database, auth and cron jobs conjured for them — v0 connects to backends but does not opinionate one the way Lovable Cloud or Replit do. Use Lovable or Replit.

ranked.name: Dyad
ranked.one_liner: Runs on your machine, your keys, nothing leaves
ranked.use_it_when: Your code or data cannot go to a third-party builder, or you want to burn your own API credits (or a local Ollama model) instead of buying someone's credit currency.
ranked.cost: Free and open source. Optional Dyad Pro $20/mo, Max $79/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: The app is a free download with no sign-up required. Core code is Apache 2.0; everything under src/pro is fair-source under the Functional Source License 1.1, which is not an OSI open-source licence — check it before you build a competing product on it. Free means free of subscription, not free of cost: you supply API keys and pay the model provider directly, unless you run local models. Dyad Pro is $20/mo for 200 AI credits, pooled access to OpenAI/Google/Anthropic models, Agent mode and large-codebase modes; Max is $79/mo for 900 credits.
ranked.good_at: No lock-in of any kind. Files live on your disk from the first prompt, you choose the model per request, and one-click connectors exist for Supabase and Neon plus GitHub and Vercel deploy. It is the only entry here where an air-gapped or offline-model workflow is possible.
ranked.the_catch: macOS and Windows only — the download page lists no Linux build, which is awkward for a tool aimed at people who self-host. It is also a small project against four funded ones: the marketing site still advertises Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash as headline models, which tells you how closely the surface is maintained. And nothing is provisioned for you — no hosting, no domain, no database unless you connect one and configure its security yourself.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants a URL to send someone in ten minutes, or anyone on Linux. Use Replit for the former, Bolt for the latter.

also_considered.name: Base44 (Wix)
also_considered.why_not: Code export and two-way GitHub sync start at the $40/mo Builder tier — the free and $16 Starter plans give you no way to take the app out.

also_considered.name: Firebase Studio (Google)
also_considered.why_not: Being discontinued: Google's own docs state new signups and workspace creation were disabled on 22 June 2026 and the product sunsets 22 March 2027. Excluded for that reason.

also_considered.name: bolt.diy
also_considered.why_not: MIT-licensed and self-hostable, but it runs on the WebContainers API, which the repo states requires a licence for production use in a commercial, for-profit setting. Free to download is not free to ship.

also_considered.name: Bubble
also_considered.why_not: Mature and genuinely capable, but there is no application code to export — if 'host it yourself' is the requirement, it fails on the first question.

also_considered.name: Claude Code / Cursor
also_considered.why_not: They will build the app from a prompt and the code is yours, but they assume you already have a working dev environment, runtime and deploy target. Different job.

watch_list: Where Google sends prompt-to-app users after Firebase Studio's 22 March 2027 sunset — a free, Gemini-backed successor with real quotas would reorder the free end of this list immediately.
Whether Lovable unlocks code download on its free tier. That single change would move it up, because its first-draft quality is the best here.
Whether pre-publish security scanning becomes a hard gate rather than an advisory. Right now every vendor puts RLS correctness on the buyer while marketing the opposite.
Bolt's token economics. The 1M free / 10M Pro allowances and the one-month rollover are the whole basis of the rank-1 pick; a cut would change it.
Replit's credit rules — if Core credits start rolling over, or agent work and hosting get separate meters, the third-place catch mostly disappears.
A credible independent benchmark for generated-app quality and security. There is none today, and the vacuum is why vendor 'comparison' pages fill the search results.

code.autocomplete.question: I just want fast, accurate completion in the editor I already use. Who is worth paying, and what do they do with my code?

method.how: Three things set the order. First: does it plug into the editor you already have, or does it want you to move house — a tool that only works if you abandon your IDE is a different purchase, and it ranks below one that doesn't. Second: what happens to your code by default, not what the marketing page says is possible. GitHub flipped individual Copilot accounts to training-on-by-default on 24 April 2026, which is the single most important fact on this page and is off by one checkbox. Third: is the completion itself metered? Inline completion is the thing you trigger hundreds of times an hour, and a tool that draws it from the same credit pot as agent runs will run dry mid-afternoon. Raw suggestion quality came last, because no reproducible independent measure of it exists — see blind_note.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No acceptance rates were measured, no suggestion quality was compared, no editor was used for a working day. Every price, credit allowance, quota and data-policy statement was read from the vendor's own pricing page, docs or repository on 2026-08-29, and is quoted as the vendor states it. JetBrains AI is absent from the ranking specifically because its pricing page would not render a readable price.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent, reproducible benchmark for inline code completion. SWE-bench and its relatives measure agents finishing tickets, not whether the grey text after your cursor is the line you wanted, and no public benchmark measures acceptance rate across these products on the same codebase. Every quality claim below is either a vendor's own or is absent. Be warned that search results for 'best AI code completion' are almost entirely vendors ranking themselves and affiliate blogs ranking whoever pays — the one genuinely useful independent signal in 2026 was press coverage of GitHub's data-policy change, not any bake-off.
method.extra_note: Editor coverage, training policy and per-tier limits are given for every entry because those are the three things buyers get caught by. Where a vendor does not publish a number, that silence is stated rather than filled in.

ranked.name: GitHub Copilot
ranked.one_liner: Widest editor support, and completions never touch your credits
ranked.use_it_when: You want completion inside the editor you already use — VS Code, Visual Studio, a JetBrains IDE, Neovim, Vim, Eclipse or Xcode — and you want the completion itself uncapped rather than drawn from a metered pot.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $10-$100/mo. Business $19/seat, Enterprise $39/seat.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, capped at 2,000 completions and 50 chat requests per month. Pro: $10/mo or $120/yr, unlimited completions, 1,500 AI Credits/month (1,000 base plus 500 flex). Pro+: $39/mo or $468/yr, 7,000 credits (3,900 plus 3,100). Max: $100/mo or $1,200/yr, 20,000 credits (10,000 plus 10,000). Business: $19/seat/mo, 1,900 credits per user. Enterprise: $39/seat/mo, 3,900 credits per user. One credit is $0.01. GitHub's docs state included credits do not carry over between months — unused credits are forfeited and the allowance resets at 00:00:00 UTC on the first of each calendar month. Code completions and next-edit suggestions are explicitly not billed in credits and remain unlimited on all paid plans.
ranked.good_at: Being everywhere and not charging you for the bit you use most. GitHub lists Copilot for VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, Vim, Eclipse, Xcode, Raycast and Azure Data Studio — nothing else here comes close to that spread. And the credit meter that everyone complains about does not touch inline completion or next-edit suggestions, which are unlimited on every paid plan. At $10/mo that is the cheapest uncapped completion on this list.
ranked.the_catch: Since 24 April 2026 GitHub uses your interaction data — inputs, outputs, code snippets, code context, comments, file names, repository structure — to train models by default on Copilot Free, Pro and Pro+. Business and Enterprise are not affected. It is a single opt-out under Privacy at github.com/settings/copilot, and nothing in the editor tells you it is on. Separately, on 1 June 2026 Copilot moved from premium requests to token-metered AI Credits: one prompt no longer costs one unit, cost now varies with model, context size and output length, and when the pool empties there is no fallback to a cheaper model — usage stops unless you set an additional spend budget. Credits do not roll over. Chat is still limited to VS Code, JetBrains and Visual Studio even though completion runs in nine editors.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants the strongest next-edit prediction and will change editors to get it — use Cursor. Anyone whose code contractually cannot leave their infrastructure — use Tabnine, or llama.vscode if you have the hardware.

ranked.name: Cursor
ranked.one_liner: The best Tab model, if you'll move into its editor
ranked.use_it_when: You are willing to adopt Cursor as your daily editor, and what you actually want is multi-line, multi-file next-edit prediction rather than single-line autocomplete.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $20/$60/$200 per month. Teams $40-$120/seat/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Hobby: free, with limited agent requests; the docs list unlimited Tab completions only for Pro and above. Pro: $20/mo. Pro Plus: $60/mo. Ultra: $200/mo. Teams Standard: $40/user/mo. Teams Premium: $120/user/mo. Enterprise: custom, with pooled usage. A Start plan at ₹649/mo is listed for India only. Usage above Tab is metered in tokens per million across two pools that reset with your monthly billing cycle: a Cursor Models pool (documented as Grok 4.6, Grok 4.5 and Composer 2.5) included on all plans, and an Other Models pool for third-party frontier models included from Pro upward. The docs do not state whether unused pool allowance rolls over.
ranked.good_at: Tab. Cursor absorbed the Supermaven team in 2024 and Supermaven's own shutdown notice tells its remaining VS Code users to migrate to Cursor because the work went into Cursor Tab. Unlimited Tab completions on every paid tier, and the docs state requests are never downgraded in quality or speed when you hit a limit — you either buy on-demand usage or upgrade.
ranked.the_catch: Two. First, the meter: Tab is unlimited but everything else is token-priced against pools whose rollover behaviour is not documented, so the $20 is a floor, not a price. The cheap pool is currently built on one model family from one supplier — if that relationship changes, so does your bill. Second, Privacy Mode. Cursor's security page says Privacy Mode is available to anyone, free or Pro, and that with it on Cursor will not train on your data — which means with it off, Cursor or its model providers may. The page does not state that it is on by default. Check the setting before your first prompt, not after. And the free Hobby tier is not a way to get good completion: unlimited Tab starts at $20.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone tied to JetBrains, Visual Studio, Eclipse or Xcode — Cursor is an editor, not a plugin, so use Copilot. Anyone with a hard no-egress rule — Tabnine or llama.vscode.

ranked.name: Zed
ranked.one_liner: Cleanest data defaults here, and ten dollars a month
ranked.use_it_when: You want a fast editor that does not retain your code by default, and you are happy to point completion at your own API keys or a local model when the free allowance runs out.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro $10/mo. Business $30/seat/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Personal: free forever, 2,000 accepted edit predictions per month, plus unlimited use with your own API keys or external agents. Pro: $10/mo with a free trial — unlimited edit predictions and $5 of tokens included, usage-based billing beyond that. Business: $30/seat/mo with no minimum seat count. Note the free tier counts accepted predictions, not offered ones.
ranked.good_at: Data handling, stated plainly and verifiable in the docs. Zed says it does not retain your prompts or code context by default; that its agreements with model providers prohibit training on your prompts or code context; and that edit-prediction requests are processed transiently unless you opt in. Training data collection requires three things at once — your explicit consent, an open-source project, and a non-excluded file. Nobody else here has defaults that good. It also supports pointing the editor at a local model server, so completion can run entirely on your machine.
ranked.the_catch: The Windows build is still marked Preview on the download page — macOS is the only build labelled Stable, and Linux installs from the command line. If your team is on Windows this is not yet a daily driver. The $5 of included tokens on Pro is a small agent budget that a couple of long sessions will clear, and past it you are on usage-based billing. And unlike Copilot or Tabnine, Zed is an editor: there is no plugin that brings any of this into the IDE you already have.
ranked.wrong_for: JetBrains and Visual Studio users, and Windows teams — use Copilot. Anyone who needs a vendor contract and an air-gapped deployment — Tabnine.

ranked.name: llama.vscode
ranked.one_liner: Genuinely offline completion, free, MIT — you supply the VRAM
ranked.use_it_when: Your code cannot leave the machine or the network, and you can run a llama.cpp server. This is the self-hosted answer that is actually still being developed.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT licence. You pay in hardware and setup time.
ranked.pricing_detail: No subscription, no seats, no telemetry to buy off. The extension is MIT-licensed and comes from the llama.cpp organisation. Running cost is your own hardware: the README sizes FIM models by VRAM — Qwen2.5-Coder 30B above 64GB, 7B above 16GB, 3B below 16GB, 1.5B below 8GB, with CPU-only operation possible at lower quality. A sibling project, llama.vim, covers Vim and Neovim.
ranked.good_at: Nothing leaves. After the model download it works fully offline, which is a different and stronger claim than 'we promise not to train on it'. It is also alive: 48 releases, the most recent v0.0.48 on 31 May 2026 — which matters, because the better-known self-hosted option, Tabby, has not shipped since January 2025.
ranked.the_catch: Suggestion quality is a direct function of your graphics card, and most laptops land in the bracket the README describes as lower quality. A 1.5B fill-in-the-middle model is not Copilot and will not pretend to be — expect competent line completion and little else. There is real setup: you run and maintain the inference server yourself, and when it is down, so is your completion. And the MIT licence covers the extension, not the weights — model licences vary by family and by size within a family, and some are research-only. Read the licence of the specific model file you download before you ship anything commercial on it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants chat and agent features at parity with the commercial tools — use Copilot or Cursor. Teams who need someone to call at 3am — Tabnine.

ranked.name: Tabnine
ranked.one_liner: Air-gapped completion with a contract and a support line
ranked.use_it_when: Procurement or regulation requires that code never leaves your infrastructure, and you need a supported vendor rather than a repository you maintain yourself.
ranked.cost: No free tier. $39/user/mo (Code Assistant) or $59/user/mo (Agentic), annual.
ranked.pricing_detail: Code Assistant Platform: $39 per user/month on an annual subscription. Agentic Platform: $59 per user/month on an annual subscription. Both prices are stated as annual subscriptions on the pricing page — the monthly-looking figure is a yearly commitment. Deployment is SaaS, VPC, on-premises or fully air-gapped at the same listed prices, with custom quotes via sales. There is no free tier listed.
ranked.good_at: The deployment story. Tabnine states zero code retention, no training on your code and no sharing with third parties, and that in air-gapped or secure environments no data leaves your infrastructure. It also ships provenance and attribution features aimed at licensing risk in generated code — a thing none of the others sell. Official plugin coverage: VS Code, JetBrains IntelliJ-platform IDEs, Eclipse, Visual Studio 2022 and Visual Studio 2026.
ranked.the_catch: The free tier is gone — nothing on the pricing page costs less than $39, and that is billed annually. You are paying roughly four times Copilot Pro for completion quality that no independent benchmark shows to be ahead of anyone, because no such benchmark exists. Editor coverage is also narrower than the marketing implies: Tabnine's own docs say plugins for IDEs outside those four are either legacy builds that do not support advanced completions and chat, or community-made. And air-gapped deployment means you inherit the operational burden anyway, without the freedom of a self-hosted open project.
ranked.wrong_for: Individual developers — this price only makes sense as a compliance purchase. Use Copilot at $10, or llama.vscode if the point was keeping code local.

also_considered.name: Supermaven
also_considered.why_not: Discontinued. Its own blog announced 'Sunsetting Supermaven' on 21 November 2025, with prorated refunds issued and VS Code users told to migrate to Cursor. The pricing page still advertises Free, $10 Pro and $10/user Team with no shutdown banner — do not buy from it.

also_considered.name: Devin Desktop (was Windsurf)
also_considered.why_not: windsurf.com now 302-redirects to devin.ai/desktop; Cognition states Devin Desktop is the new name for Windsurf. Its free plan is the best free completion offer on the market — unlimited Tab completions and unlimited inline edits at $0 — but the download page currently shows macOS, the editor is now the front end for an agent business, and the brand has changed twice in two years. Worth trying, not worth building a workflow on yet.

also_considered.name: Tabby (TabbyML)
also_considered.why_not: The better-known self-hosted option: Apache 2.0 with a separately licensed ee/ directory, free for up to 5 users, $19/seat for Team up to 50, and plugins for VS Code, Neovim and the JetBrains family. Dropped because the newest release on its GitHub releases page is v0.32.0 from 25 January 2025 — nineteen months stale in a category that moved twice in that time.

also_considered.name: JetBrains AI
also_considered.why_not: Excluded because we could not read a price. The buy page renders prices in JavaScript that would not resolve, and the docs pages on subscriptions returned 404. Check current pricing yourself — if you live in a JetBrains IDE it is the obvious first thing to trial, we just will not quote a number we could not see.

also_considered.name: Amazon Q Developer
also_considered.why_not: Free tier is 50 agentic requests per month; Pro is $19/user/mo. The pricing page indicates free-tier data handling is 'opt-out available' while Pro is 'automatically opted out' — meaning the free tier's default is the wrong way round. Fine if you are already deep in AWS, unremarkable otherwise.

also_considered.name: Continue
also_considered.why_not: Still Apache 2.0, but the project has pivoted: its README now describes source-controlled AI review checks enforceable in CI, not editor autocomplete. It is no longer the local-model completion extension people remember recommending.

watch_list: Whether GitHub reverses training-on-by-default for Copilot Free, Pro and Pro+. That one setting is the reason the rank-1 pick carries a warning rather than a clean recommendation.

Whether Copilot AI Credits ever roll over, and whether inline completion stays outside the meter. Completions being credit-free is the entire basis for ranking Copilot first — if that changes, so does this list.
Cursor's Cursor-Models pool. The cheap tier currently rests on one external model family; a repricing or a supplier change would move Cursor's real cost significantly.
Zed's Windows build leaving Preview. That alone would push Zed above Cursor for a lot of teams, given its data defaults.

Whether Cognition keeps shipping the Windsurf-derived Tab model inside Devin Desktop, or lets it rot while the agent gets the attention. Unlimited free Tab would be a rank-2 pick if it looked durable.
Local FIM model quality at 7B and below. The gap between llama.vscode on a laptop and a hosted frontier completion is the only reason the self-hosted option is fourth rather than second.

docs.ask-spreadsheet.question: I want to ask my spreadsheet questions in plain English — which tools show their working so I can check the number?

method.how: Ranked on one thing above everything else: when the tool hands you a number, can you see the formula, the query or the Python that produced it? A confidently wrong total is the failure mode in this category, and an auditable trail is the only defence — so tools that print code or cite cells outrank tools that write prose. Second tiebreak was where the data goes and what happens at scale: whether the vendor documents a row or file-size ceiling, or whether the tool silently reads part of your sheet and answers anyway. Nothing here is trustworthy unattended; every pick is ranked as a thing you check, not a thing you believe.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No accuracy runs, no timing, no shared test workbook. Prices, limits and licences were read from the vendors' own pages on 2026-08-29; where a page renders its price in JavaScript and the number could not be read at source, this entry says 'check current pricing' rather than quoting one.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark was used, because none of these vendors publishes results against a common public test set for spreadsheet question-answering. Treat search results in this category with suspicion: the top-ranking 'best AI spreadsheet tools 2026' listicles are published by the vendors themselves (Julius, Coefficient, Querri and others all rank their own product), and every accuracy claim below is attributed to whoever made it.

ranked.name: ChatGPT (data analysis / code interpreter)
ranked.one_liner: Uploads a copy, writes Python, shows every line it ran.
ranked.use_it_when: You have one file and one question, the data can leave your building, and you want to read the actual filter and aggregation before you quote the number in a meeting.
ranked.cost: Free tier (3 file uploads/day). Plus $20/mo. Pro $100 or $200/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Plus $20/month. Pro comes in two tiers, $100/month (OpenAI says 5x Plus usage) and $200/month (20x Plus). OpenAI's help centre states there is no annual billing for Go, Plus or Pro. The Go, Business and Enterprise per-seat prices are rendered in JavaScript on OpenAI's pricing page and could not be read at source on 2026-08-29 — check current pricing. Storage caps: 25GB individual, 100GB org; upload rate 80 files per 3 hours, and 3 per day on Free.
ranked.good_at: The code is the product. Every number arrives with the Python that made it, so you can see which rows were dropped, how blanks were treated and whether it filtered the year you asked for. It also copes with genuinely messy files — merged headers, mixed types, stray footer rows — better than anything that has to work inside a live grid.
ranked.the_catch: It answers about a copy of your file sitting on OpenAI's servers, and it will happily answer from a partial read. OpenAI's file FAQ puts spreadsheets at roughly 50MB (512MB hard limit per file) and notes the 2M-token text limit does not apply to them — so the real ceiling is undocumented, and when a big or wide sheet gets sampled the answer looks exactly as confident as a correct one. The sandbox also resets between sessions, so on day three you re-upload, it re-derives the number a slightly different way, and the two don't match.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose data cannot leave the building — use PandasAI. Anyone who needs the answer written back into the live workbook with formulas intact — use Claude for Excel.

ranked.name: Claude for Excel
ranked.one_liner: Answers cite the exact cells, inside your live workbook.
ranked.use_it_when: The spreadsheet is a real model with dependencies — you want to ask why C42 is what it is, flex an assumption, and have downstream cells recompute rather than get a paragraph about it.
ranked.cost: Add-in is free; needs Claude Pro $17-20/mo, Max from $100/mo, or a Team/Enterprise seat.
ranked.pricing_detail: Claude Pro $17/month on annual, $20 monthly. Max from $100/month. Team standard seat $20/month annual ($25 monthly); Team premium seat $100/month annual ($125 monthly). Enterprise $20/seat/month plus usage at API rates, annual only. Generally available on Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise. Your Excel usage counts against the same account limits as everything else you do with Claude, so a heavy modelling day eats your chat budget.
ranked.good_at: Cell-level citations you can click to jump to the referenced cell — the closest thing here to a real audit trail. It updates values while keeping formula relationships intact, traces #REF! and #DIV/0 to a root cause, and works across multi-tab workbooks. It edits the file you already have rather than a copy of it.
ranked.the_catch: Anthropic's own documentation says it is not recommended for audit-critical calculations without verification, and warns that downloaded or vendor-supplied workbooks can carry prompt injections that have been shown in testing to manipulate the add-in into extracting or destroying data. Two governance holes worth knowing before rollout: Claude for Excel activity is not included in Enterprise audit logs or the Compliance API, and it does not inherit your org's custom data retention settings. Chat history lives in browser IndexedDB — local, unsynced, and gone when someone clears site data. No macros, no VBA, no data tables; and it will not run on Excel 2016/2019 perpetual or volume licences, on iPad, or on Android.
ranked.wrong_for: Google Sheets users — use Gemini in Sheets. Anyone wanting statistics, regressions or plots rather than model tracing — use ChatGPT or Julius.

ranked.name: Microsoft 365 Copilot in Excel
ranked.one_liner: The Excel default; only safe if you force it to show formulas.
ranked.use_it_when: Your organisation already runs Microsoft 365, the file lives in SharePoint or OneDrive, and you need something IT will actually approve rather than a tool you smuggle in.
ranked.cost: Copilot Business add-on $18/user/mo billed annually; enterprise M365 Copilot $30/user/mo annually. Eligible M365 licence required.
ranked.pricing_detail: Microsoft 365 Copilot Business add-on: $18.00 user/month billed annually (Microsoft's page shows this reduced from $21.00), or $25.20 user/month billed monthly. Bundled: Microsoft 365 Business Standard with Copilot $23.50 annual / $28.20 monthly; Business Premium with Copilot $32.00 annual / $38.40 monthly. Enterprise Microsoft 365 Copilot: $30 user/month billed annually, $31.50/month on monthly billing with an annual commitment. All of it is an add-on — a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription is mandatory on top.
ranked.good_at: It is already where the file is, and it can leave evidence behind: ask for a formula column and the formula lands in the sheet where anyone can read it, and Advanced Analysis with Python writes visible Python rather than prose. For a finance team that will never install a third-party add-in, this is the realistic option.
ranked.the_catch: By default it answers in prose with no visible working at all — the audit trail only exists if you specifically ask for a formula column or switch to Python analysis, and most users won't. Microsoft's own getting-started page says your data must be formatted as a table or supported range for Copilot to read it, so a normal human spreadsheet with a title row and merged headers gets partial or refused answers. And the price is per seat, annually, stacked on a licence you already pay for — the true cost is the add-on plus the base plan, not the $18 headline.
ranked.wrong_for: One person, one file, one question, no procurement cycle — use ChatGPT or Julius. Anyone who needs cell-by-cell citations for a financial model — use Claude for Excel.

ranked.name: Gemini in Google Sheets
ranked.one_liner: Sheets' own AI, with a Show code button worth using.
ranked.use_it_when: The data already lives in Google Sheets and you want trends, a regression or a chart without exporting anything to a third party.
ranked.cost: Google AI Pro $19.99/mo for individuals. Included at varying levels with Google Workspace Business plans — check current pricing.
ranked.pricing_detail: Consumer plans read at source: Free $0; Google AI Plus $4.99/month; Google AI Pro $19.99/month (includes Gemini in Gmail, Docs and other Workspace apps); Google AI Ultra from $99.99/month, with a $199.99/month option. Google Workspace Business per-seat prices are rendered in JavaScript and could not be read at source on 2026-08-29 — check current pricing. Google's comparison table shows Business Starter with 'limited' Gemini and Standard, Plus and Enterprise with 'expanded access', with 16% off on a one-year commitment.
ranked.good_at: Two buttons most rivals don't have: 'Show code' reveals the formula it generated, and 'Analysis steps' reveals the reasoning behind an analysis or chart. You can also point it at one specific table when a sheet contains several, which cuts the commonest source of wrong answers — it silently analysing the wrong block.
ranked.the_catch: Google publishes no row, column or size limit for Sheets analysis anywhere in the documentation, so you discover the ceiling by hitting it: on large or untidy ranges it declines, or quietly narrows what it looked at. The AI tier you get is bundled into a plan rather than bought directly, so Business Starter users get 'limited' Gemini and no clear statement of what that excludes — and I could not read the Workspace seat price at source to tell you what upgrading costs.
ranked.wrong_for: Excel workbooks, especially real financial models — use Claude for Excel or Copilot. Anything needing a reproducible script you can rerun next month — use ChatGPT or PandasAI.

ranked.name: PandasAI
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed library; the dataframe and the generated code stay yours.
ranked.use_it_when: The data legally cannot go to a vendor, or you want the plain-English question to compile down to code you can commit, review and rerun on a schedule.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT expat licence (except the pandasai/ee directory). You pay only your LLM provider.
ranked.pricing_detail: The README states PandasAI is available under the MIT expat licence except for the pandasai/ee directory, which carries its own separate licence — read that file before shipping anything commercial built on the enterprise parts. Managed PandasAI Cloud and a self-hosted Enterprise offering exist but are contact-sales only, with no published price. Your running cost is whatever your model provider charges; the library talks to models through LiteLLM, with OpenAI shown as the default in the docs.
ranked.good_at: The only pick here where the data can genuinely stay on infrastructure you control: the dataframe is loaded in your process, and if you point LiteLLM at a locally hosted model, nothing leaves at all. Because the output is code, the answer is reproducible next quarter — which the hosted chat tools are not.
ranked.the_catch: It is a library, not a product. There is no interface for the colleague in finance who actually has the question; you write the loader, the prompt plumbing and whatever UI exists. 'Self-hosted' is not the same as private — out of the box it calls a hosted model through LiteLLM, so unless you also host the model, your schema and sampled rows still leave. And check the pulse before you build: the latest release read at source was 3.0.0, dated 7 October 2025.
ranked.wrong_for: Non-programmers, and anyone who needs an answer this afternoon — use ChatGPT or Julius. Teams that need governance and audit logs rather than a repo — use Copilot.

also_considered.name: Julius AI
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely good at this and it shows its Python, with a 32GB sandbox and no enforced file-size limit per its FAQ — but it is credit-metered ($20/mo for 2,000 credits, $45 for 5,000, $200 for 25,000), and a day of iterating on one messy file burns through them faster than the plan names suggest.

also_considered.name: Quadratic
also_considered.why_not: Best idea in the category — AI writes Python, SQL and formulas into cells you can open and check — but $18/user/mo annual ($20 monthly) with an AI credit budget attached, and self-hosting is Enterprise-only.

also_considered.name: Rows
also_considered.why_not: Excluded: its own pricing page now says 'Rows has joined Superhuman' and pushes visitors to Superhuman Docs. Don't start a workflow here.

also_considered.name: GPT for Work (GPT for Sheets)
also_considered.why_not: Bulk cell-filling and enrichment, not question-answering — and the credits expire 12 months after your most recent purchase, minimum $29.

also_considered.name: Equals
also_considered.why_not: Still trading, but it is a spreadsheet-plus-SQL product aimed at analysts who already write queries; no price shown on the homepage, and it solves a different problem than 'ask my file a question'.

watch_list: Whether Microsoft's $18/user/month Copilot Business price holds or snaps back to the $21 it is shown as reduced from.
Whether Anthropic brings Claude for Excel activity into Enterprise audit logs and the Compliance API — today that gap alone blocks it in regulated teams.

Whether any vendor publishes a hard, documented row or file-size ceiling instead of silently sampling. That single change would reorder this list, because silent truncation is the direct cause of the confidently wrong number.
Whether a credible independent accuracy benchmark for spreadsheet question-answering appears and vendors start reporting against it. Right now the category is graded entirely by its own marketing.
Whether PandasAI keeps shipping — 3.0.0 on 7 October 2025 was the latest release read at source, and a stalled repo would drop it off this list.
Whether Superhuman keeps Rows' AI analyst alive as a standalone product or folds it away entirely.
