docs.pdf-tables.question: I need the tables out of a pile of PDFs. Some are scans. Some tables run over three pages. What actually works?

method.how: Ranked on the two things that actually break table extraction: whether the tool reads a scan at all, and what it does when a table continues onto the next page. Nothing on this list solves the second problem properly - Microsoft and AWS both ship blog posts and sample repos telling you to stitch cross-page tables yourself, and Docling has an open issue for it - so tools were ordered by how cheaply and predictably you can bolt that stitching on top. Accuracy ordering leans on the two independent benchmarks I could find rather than on vendor leaderboards. Price per page was read at source on 2026-08-29; where a vendor quotes two different prices in the same week, both are printed.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. I ran no PDFs through anything. Prices and hard limits were read from vendors' own pages and APIs on 2026-08-29 (Azure figures pulled from the Azure retail prices API, East US, USD). Accuracy statements are other people's measurements, attributed. Nobody paid for anything.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: Two roughly independent benchmarks exist and both are cited here. OmniDocBench (OpenDataLab, CVPR 2025, Apache-2.0 dataset) publishes table TEDS scores - Gemini 3 Flash 89.29, MinerU-Pipeline 81.88, Marker 65.77, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 94.76 on its leaderboard. 'Beyond String Matching: Semantic Evaluation of PDF Table Extraction' (Horn and Keuper, arXiv 2603.18652, submitted to BMVC 2026) scored 21 parsers over 451 tables and put Gemini 3 Pro top at 9.55/10, Gemini 3 Flash 9.50, GROBID last at 2.10 - but on synthetic LaTeX documents, which the authors themselves say do not capture real-world table diversity, and it does not separate scans from native text. Older but hands-on: MuckRock/DocumentCloud with OpenNews (2024) ran eight tools over real scanned and multi-page documents. Everything else you will find is a vendor ranking itself: RD-TableBench is published by Reducto, the IDP Leaderboard by Nanonets, the 'table extraction benchmark' posts by LlamaIndex. Search results for this category are almost entirely vendor comparison pages. Treat any number with a logo on it as marketing. LlamaIndex has publicly argued OmniDocBench is now saturated, so its ordering is less discriminating than it was.

ranked.name: Azure AI Document Intelligence (prebuilt-layout)
ranked.one_liner: Boring, cheap, reads scans, gives you real cell coordinates
ranked.use_it_when: You have mixed native-text and scanned PDFs, you need row/column indices, spans and bounding boxes you can audit against the page, and you are willing to write your own cross-page stitching.
ranked.cost: Free 500 pages/mo. Layout $10 per 1,000 pages.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read from the Azure retail prices API on 2026-08-29 (East US, USD). Pay-as-you-go S0: 'S0 Batch Layout Pages' and 'S0 Pre-built Pages' both $10 per 1,000 pages; 'S0 Read Pages' (plain OCR, no table structure) $1.50 per 1,000 falling to $0.60 above 1M; custom extraction $30 per 1,000; add-on features $6 per 1,000; query fields $10 per 1,000; custom model training $3/hour. Free F0 tier is 500 pages/month but capped at 4 MB and 2 pages per document, so it demos rather than works. S0 caps: 500 MB and 2,000 pages per document, 15 analyse transactions/sec by default. Monthly commitment tiers drop the prebuilt rate to $9.50 per 1,000 at 20K pages/month and $7.50 per 1,000 at 1M. Disconnected containers are annual-only and start at $8,640/year for 100K prebuilt pages - budget for that before you promise anyone an air-gapped deployment.
ranked.good_at: Structured output that survives contact with a scan. You get every cell with rowIndex, columnIndex, rowSpan, columnSpan, a confidence and a bounding region on a specific page, which means you can programmatically check the extraction against the pixels instead of trusting it. MuckRock/DocumentCloud's 2024 test found Azure and Textract both 'performed admirably' on their hardest scanned flight log and election documents, where the free tools failed on handwriting. 500 MB and 2,000 pages per file is the most generous ceiling of anything here.
ranked.the_catch: It does not merge a table that continues onto the next page. Microsoft's own answer to this is a 2024 Tech Community post titled 'A heuristic method of merging cross-page tables based on Document Intelligence layout model' - that is, write the heuristic yourself. You will spend day three deciding whether two adjacent tables with matching column counts are one table or two, and you will get it wrong on documents where a header repeats. Second trap: v2.1 of the REST API retires 15 September 2027 and the preview API versions from 2023-2024 died 30 June 2026, so anything you write against an old SDK has a clock on it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who just wants markdown to shove at an LLM and does not care about coordinates - use Gemini and pay less. Anyone whose documents cannot leave their own hardware without an annual six-figure container commitment - use Docling.

ranked.name: Gemini 3 (Gemini API, direct)
ranked.one_liner: Best measured table accuracy, zero provenance, invents numbers
ranked.use_it_when: You want markdown or JSON tables out of messy documents fast, the tables are the point rather than the audit trail, and you can afford to spot-check the output against the page yourself.
ranked.cost: Free tier on Flash. Paid from $0.75/M input tokens; a PDF page is 258 tokens.
ranked.pricing_detail: Read at ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing on 2026-08-29. Gemini 3.7 Flash and 3.6 Flash: $0.75/M input and $3.75/M output through 31 December 2026, rising to $1.50 and $7.50 on 1 January 2027 - a doubling already on the published page, so do not build a margin on the current number. Gemini 3.5 Flash $1.50/$9.00. Flash-Lite $0.30/$2.50. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview $2.00/$12.00 for prompts up to 200K tokens, $4.00/$18.00 above, and no free tier on Pro at all. Each PDF page counts as 258 image tokens, so input is negligible (about $0.0002/page on Flash) and the bill is entirely output tokens - a dense table page can emit several thousand, which is where a per-page cost in the half-penny to two-penny range comes from. On Gemini 3 models native embedded text is extracted and not charged as image tokens. Hard cap: 50 MB or 1,000 pages per PDF, the same for inline data and the Files API.
ranked.good_at: Raw table accuracy on the only two independent benchmarks I could find. Horn and Keuper (arXiv 2603.18652, BMVC 2026 submission) put Gemini 3 Pro first of 21 parsers at 9.55/10 and Gemini 3 Flash second at 9.50, both ahead of every dedicated OCR tool tested; the OmniDocBench leaderboard shows Gemini 3 Flash at 89.29 table TEDS against MinerU-Pipeline's 81.88 and Marker's 65.77. It also handles the thing everything else fumbles - you can put ten consecutive pages in one prompt and ask it to return the continued table as one table - because it sees the pages together.
ranked.the_catch: It has no idea when it is wrong, and neither will you. There are no bounding boxes, no per-cell confidences and no link back to a pixel, so a transposed digit in a financial table is indistinguishable from a correct one until someone downstream notices. Both benchmarks that rank it top measured semantic similarity to ground truth, not per-cell numeric fidelity, and Horn and Keuper used synthetic LaTeX documents and say so. The 1,000-page and 50 MB caps mean anything larger needs splitting, which puts you back in the cross-page stitching business you were trying to avoid. And Pro has no free tier, so the model that actually won the benchmark is the one you cannot try for nothing.
ranked.wrong_for: Regulated extraction, anything where a wrong number is a reportable event, or anything you must be able to defend cell by cell - use Azure. Data that cannot go to Google - use Docling.

ranked.name: Docling
ranked.maker: IBM Research Zurich / LF AI & Data Foundation
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed, self-hosted, reads scans, no per-page bill
ranked.use_it_when: The documents cannot leave your infrastructure, or the volume is high enough that $10 per 1,000 pages becomes a real line item, and you have somewhere to run a GPU.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT licence, commercial use included. You pay for compute.
ranked.pricing_detail: No licence cost and no usage cap. Version 2.124.0 on PyPI, released 31 August 2026. MIT on both the code and the project's own models, which is the important part - unlike Marker, there is no revenue or funding threshold above which you owe someone money. Your costs are GPU time and engineering. OCR engines are pluggable extras (EasyOCR, RapidOCR, TesserOCR, macOS native), and there is a VLM pipeline (--pipeline vlm, GraniteDocling) for harder pages.
ranked.good_at: Being genuinely free to use commercially while still handling scans. It is the only option here where table structure recognition, OCR and a VLM fallback all run on your own hardware under a permissive licence, and it is maintained by a real research group under LF AI & Data rather than a startup that might get acquired. Output is a structured document model, not just markdown, so you keep cell structure.
ranked.the_catch: Same cross-page failure as the paid tools, documented in the open: docling issue #2976, 'Continued table across pages is split into multiple tables'. Beyond that, accuracy on scans depends entirely on which OCR extra you bolt on, and the defaults are not the best available - the fair comparison is not 'Docling vs Azure' but 'Docling plus whichever OCR engine you configured vs Azure', and you own the tuning. Running it fast enough to matter means a GPU; on CPU, a few hundred scanned pages will take long enough that you will start pricing up Azure again.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants this working this afternoon with no infrastructure - use Azure or Gemini. Anyone whose documents are clean native-text PDFs and who does not need OCR at all - Camelot is lighter.

ranked.name: Reducto
ranked.one_liner: Pitched at the documents that break everything else; vendor-graded
ranked.use_it_when: You have already lost a week to a specific class of ugly document - dense financial tables, rotated scans, forms with nested headers - and Azure's output is measurably not good enough on your own sample.
ranked.cost: 15,000 free credits. Listed $0.015/page; new r-1 model announced at $0.01/page.
ranked.pricing_detail: Two prices are in the market this week and you should establish which applies to you before committing. The pricing page on 2026-08-29 showed Standard pay-as-you-go at $0.015 per credit with 15,000 credits free, up to 5 Studio seats, no page minimum or commitment. A press release dated 1 September 2026 announced a new model, r-1, at '1 cent a page' described as an all-in cost with 'no additional model charges or feature-based multipliers'. Batch (async, 12-hour completion guarantee) takes 20% off. Growth and Enterprise are contact-sales only, and the things a compliance team will demand - zero data retention, BAAs, data residency, VPC or on-premise, SSO/SAML, RBAC - are all behind that call, not on the self-serve tier. There is a startup programme (under $15M funding, $3M revenue, 50 staff) and a Y Combinator deal.
ranked.good_at: Being purpose-built for the long tail rather than the average page, and being straightforward to buy - no cloud account, no IAM, no region selection. It is one of the few vendors that treats complex table structure as the product rather than a feature of an OCR API.
ranked.the_catch: Every accuracy number attached to it is its own. RD-TableBench, the benchmark most often cited for Reducto's superiority, is published by Reducto; the r-1 launch claim of 'reduces errors by up to 20%' cites 'Reducto's evaluations' against unnamed comparators, with no named third-party benchmark. It appears in neither of the independent benchmarks cited above. You are buying on a vendor's self-assessment at up to 50% more per page than Azure, and the free 15,000 credits are exactly enough to find out whether that is justified on your documents - so use them properly before you sign anything.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose documents are ordinary - you are paying a premium for a hard-case model you do not need; use Azure. Anyone who needs an independently verified accuracy figure to justify the spend - that does not exist here yet.

ranked.name: Camelot 2.0 (with pdfplumber as the fallback)
ranked.one_liner: Free Python, excellent on clean PDFs, hopeless on bad scans
ranked.use_it_when: The PDFs are machine-generated, you can select the text in a viewer, and you want a dependency rather than a vendor. Government and financial filings, generated reports, anything that started life in a typesetter.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT licence, commercial use included.
ranked.pricing_detail: No cost. Version 2.0.0 on PyPI, released 4 June 2026, MIT. Five parsers: lattice for ruled tables, stream for whitespace-aligned ones, network and hybrid for text-alignment cases, plus an optional neural ml flavour (Table Transformer) for borderless tables, and flavor='auto'. Scanned PDFs need the optional extras - pip install 'camelot-py[ml,ocr]' - which pulls in the neural backend and an OCR engine. pdfplumber is separately MIT and is the better tool when you need the raw lines and character positions to reason about cell boundaries yourself.
ranked.good_at: Precision on documents that have a text layer, at zero cost and with no network call. MuckRock/DocumentCloud found the text-layer tools 'work really well on text-based, machine-generated PDFs', with pdfplumber particularly good at extracting lines and cell structures. When a PDF is clean, these give you exact character positions rather than a model's opinion, which is a different and often better guarantee than anything above.
ranked.the_catch: The moment a document is a photocopy, you are outside its competence and the failure is quiet - you get a table-shaped object full of wrong text rather than an error. The [ocr] and [ml] extras exist but drag in Table Transformer and a torch install, at which point you have accepted a heavy ML dependency to do badly what Azure does well for a penny a page. Borderless tables in stream mode remain the classic pain: column detection is whitespace heuristics, and one wide cell will shift every column to its right.
ranked.wrong_for: Scanned or photographed documents, handwriting, anything with merged header cells - use Azure or Docling. Anyone who needs one tool to cover a mixed pile of native and scanned PDFs; this is the clean-input half of that job only.

also_considered.name: Amazon Textract (AnalyzeDocument, TABLES)
also_considered.why_not: Good on scans - the same 2024 MuckRock test rated it alongside Azure - but $15 per 1,000 pages for tables against Azure's $10, and it has the identical cross-page problem: AWS's answer is a machine-learning blog post and the aws-samples/amazon-textract-multipage-tables-processing repo. Async caps at 500 MB and 3,000 pages; synchronous is 10 MB and one page. Free tier is 100 Analyze Document pages/month and only for three months. Pick it if you are already deep in AWS, otherwise Azure is cheaper for the same job.

also_considered.name: Google Document AI (Layout Parser)
also_considered.why_not: Layout Parser is $10 per 1,000 pages, the same as Azure, but synchronous requests cap at 10 pages per document and batch at 200 - a real constraint if your documents are long. Form Parser is $30 per 1,000. Also the shakiest platform commitment here: Document AI Warehouse and Human-in-the-Loop were both deprecated in January 2024, and a long list of pretrained processor versions shut down on 30 June 2026, so anything you pin will need re-pinning. Excluded on that basis for anything meant to last.

also_considered.name: LlamaParse (LlamaCloud)
also_considered.why_not: Credit-priced at $1.25 per 1,000 credits, and the tier that handles hard tables is the expensive one: Fast is 1 credit/page ($0.00125), Cost-effective 3, Agentic 10 ($0.0125), Agentic Plus 45 ($0.056/page - nearly six times Azure). Layout extraction adds 3 credits. Free plan is 10K credits/month, which at Agentic Plus is about 220 pages. Perfectly good, but the advertised cheapness and the mode you will actually end up using are two different numbers.

also_considered.name: Unstructured
also_considered.why_not: $0.015 per page after 10,000 free pages, with an Apache-2.0 open-source library if you self-host. Strong as a general document-partitioning pipeline for RAG, weaker than the dedicated parsers when the deliverable is a correct table specifically. If you want free and self-hosted, Docling is the better table tool; if you want hosted, Azure is cheaper.

also_considered.name: Marker (Datalab)
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely capable - VLM fallback on scanned pages, and --use_llm explicitly does multi-page table merging, which is more than most manage. But the licence is a trap: the code is Apache-2.0 while the model weights are a modified AI Pubs Open RAIL-M that is free only for research, personal use and companies under $5M in funding or revenue. Above that you owe Datalab a licence fee. It also scored 65.77 table TEDS on the OmniDocBench leaderboard, well behind the VLMs. Read the weights licence before you ship it.

also_considered.name: Adobe PDF Extract API
also_considered.why_not: 500 free Document Transactions per month, and then I could not read a per-transaction price anywhere on Adobe's own pricing pages on 2026-08-29 - both the main pricing page and the pay-as-you-go page route you to 'contact sales'. Nor could I establish how many pages constitute one Document Transaction for Extract, which is the number that determines whether it is cheap or ruinous. Check current pricing directly with Adobe; do not plan around it until you have that in writing.

watch_list: Reducto's r-1, announced 1 September 2026 at 1 cent a page all-in. If an independent benchmark confirms the claims at that price it undercuts Azure on both accuracy and cost and moves to the top of this list. Until then it is a vendor's word.

Whether any vendor ships cross-page table stitching as a first-class API field rather than a sample repo. Every paid tool here charges per page and hands the hardest part of a multi-page table back to you. The first one to return a continued table as one object with page provenance wins this category outright.

Gemini Flash pricing doubles on 1 January 2027 - input $0.75 to $1.50, output $3.75 to $7.50 per million tokens - already published on Google's own page. That roughly halves the cost gap between rolling your own with an LLM and paying Azure.

OmniDocBench saturation. LlamaIndex has publicly argued the benchmark no longer discriminates between top models; a credible successor would change the evidence base this list rests on, and right now that evidence base is thin.
Docling's VLM pipeline (GraniteDocling). If it closes the gap on scanned tables without needing a serious GPU, the case for paying per page at moderate volume mostly evaporates.
Azure REST v2.1 retires 15 September 2027 and v3.0 on 30 March 2029. Anything built on an older SDK has a dated migration attached to it.

marketing.ad-creative.question: I need forty versions of one static ad by Friday. Which tool does that without wrecking the brand?

method.how: Ranked on three things: how many genuinely different variants you get out per hour without re-editing each one; whether the tool pushes to your ad account or just hands you files; and whether the pricing model punishes the volume that creative testing actually needs. The ad-account distinction matters more than the marketing suggests — Pencil connects to Meta, TikTok, Google, DV360 and LinkedIn; The Brief serves to 40+ networks from Ultra up; Canva, Bannerbear and ComfyUI export files and leave you uploading by hand. Nothing here is excellent: the AI generators produce templated sameness and the tools with real layout control need you to build the template first. Compliance is now part of the buying decision — EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations for artificially generated or manipulated content applied from 2 August 2026, and Google already makes election advertisers tick an 'Altered or synthetic content' box in campaign settings, so ask any vendor what provenance metadata survives their export.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No ads were run, no creative was scored against real spend. Prices read from vendors' own pages on 2026-08-29. Where a vendor renders prices in JavaScript we could not read them and say so rather than guess — Placid is the case here.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark exists for ad-creative generation quality. Search results for this job are dominated by vendors ranking themselves: the first page of results is almost entirely 'best AI ad creative tools 2026' posts published by companies selling competing ad tools. Treat every ranking you find here, including this one, as unaudited. Platform policy text was read at source where fetchable — Google's policies were; Meta's Advertising Standards are rendered client-side and could not be quoted at source.

ranked.name: The Brief (formerly Creatopy)
ranked.one_liner: Bulk resize and batch-edit hundreds of on-brand static ads
ranked.use_it_when: You have one approved concept and need it in thirty placements, sizes and locales, on brand, with the type still fitting — then served to the networks rather than zipped up.
ranked.cost: From $29/mo (annual). Team $49/seat/mo. Enterprise custom.
ranked.pricing_detail: Pro $29/mo ($348/yr), 1 seat, 250GB. Ultra $79/mo ($948/yr), 1 seat, 1TB. Team $49/seat/mo ($588/seat/yr), 2-10 seats, 1TB. Enterprise custom, billed monthly, quarterly or annually. Displayed prices are the annual-billed rates — the page advertises 'Yearly save 26%' but does not publish the monthly-billed figure. Ad serving (25+ networks, 100,000 monthly impressions), automated A/B testing and AI translation start at Ultra. API access, white-label editor, SSO/SAML and DAM integrations are Enterprise only.
ranked.good_at: Taking one approved layout and mechanically producing every size, format and locale variant — 'edit 100 ads at once', AI resize across formats — without the headline breaking out of the frame each time.
ranked.the_catch: Two. First, the rebrand: Creatopy became The Brief in 2026 and every old URL 302s across, so your bookmarks, internal docs and template links all move with it mid-project. Second, the price you see is not the price a creative tester pays — automated A/B testing and ad serving, the two features that make this a testing tool rather than a resizer, are gated one tier above the advertised $29, at $79. And the $29 is the annual-billed rate; the monthly number is not on the page.
ranked.wrong_for: One-off ads, or anyone without an existing concept — it resizes and remixes, it does not invent. Use Canva to make the thing in the first place, or Pencil if you want generation wired directly into the ad account.

ranked.name: Canva
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest competent way to make and vary static ads
ranked.use_it_when: No budget, no designer, and you need presentable variants of a spreadsheet of headlines today. Also the only genuinely free option here that produces finished ads.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro $180/yr. Business $250/yr per person.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, 1 seat, 1 brand kit (3 colours only), 5GB storage, up to 200 Standard AI uses or 20 Premium AI uses. Pro: $180/yr, 1 seat, 5 brand kits, 100GB, '10x more AI than Canva Free'. Business: $250/yr per person, 100 brand kits with approvals, 500GB, '20x more AI than Canva Free'. Enterprise: custom, 1TB, SSO, dedicated support at a 150-seat minimum. Note Business is priced per person — a five-person team is $1,250/yr, not $250.
ranked.good_at: Bulk Create plus the template library: the fastest route from a CSV of headlines and offers to a folder of exportable, on-brand ad files. Nothing else at this price gets a non-designer to acceptable output.
ranked.the_catch: The AI allowance is published as a multiple of the free tier — '10x more AI than Canva Free' — not as a number, and Standard, Premium and Ultra AI uses burn at different rates, so you cannot work out how many generations you get before you pay. And it exports files: nothing reaches your ad account, so a human still uploads, names and tags forty assets in Ads Manager afterwards.
ranked.wrong_for: Teams running high-volume creative tests every week — the manual export-and-upload loop eats the time the tool saved. Use Bannerbear if you have a developer, or The Brief if you do not.

ranked.name: Pencil
ranked.one_liner: Generates ads and launches them straight into your ad accounts
ranked.use_it_when: Small team that wants generation, auto-resizing to 1:1, 9:16, 4:5, 16:9 and 1.91:1, and launch in one loop rather than three tools.
ranked.cost: Core $14/mo (50 generations). Growth $55/mo (250). Pro custom.
ranked.pricing_detail: Core $14/mo billed monthly, or $11/mo billed annually ($132/yr), 50 generations per month. Growth $55/mo monthly, or $44/mo billed annually (about $528/yr), 250 generations per month. Pro: custom pricing, unlimited generations. Annual billing saves 20%. Generations are the metered unit, so a round of variations against one concept can consume a meaningful share of a month's Core allowance.
ranked.good_at: Being the only cheap tool on this list that connects directly to the ad accounts — launch and track on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Google Display, DV360 and LinkedIn without an export step.
ranked.the_catch: The headline feature is creative performance prediction, and it is entirely vendor-self-reported. Pencil states that predictions begin on Core and get more accurate the more you test and the richer your data; it publishes no validation methodology and no independent audit exists. You are being invited to kill creative on a score nobody outside the vendor has checked. Separately, 50 generations a month on the $14 tier is one afternoon of real testing — the useful tier is $55.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who has to defend a creative decision to a client or a finance director with evidence. Run the split test in Ads Manager, or use Marpipe's multivariate approach, and treat the prediction score as a tie-breaker at most.

ranked.name: Bannerbear
ranked.one_liner: API that stamps thousands of ad variants from your templates
ranked.use_it_when: You have a developer and a product feed, and you want variants generated deterministically on a schedule — same template, thousands of data-driven permutations, no model randomness.
ranked.cost: Automate $49/mo. Scale $149/mo. Enterprise $299/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Automate $49/mo: 1,000 images or videos per month, 10GB bandwidth, no team members or roles, email support. Scale $149/mo: 10,000-40,000 credits depending on sub-tier, 50GB, team members and roles. Enterprise $299/mo: 50,000-2,000,000 credits, 100GB, bring-your-own S3 storage. Unlimited templates on every plan. Free trial is 30 API credits, no card required. No annual discount is published.
ranked.good_at: Repeatable, predictable output at volume. A generative tool gives you a different image each time; this gives you the same layout with the data swapped, which is what a clean creative test actually needs.
ranked.the_catch: There is no overage. Bannerbear's own FAQ says it is not possible to exceed your monthly credit limit — generation simply stops until you upgrade, which is a bad thing to discover mid-flight on a Friday. No annual discount is published either, so it is full price twelve months a year. And it renders: it will not tell you what to put in the template, and it does not touch your ad account.
ranked.wrong_for: Marketers with no engineering support — this is an API first and a UI second. Use The Brief for the same job with a person driving it.

ranked.name: ComfyUI with local models
ranked.one_liner: Self-hosted image generation for teams whose data cannot leave
ranked.use_it_when: Regulated, NDA-bound or pre-launch work — unreleased product shots and unannounced pricing that cannot be uploaded to a vendor's cloud under any circumstances.
ranked.cost: Free, GPL-3.0. You pay for the GPU.
ranked.pricing_detail: The software is free under GPL-3.0 and runs fully offline; the core downloads nothing unless you ask it to. Your costs are hardware or rented GPU time. Model weights are licensed separately and this is where people get caught: the FLUX.1 [dev] licence states you may only access, use or create derivatives of the model for Non-Commercial Purposes, while separately stating you may use Output for any purpose including commercial. Commercial use of the model itself goes through Black Forest Labs licensing. Read the weights licence for whatever checkpoint you actually load — free to download is not free to use commercially.
ranked.good_at: Nothing leaves your network. Full control of the pipeline, reproducible seeds and workflows, and no per-generation meter — the only option here that scales to thousands of images without a credit counter.
ranked.the_catch: It generates images, not ads. There is no text layout engine, no safe-area handling for platform placements, no size-variant system and no brand kit, so you will build a compositing step yourself before anything is shippable. Budget days of engineering and a GPU, not an afternoon. Plus the licence trap above, which is a genuine commercial risk rather than a footnote.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone on a deadline, and anyone without engineering. If your data is allowed to leave the building, every other tool on this list is a better use of the week.

also_considered.name: AdCreative.ai
also_considered.why_not: The obvious search result and the one to be careful with: TrustScore 3.4/5 across roughly 4,479 reviews, with recurring recent reports of trials converting into annual plans and refunds taking months. $39/mo buys 10 credits.

also_considered.name: Smartly
also_considered.why_not: Enterprise ad-ops platform with sales-only pricing — its old pricing page now just says to contact them. Overkill unless someone else signs the media plan.

also_considered.name: Marpipe
also_considered.why_not: Has moved towards catalogue and feed ads: free feed tier, $199/mo Startup (500 SKUs), $999/mo Enterprise. Strong for multivariate SKU testing, wrong tool for concept variations.

also_considered.name: Icon
also_considered.why_not: Now a human UGC video service — $1,000/mo for six filmed and edited ads. Video only; no static creative at all.

also_considered.name: Templated.io
also_considered.why_not: A cheaper Bannerbear ($29/$79/$179 a month, 1,000/5,000/25,000 credits) but every price on the page is billed annually and the monthly rate is not shown.

also_considered.name: Placid
also_considered.why_not: Comparable render API and the only one whose credits roll over, up to double your monthly budget — but its prices render client-side and we could not read a figure at source. Check current pricing.

watch_list: EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations for artificially generated or manipulated content applied from 2 August 2026. The first vendor to ship real provenance and disclosure support — rather than stripping metadata on export — moves up this list.

Google already requires election advertisers to tick 'Altered or synthetic content' in campaign settings, with auto-generated disclosures on some formats. If that requirement spreads beyond election ads, any tool that discards C2PA metadata at export becomes a liability.

Meta's Advertising Standards are rendered client-side and could not be quoted at source. If Meta publishes a plain, fetchable AI-disclosure rule for ordinary commercial ads, this list gets reordered around who supports it.
The Creatopy-to-The Brief migration. If support, template libraries or export specs degrade through the rebrand, it loses the top spot to Canva on price and Pencil on integration.

The platforms' own creative tools — Meta's Advantage+ creative and Google's asset generation in Performance Max — are free and already inside the ad account. When their output stops looking generic, most of the $29-$79 tier here loses its reason to exist.

Any independent, third-party validation of creative performance prediction. Pencil's scores, and everyone else's, are currently vendor claims; a credible external benchmark would change what that $14 tier is worth.

Google Ads political content policy — synthetic content disclosure
Google Ads misrepresentation policy — manipulated media
EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations

meetings.notetaker.question: Which AI notetaker actually takes usable meeting notes without landing me in a wiretap lawsuit?

method.how: Ranked on three things, in this order: what the tool does about consent, whether the vendor trains on your conversations, and only then note quality. That order is deliberate — a notetaker that produces beautiful minutes and quietly records a Californian client is a liability, not a productivity tool. Prices and policy claims were read at each vendor's own pricing and security pages on 29 August 2026. Where a vendor's page contradicted third-party pricing trackers, the vendor page won.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No side-by-side transcription accuracy run, no word-error-rate measurement, no long-term use of any tool. Prices, tier limits, retention windows and model-training claims were read from vendors' own pages on 2026-08-29 and are quoted as vendor claims, not verified facts. Legal summaries below are reporting of published law-firm commentary and court filings, not legal advice.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for meeting-note quality. No WER leaderboard, no neutral test corpus, nothing. Every 'we tested 14 notetakers' post you will find is either a competitor's content-marketing page or an affiliate roundup, and the vendors themselves rank first in searches for their own competitors' names. The only non-vendor evidence used here is court material: In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation, No. 5:25-cv-06911 (N.D. Cal.), and a June 2026 Mayer Brown client note on notetaker wiretap exposure. Treat every accuracy claim on this page, including the vendors', as unverified.

ranked.name: Circleback
ranked.one_liner: Cleanest consent story, no training on your calls, sharp action items
ranked.use_it_when: You need notes for external calls with clients, candidates or patients, and someone will eventually ask you to prove what happened to the recording.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $15-$35/user/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free $0 (unlimited meetings, 30-day meeting and recording history). Pro $15/user/mo. Business $25/user/mo. Enterprise $35/user/mo. Read at circleback.ai/pricing on 2026-08-29: the monthly and annual toggles showed the same per-seat figure, so there is no annual discount to chase. Storage, not meeting count, is what you buy: 30 days free, 1 year on Pro, 2 years on Business, unlimited on Enterprise.
ranked.good_at: The compliance answers are all in one place and all say the right thing: SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA with a BAA available, EU-US Data Privacy Framework, and a flat 'we do not use customer data to train models'. Admins can set workspace-level retention. You can run it as a bot in the call or as a bot-free desktop app, which means you can pick per-meeting whether other participants see something in the attendee list. Action items come out assigned to named people rather than as a bulleted mush.
ranked.the_catch: Your recordings age out from under you. On the free tier history is 30 days; on Pro, recordings are kept one year. If you picked Circleback because you wanted an auditable record of what a client agreed to, the audit trail expires on a schedule set by how much you pay, and the cheapest fix is a $35/seat Enterprise contract. There is also no individual-priced tier below $15/seat, so a solo user pays team money.
ranked.wrong_for: People who mostly take notes in internal meetings and want the best-written summary for the lowest money — use Granola. People whose conversations legally cannot leave their own machines — use anarlog.

ranked.name: Granola
ranked.one_liner: Best notes on the list; also the easiest way to record someone silently
ranked.use_it_when: Internal meetings, one-to-ones and calls with colleagues who already know you take notes, on a Mac or Windows machine you control.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $14-$35/user/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Basic free (AI notes, AI chat, shared folders, templates, multi-language, model-training opt-out — but 'limited meeting history', with no number given on the pricing page). Business $14/user/mo adds unlimited history, advanced models, HubSpot/Notion/Slack/Attio/Affinity/Zapier, MCP and API. Enterprise $35/user/mo adds SSO, org-wide auto-deletion periods, org-wide training opt-out and org-wide notification that Granola is in use. No annual discount stated on the page.
ranked.good_at: It merges what you typed with what was said, which is a genuinely different product from a transcript summariser and produces the most readable notes here. It stores no audio file on desktop — transcript and your notes only — so there is simply less to leak or subpoena. No bot joins the call, so no dead-eyed 'Notetaker' avatar sitting in your client's participant list. Works across Zoom, Meet and Teams because it listens to device audio rather than integrating per-platform, and there is a mobile app for in-person meetings.
ranked.the_catch: The bot-free design is the legal problem, not the feature. Because nothing joins the call, the other participants get no indication whatsoever that they are being transcribed — and org-wide notification that Granola is being used is an Enterprise-only control at $35/seat. In California, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Washington, Massachusetts, Maryland, Florida and the other all-party-consent states, that is precisely the fact pattern regulators and plaintiffs' lawyers are pointing at. Second catch: by default Granola trains on anonymised customer data to improve the product. You can opt out in Settings, but it is opt-out, not opt-in, and it is off by default only for Enterprise.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone recording externals in a two-party-consent state without a separate disclosure habit — use Fathom, which puts a notice in the chat. Anyone in a regulated industry needing a BAA — use Circleback.

ranked.name: Fathom
ranked.one_liner: The most honest about being in the room, and free for real
ranked.use_it_when: Sales and client calls where you want the recording to be obviously a recording, and you do not want to pay anything to start.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $15-$29/user/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free $0 with unlimited recordings, unlimited storage and unlimited recording length — but chronological summaries only. Premium $15/user/mo unlocks the 14 meeting-type summary templates, AI action items and follow-up emails. Team Edition $19/user/mo adds cross-team search and unlimited CRM sync (Premium caps CRM sync at 3 users per email domain). Team Edition Pro $29/user/mo. Prices read at fathom.video/pricing on 2026-08-29; the page did not display a separate annual rate, and third-party pricing trackers quote different figures — assume the monthly number is what you pay unless sales says otherwise.
ranked.good_at: Consent transparency, by some distance. Fathom's own documentation states there is no way to silently record: the bot is visible in the participant list, a recording banner shows and cannot be auto-hidden, newer versions post a notice in the meeting chat when recording starts, and the notetaker's display name is customisable so it can read as a recorder. There is an 'Auto Request Recording Consent' setting that emails external attendees in advance, and if anyone declines, auto-record switches itself off. A bot-free desktop mode exists too. The free tier is a working product, not a demo.
ranked.the_catch: The consent email — the feature that makes Fathom defensible in an all-party-consent state — is off by default, must be turned on per user (or org-wide on Team), and only fires 24 hours before the meeting. Same-day meetings, which is most of them, send nothing at all. And if attendees simply do not reply, Fathom joins and records anyway. So the compliance story you are buying is one you have to configure and then still cannot rely on for anything booked this morning. On the free tier, the summary you get is a chronological dump; the useful templates are a paid upgrade.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who finds a visible bot socially awkward in client calls — use Granola or Circleback's bot-free mode. Anyone needing HIPAA cover — use Circleback.

ranked.name: anarlog
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed, runs on your machine, nothing leaves unless you say so
ranked.use_it_when: Your legal or security team has already said no to every cloud notetaker, or you are under NDA and the transcript genuinely cannot go to a third party.
ranked.cost: Free and open source. Optional cloud $15-$20/user/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: The desktop app is free and MIT-licensed; bring your own API key, or run transcription and summarisation entirely locally via Ollama, LM Studio or an OpenAI-compatible server. Optional hosted extras: Pro $15/mo or $150/yr for individuals; Team $20/person/mo or $200/person/yr; Enterprise custom. Verified MIT in the repo LICENSE file — that means commercial use, forking and reselling are all permitted for the community app.
ranked.good_at: It is the only option here where you can prove, by reading the source, that audio never left the machine. Transcripts, notes, attachments and recordings sit in a local SQLite database and plain files you can read and export as Markdown. No bot joins the call — it captures device audio. Cloud sync is opt-in rather than the default. Roughly 9,000 GitHub stars and active commits, so it is not an abandoned weekend project.
ranked.the_catch: Three names in about a year. It launched as Hyprnote, became Char, and is now anarlog — and char.com is a different product the same team is now building, which is where their attention is. The repo's own note confirms it: anarlog is the community app, char is what the team is building. Beyond the branding churn: macOS is the real platform, Windows x64 and Linux builds are labelled beta, on-device transcription models are only supported on some Macs, and the source-visible enterprise components are commercially licensed, not MIT — so 'MIT-licensed' covers the community app and not everything in the repo. Local transcription quality is below what the cloud vendors ship.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants notes to appear in Slack, Notion and HubSpot without configuring anything — use Circleback or Fireflies. Windows-first teams should wait for the beta label to come off.

ranked.name: Fireflies.ai
ranked.one_liner: Loudest about recording, cheapest at scale, most fiddly quotas
ranked.use_it_when: A large team needs one searchable archive of every call wired into a CRM, and per-seat cost across fifty people matters more than note elegance.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Paid $10-$39/seat/mo depending on billing term.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free $0: unlimited transcription (asterisked on the page), limited AI summaries, 400 minutes of storage per team, 20 AI credits. Pro $18/seat/mo monthly or $10/seat/mo annual, 8,000 minutes storage per seat. Business $29 monthly or $19 annual, unlimited storage, 30 AI credits, conversation intelligence. Enterprise $39/seat, annual only, 50 AI credits, SSO+SCIM, audit logs, HIPAA, custom data retention. Fireflies states customer data is never used for AI training.
ranked.good_at: Disclosure. It is the noisiest tool here about the fact that it is recording: a pinned message in the meeting chat, a spoken audio notice about ten seconds after the desktop app starts capturing, an 'AI Taking Notes' camera watermark, an advance email to participants an hour before with an opt-out link, and in-meeting slash commands so anyone can pause or eject the bot mid-call. On Zoom and the Google Meet SDK, participants see the platform's own recording approval pop-up. For an all-party-consent jurisdiction, that stack of signals is the strongest evidentiary position on this list.
ranked.the_catch: The advertised price is the annual price. Pro is $10 on the pricing page and $18 if you actually pay monthly — an 80% premium for not committing a year up front — and Enterprise cannot be bought monthly at all. Then there are AI credits, a second currency layered on top of seats: 20 on Free and Pro, 30 on Business, 50 on Enterprise, and running out mid-month is how people discover them. Storage is capped in minutes, not meetings, so a team on the free tier burns 400 minutes in about five long calls. Custom data retention and private storage are Enterprise-only.
ranked.wrong_for: Solo users and small teams who will never touch the analytics — the free tier's 400-minute team cap makes it a trial, so use Fathom's free tier instead. Anyone who wants a bot-free, discreet recorder — use Granola.

also_considered.name: Otter.ai
also_considered.why_not: Otter's own privacy page says it de-identifies user data and trains its models on it, with no opt-out mentioned; and on 13 August 2026 a judge let the core Federal Wiretap Act, CIPA s.631 and Illinois BIPA voiceprint claims in In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation proceed to discovery, on allegations it took consent from hosts only. Free tier is 300 minutes a month; Pro $16.99/mo or $8.33 annual; Business $30/mo or $19.99 annual.

also_considered.name: Zoom AI Companion / ZoomMate
also_considered.why_not: Rebranded and repackaged during 2026 — what was bundled free with paid Zoom now reads as a separately-subscribed product with a 3-summaries-per-month free allowance. Could not read a reliable per-seat price at Zoom's own pages, so check current pricing before assuming it is included in what you already pay.

also_considered.name: Meetily
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely self-hosted and open source, 100% local with Whisper/Parakeet and Ollama summarisation on macOS and Windows. Ranked below anarlog only because setup is heavier and the notes are rawer; pick it if you want Rust and local-only with no cloud tier existing at all.

also_considered.name: Read AI
also_considered.why_not: Adds engagement scoring and sentiment on participants, which is a second consent problem stacked on the recording one — hard to justify to an external attendee in an all-party-consent state.

also_considered.name: tl;dv
also_considered.why_not: Solid recorder with good clipping, but its comparison content ranks aggressively against every tool on this list, which makes independent assessment of its own claims difficult and the roundups unusable.

also_considered.name: Airgram
also_considered.why_not: Discontinued — shut down, migrate off it. Named here only because it still appears in old roundups and comparison tables.

watch_list: In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation, No. 5:25-cv-06911 (N.D. Cal.) reaching discovery or a class certification ruling — a finding that host-only consent is insufficient would force every bot-based vendor to change defaults, and would push the bot-free tools to add participant notification.
Whether Granola makes participant notification available below the $35/seat Enterprise tier. If it does, it takes the top spot.
Whether Fathom flips 'Auto Request Recording Consent' to on by default and fires it for same-day meetings, which is currently the hole in its otherwise best-in-class consent tooling.
anarlog's Windows and Linux builds losing the beta label, and whether the team's attention stays on it now that char.com is their commercial product.
Any vendor shipping per-jurisdiction consent behaviour — automatically requiring all-party opt-in when an attendee's domain or dial-in maps to a two-party-consent state. Nobody does this yet.

Zoom and Microsoft folding competent notetaking into the base subscription. Native platform capture with the platform's own recording banner is the strongest consent posture available, and it would make most of this list a nice-to-have.

research.deep-research.question: I want a researched report with citations that survive checking. Which deep research tool actually gets its sources right?

method.how: Ranked on two things a buyer can check: how much the tool actually reads, and whether the citations it attaches hold up. Where an independent benchmark measured citation accuracy at product level I used it; where only model-level papers exist I said so. Nothing in this category is good yet - the best published figure for 'does this source support this sentence' is Claude Opus 4.5 at 76.8% factual accuracy in the May 2026 'Cited but Not Verified' paper, meaning roughly one citation in four still fails a check even at the top. Price and readable quotas broke ties, and two of the big vendors have quietly stopped publishing quotas at all.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No reports were run, no citations were hand-checked by me. Prices, quotas and vendor claims read from vendors' own pages on 2026-08-29; benchmark figures read from the papers and leaderboards named in blind_note. Where a vendor would not show a number at source, this entry says so rather than guessing.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: Four independent sources used. DeepResearch Bench (arXiv 2506.11763) is the only one that scored the shipping consumer products head to head - Gemini Deep Research 48.88 RACE / 81.44% citation accuracy / 111.21 effective citations, OpenAI Deep Research 46.98 / 77.96% / 40.79, Perplexity Deep Research 42.25 / 90.24% / 31.26, Grok Deeper Search 40.24 / 83.59% / 8.15 - and it dates from June 2025, so treat it as a year stale. DeepResearch Bench II (2026, 9,430 rubrics over 132 expert reports) puts OpenAI o3 at 45.40, Gemini at 44.60 and 41.98, Perplexity Research at 38.58, but its top five are all vendor systems you have probably never heard of, which is what a leaderboard looks like when vendors submit their own runs. On citations specifically: arXiv 2604.03173 (April 2026) found 3-13% of cited URLs were fabricated and 5-18% did not resolve, with Gemini 2.5 Pro Deep Research worst at 13.3% and Claude models best at 3.0-3.2%; arXiv 2605.06635 (May 2026) found the link usually works and the page is usually on-topic, but the claim is only actually supported 24-77% of the time depending on model. Beyond those four papers, search results for this category are almost entirely vendors ranking themselves and affiliate listicles - treat any 'best deep research tool' page, including the ones in the sources below, as marketing until you find the primary number.

ranked.name: Gemini Deep Research
ranked.one_liner: Reads the most, cites the most, fabricates the most links
ranked.use_it_when: You want the widest sweep of a topic and you are going to click through the citations anyway. Also the only one of the majors with a usable free tier for this.
ranked.cost: Free tier included. Paid $4.99-$199.99/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Deep Research is listed as available on the Free plan (Google warns it 'may be unavailable during periods of high demand'). Google AI Plus $4.99/mo, AI Pro $19.99/mo, AI Ultra from $99.99/mo with a $199.99/mo 20x option - all read from gemini.google/subscriptions on 2026-08-29. Google's own subscription and help pages give no per-day Deep Research count, only vague multipliers ('2x', '4x', 'up to 20x higher usage'). 9to5Google reported the actual caps in April 2026 as 3/day on Plus, 20/day on Pro, 75/day on Ultra 5x and 200/day on Ultra 20x, and listed Plus at $7.99 rather than the $4.99 Google shows today - so the quota figures may have moved too. Google does not publish a report length limit.
ranked.good_at: Volume of grounded material. On DeepResearch Bench it produced 111.21 effective citations per report against OpenAI's 40.79 and Perplexity's 31.26, and took the top RACE score at 48.88. If your worry is that the report missed a whole branch of the topic, this is the one that misses least. Exports straight to a Google Doc with links intact.
ranked.the_catch: It is the worst offender on fabricated links. The April 2026 reference-hallucination paper (arXiv 2604.03173) measured Gemini 2.5 Pro Deep Research at 13.3% hallucinated URLs, the highest of every system tested, against 3.0-3.2% for Claude. Wide reading plus invented citations is the exact combination that makes a report look authoritative and fail review. Second catch: Google has stopped publishing Deep Research quotas in its own docs, so on day three you find out what your cap is by hitting it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who will be judged on the bibliography. If a bad citation costs you, use Elicit for academic work or Claude Research (also_considered) for anything you will verify by hand.

ranked.name: ChatGPT deep research
ranked.one_liner: The balanced default; nobody will publish its quota
ranked.use_it_when: A hard multi-hop question where the answer has to be assembled from several sources that do not cite each other, and you want a long structured report at the end.
ranked.cost: Limited free tier. Plus $20/mo. Pro $100 or $200/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: ChatGPT Plus is $20/month billed monthly (OpenAI help centre, read 2026-08-29). Pro now comes in two tiers: 'Pro $100 unlocks 5x higher usage than Plus' and 'Pro $200 unlocks 20x usage than Plus', both including deep research (OpenAI help centre). Free and Go plans get 'Limited deep research' per the pricing page; the Go price would not render at source, so check current pricing. OpenAI no longer publishes deep research task counts anywhere - its own help article now says only 'Deep research usage varies by plan. Your in-product usage counter shows your remaining tasks.'
ranked.good_at: Depth on genuinely hard questions. OpenAI claims 26.6% on Humanity's Last Exam and 72.57% (cons@64) on GAIA for the model powering it, and it takes 5-30 minutes per run reading what it describes as 'hundreds of online sources'. In DeepResearch Bench II's 2026 rubric scoring, OpenAI o3 was the highest-placed of the mainstream consumer products at 45.40. Report structure is the best of the five - it reads like something a person wrote.
ranked.the_catch: You cannot budget it. There is no published per-plan quota, only an in-product counter, and when you exhaust the full version you are moved onto a 'lightweight' deep research that OpenAI does not distinguish clearly in the output - so a shallower report arrives looking exactly like a deep one. OpenAI's own launch page also admits it 'currently shows weakness in confidence calibration' and 'may struggle with distinguishing authoritative information from rumors'.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs a fixed monthly number of runs to plan around - Gemini Pro's reported 20/day is at least a number. Anyone doing literature work should use Elicit.

ranked.name: Advanced Deep Research
ranked.one_liner: Fewest citations, but the highest share of them stick
ranked.use_it_when: You want a fast, tight, mostly-correct answer with sources in a couple of minutes rather than a thirty-minute essay - and when precision matters more than coverage.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro $20/mo. Max $200/mo or $2,000/yr.
ranked.pricing_detail: Perplexity Max is '$200/monthly or $2000/annually' per its own help article; Pro is stated at $20/month in Perplexity's Max announcement post. The public pricing page would not render at source. No plan publishes a Research or Deep Research quota anywhere - the Pro help article says only 'a high volume of daily searches', and the free tier gets 'a limited number of answers per day' with no figure. Max includes unlimited Labs. Note the annual Max price is 10x the monthly, i.e. no annual discount at all.
ranked.good_at: Citation precision per source cited. On DeepResearch Bench it scored 90.24% citation accuracy, the best of the four products measured, and completes most runs in 2-4 minutes against OpenAI's 5-30. Advanced Deep Research adds a code sandbox for calculations and can read documents you upload.
ranked.the_catch: It is thin. That 90.24% is measured over 31.26 effective citations per report against Gemini's 111.21 - it is accurate partly because it commits to less, and it placed last of the mainstream products on DeepResearch Bench II at 38.58. Perplexity's own page for Advanced Deep Research claims it 'matches or outperforms competitors' on industry benchmarks while publishing no scores at all, which is the tell. And no published quota on any tier means a $200/mo Max subscription buys you an unspecified amount of the thing you bought it for.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone writing a long report that has to survey a whole field - use Gemini for coverage. Anyone who needs the annual plan to save money; it does not.

ranked.name: Elicit
ranked.one_liner: The only one whose citations you can actually verify
ranked.use_it_when: The topic is covered by published research and a wrong citation would be fatal - evidence reviews, clinical or scientific claims, anything a reviewer will check.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro $49/mo ($588/yr). Scale $169/mo ($2,028/yr).
ranked.pricing_detail: Basic free: 'limited usage' for Research Agent and Research Reports, unlimited search over 138 million papers. Pro $49/mo or $588/yr, with a systematic review workflow that screens 5,000 papers. Scale $169/mo or $2,028/yr for '5x usage' and 30 extraction columns at a time. Enterprise custom, screening 40,000 papers and 40 columns. Elicit describes every tier's allowance as 'limited', 'standard' or '5x usage' and publishes no credit counts, so you cannot work out how many reports a month you get before paying.
ranked.good_at: Grounding. It extracts from the full text of specific papers into a table you can inspect row by row, so a claim traces back to a passage rather than to a URL. Elicit claims 99.4% extraction accuracy (1,502 of 1,511 data points) - vendor's own figure, not independently replicated. Nothing else on this list lets you audit the evidence at that granularity.
ranked.the_catch: It only knows academic literature. Ask it about a market, a company, a product or anything from the last six months and it has nothing to read - there is no web crawl behind it. At $49/mo it is also more than twice the price of the general tools, and the '5x usage' at $169 is meaningless without a base number to multiply.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone researching a market, a technology's commercial landscape, or current events. Use Gemini or OpenAI for that.

ranked.name: GPT Researcher
ranked.one_liner: Self-hostable, Apache-2.0, and only as good as your keys
ranked.use_it_when: The material cannot leave your infrastructure, or you want to control the crawl depth, source list and report length yourself instead of accepting a vendor's defaults.
ranked.cost: Free and open source (Apache-2.0). You pay LLM and search API costs, ~$0.40 per run per the README.
ranked.pricing_detail: Apache-2.0 licence, so commercial use is permitted. No subscription and no quota - the only cap is your own API spend. The README states 'Takes ~5 minutes per deep research' and 'costs ~$0.4 per research (using o3-mini on high reasoning effort)'; that figure is from the maintainers, on one model, and will move with whatever model you point it at. Defaults are breadth 4, depth 2, concurrency 4, with a recommended total_words of 2500; multi-agent runs produce a 5-6 page report. You also need a search API key on top of the LLM key.
ranked.good_at: Control and privacy. It is the only entry where you set the number of sources, the recursion depth and the report length yourself, run it inside your own network, and see every prompt. Aggregates 20+ sources per run by default and produces reports over 2,000 words.
ranked.the_catch: Its citation quality is entirely inherited from the model you plug in, and open systems are measurably behind here. The August 2026 error-localisation paper (arXiv 2608.24306) measured citation recall on three open deep research stacks at 58.7%, 28.5% and 7.1%, and traced 84.7% of one system's final-report errors to the orchestrator rather than the model. You are also running and debugging a Python agent, not opening a tab.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants a report in the next ten minutes without setting up two API keys. Use Gemini's free tier instead.

also_considered.name: Claude Research (Anthropic)
also_considered.why_not: Best measured citation hygiene of anything here - 3.0-3.2% fabricated URLs in arXiv 2604.03173, and Claude Opus 4.5 topped factual support at 76.8% in arXiv 2605.06635 - but those are model-level results, not tests of the Research product, and Research has no quota of its own: Anthropic's docs say only that it 'can use up your limits faster'. Pro $20/mo ($17 annual), Max from $100/mo. Pick it if you will verify every claim yourself.

also_considered.name: Grok Deeper Search (xAI)
also_considered.why_not: Thinnest sourcing of the four products on DeepResearch Bench: 8.15 effective citations per report against Gemini's 111.21, at 40.24 RACE. Fine for a quick look, not for a report.

also_considered.name: Consensus
also_considered.why_not: Cheap and honest about its limits - free tier gives 10 Pro Analyses, 10 Study Snapshots and 10 Ask Paper messages a month, Premium is $8.99/mo or $108/yr over 200M+ papers - but it is a search and summary layer, not a report generator. Elicit does the report.

also_considered.name: Undermind
also_considered.why_not: Strong recall on academic literature and the cheapest paid tier of any specialist here ($16/mo, billed annually), but the price is annual-only at that rate and it publishes no numbers for papers read or run time beyond 'hundreds' and 'a few minutes'.

also_considered.name: AI21 DeepResearch
also_considered.why_not: Tops DeepResearch Bench II at 64.38, well clear of every consumer product on that leaderboard. No consumer price readable at source on 2026-08-29, so it fails this list's own rule about quoting numbers you can see.

watch_list: A refresh of DeepResearch Bench's product leaderboard. The head-to-head numbers ranking Gemini above OpenAI are from June 2025 and predate both vendors' current models; a rerun could swap 1 and 2 outright.
Whether OpenAI or Google restore published per-plan quotas. Both now hide them behind in-product counters and vague multipliers, and both would move up if you could budget a subscription again.

The first vendor to ship a claim-level verification pass - an automatic 'does this source actually support this sentence' check before the report is handed over. Nobody does it today, and the citation papers say roughly a quarter of citations would fail it.
Perplexity publishing actual benchmark scores for Advanced Deep Research instead of 'matches or outperforms competitors'.
Open-source citation recall closing the gap. 7.1-58.7% today per arXiv 2608.24306; the same paper got +5 points recall from trivial orchestrator fixes, so this could move fast.
Elicit adding a non-academic corpus. It would go straight to the top of this list if it could read anything other than papers.

sales.cold-email.question: Which tool actually sends personalised cold email at volume without torching my domain, and what does it really cost?

method.how: Ranked on the thing that decides outcomes: sending infrastructure and deliverability control, not template libraries or AI copy buttons. Every tool was scored on what it does about warm-up, per-mailbox throttling and inbox rotation, whether mailboxes and domains are billed separately from the seat, and how honestly the pricing page states its caps. Personalisation depth broke ties, because a great email that lands in spam is worth nothing. Be clear that no tool in this category solves deliverability for you: they all sell you a throttle and a warm-up pool, then hand you the domain reputation risk.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No inbox-placement tests were run, no campaigns were sent, no accounts were bought. Prices, caps and add-on costs were read from the vendors own pricing and help pages on 2026-08-29; where a vendor page would not render its price table, that is said plainly rather than filled in from a third-party blog.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark of cold email platforms inbox placement. None exists, and search for this category is almost entirely vendors ranking themselves: the top organic results for best cold email software 2026 include lists published by Lemlist, Saleshandy, Salesforge, Woodpecker and Amplemarket, each of which appears at or near the top of its own list. EmailToolTester runs the closest thing to recurring independent deliverability testing, but it tests newsletter ESPs, not cold outreach senders. Treat every inbox rate you see quoted, including vendors own case studies, as marketing.

ranked.name: Smartlead
ranked.one_liner: The sending engine agencies run when volume actually matters
ranked.use_it_when: You are sending from dozens or hundreds of mailboxes, need inbox rotation, per-mailbox throttles, a proper API and white-label client workspaces, and you already know how to buy and configure domains yourself.
ranked.cost: Paid $39-$379/mo (annual $32.50-$314.60/mo). Warm-up may be a $59/mo add-on on the two lower tiers.
ranked.pricing_detail: Base $39/mo (2,000 contacts, 6,000 sends), Pro $94/mo (30,000 contacts, 90,000 sends), Unlimited Smart $174/mo (unlimited contacts, 150,000 sends), Unlimited Prime $379/mo (500,000 sends, 3 SmartServers, OAuth, 3+ client workspaces). Annual billing is 17% off. Unlimited email accounts on every plan at no per-mailbox charge. Add-ons stack: SmartSenders mailboxes $3.99-$9 per mailbox/mo, SmartDelivery $49-$599/mo, SmartServers $39/server/mo, whitelabel $29/mo per client workspace, SmartDialer $9/mo, 6,000 verification credits $32 one-off.
ranked.good_at: Infrastructure control. Unlimited connected mailboxes at no per-inbox fee, mailbox rotation, per-mailbox daily caps and ramp, a real API and webhooks, and multi-workspace white-labelling that agencies genuinely use. If you want to run 300 inboxes across 80 domains and script the whole thing, this is the one built for that.
ranked.the_catch: The warm-up story does not hold together on their own site. The pricing page shows warm-up as a $59/mo add-on on Base and Pro and free only on the two Unlimited tiers, while the Smartlead FAQ page still says unlimited warm-up is included on every plan including the $39 Base. Two vendor pages, two answers, on the same day. Get it in writing before you buy. Beyond that, the $39 headline is a decoy: 6,000 sends a month is about 200 a day, and the add-on menu (mailboxes, SmartDelivery, SmartServers, whitelabel) is where the real bill lives. Support is thin at the lower tiers.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone sending under a few thousand emails a month, or anyone who wants domains and mailboxes bought for them inside the product. Use Instantly for that. If you want one seat writing genuinely bespoke emails, use lemlist.

ranked.name: Instantly
ranked.one_liner: Buys your domains and inboxes for you, then sends from them
ranked.use_it_when: You are starting outbound from nothing and want domains, pre-warmed mailboxes, a lead database and the sender in one account rather than assembling four vendors.
ranked.cost: Standalone sending from $47/mo; bundles $94-$555/mo. Mailboxes $4-$10/mo each, domains $15/yr, extra.
ranked.pricing_detail: Standalone Outreach: Growth $47/mo (1,000 contacts, 5,000 sends), Hypergrowth $97/mo (25,000 contacts, 125,000 sends), Lightspeed $358/mo (100,000 contacts, 500,000 sends). Bundles that add the 450M lead database and AI agents: Starter $94/mo, Scale $194/mo, Agency $555/mo, Enterprise custom. Lead credits are a separate line: Nano $9/mo (150 credits) up to Hyper from $197/mo. Unlimited email accounts and warm-up on all plans. Infrastructure is billed apart: domains $15/yr, done-for-you Google account $5/mo, pre-warmed Google account $10/mo, done-for-you Airmail account $4/mo. Annual saves 10%.
ranked.good_at: Removing the setup wall. You can buy domains and mailboxes inside the product at $4-$10 per inbox per month, connect them without touching DNS by hand, and be sending in an afternoon. Unlimited connected accounts and warm-up are genuinely included on every plan, and the unified inbox is the least annoying of the five.
ranked.the_catch: The contact limit is not what you think. Instantly counts uploaded contacts cumulatively against your plan cap rather than resetting each month, so on Growth the 1,000 uploaded contacts is a lifetime ceiling you hit and then pay to raise, not a monthly allowance. Separately, the three-way split between Outreach plans, Credits plans and Bundles means the price you were quoted in a review is rarely the price you end up paying, and their own help centre warns that done-for-you mailboxes are paused automatically if you drop the Outreach plan. You are also renting reputation on domains you did not season yourself.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs deep per-mailbox control, scripted operations or agency white-labelling. Use Smartlead. Anyone whose value is research-heavy personalisation rather than volume should spend the money on Clay instead.

ranked.name: Clay
ranked.one_liner: Actual personalisation at scale; deliverability is still your problem
ranked.use_it_when: The email has to reference something true about each company, and you want the research, enrichment waterfall and the AI writing step in one table rather than a spreadsheet plus three scrapers.
ranked.cost: Free tier (100 data credits, 500 actions/mo). Paid from $167/mo; Growth from $446/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 100 data credits and 500 actions a month. Launch: from $167/mo monthly billing, 3,000 data credits and 15,000 actions a month. Growth: from $446/mo monthly billing, 6,000 data credits and 40,000 actions a month. Enterprise custom, annual commitment. Annual billing is materially cheaper and the page also quotes annualised figures alongside monthly ones, which makes the tiers hard to read. Seats are unlimited on all plans. Credits are priced on a slider from roughly $0.05 each and fall with volume, so the plan price and the credit price are two separate decisions. Domains and mailboxes for the native Clay Sequencer are bought as an extra.
ranked.good_at: Per-lead research that no sequencer can do. Waterfall enrichment across many data providers so you pay only for the hit, AI columns that read a website or a job ad and write a real first line, and now a native Sequencer so the send does not have to leave the platform.
ranked.the_catch: The bill is a variable, not a number. Data credits and actions are metered separately, an AI column that reruns over 5,000 rows burns both, and it is genuinely easy to spend a plans monthly allowance in an afternoon of debugging a table. The learning curve is steep enough that most teams need a contractor for the first month. And Clay does nothing for domain reputation: the Sequencer is young compared with Smartlead or Instantly, so many teams still pay for Clay and a sender.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose problem is throughput rather than relevance, or anyone on a fixed budget who cannot tolerate a variable bill. Use Smartlead or Instantly and write five good templates instead.

ranked.name: lemlist
ranked.one_liner: Per-seat multichannel for reps who write like humans
ranked.use_it_when: A small sales team runs email plus LinkedIn plus calls against a few hundred high-value accounts, and each rep needs their own identity, inbox and task list.
ranked.cost: $69/user/mo ($55 annual). Multichannel $109/user/mo ($87 annual). Enterprise quote.
ranked.pricing_detail: Email plan $69 per user/mo, $55 with annual billing: 50,000 emails/mo, email and phone finder, 650M lead database, unified inbox, deliverability hub. Multichannel $109 per user/mo, $87 annual: adds 5 senders per user, LinkedIn, SMS and WhatsApp automation, a dialler, unlimited emails and messages. Enterprise is custom for teams of 5+ and adds SSO/SAML and 5+ senders per user. lemwarm warm-up is included on all plans. Enrichment is pay-per-success on top: email verification about $0.05 a credit, phone numbers about $0.20, intent signals from 20 credits (web visits) to 400+ (LinkedIn engagement).
ranked.good_at: Sequence craft and multichannel in one timeline. Conditional steps, image and landing-page personalisation, LinkedIn and call tasks sitting in the same sequence as the email, and lemwarm included rather than upsold. It is the most pleasant of the five to actually write in.
ranked.the_catch: Per-seat pricing is the wrong shape for this job. Volume outreach means many sending identities, and lemlist charges you per user while capping senders per user (5 on Multichannel), so scaling sending forces you to buy seats for people who do not exist. Three seats on Multichannel is $327/mo before a single enrichment credit, against $174/mo for unlimited contacts on Smartlead. The intent-signal credits are also priced high enough that a curious afternoon costs real money.
ranked.wrong_for: High-volume agencies and anyone running more than about ten mailboxes. Use Smartlead or Saleshandy, where mailboxes are free and you pay for sends.

ranked.name: Warmbly
ranked.one_liner: The only real self-hostable option, and it is very early
ranked.use_it_when: Your prospect data legally cannot sit on a US SaaS, or you already run mail infrastructure and want campaigns, warm-up and a unified inbox on your own boxes under a permissive licence.
ranked.cost: Free forever self-hosted (Apache 2.0). Cloud is not launched; announced from $23/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Self-hosting is free with no licence fee. Apache 2.0, so commercial use is explicitly permitted, including running it for clients. Stack is Postgres, Redis and an event bus with one binary per service. The hosted cloud is advertised as coming soon with a free tier of 10 mailboxes with warm-up and paid plans from $23/mo for 150 sends a day; that pricing is not yet live, so treat it as a plan, not a price. Your real cost is infrastructure: domains, mailboxes or SMTP relays, IPs, and the hours to run them.
ranked.good_at: Being the only credible answer when the data cannot leave your infrastructure. Apache 2.0 with no open-core bait, distributed workers across multiple IPs, pluggable KMS and storage, and warm-up plus sending in the same self-hosted system rather than a warm-up tool bolted to a script.
ranked.the_catch: It is barely a product yet. As of 2026-08-29 the GitHub repository shows 1 star and no published releases, and the cloud version is still coming soon, so you are the QA team, the on-call and the deliverability expert. There is no vendor to escalate to when Microsoft starts rejecting your mail. Nobody has independently verified its warm-up pool, which for a warm-up network is the whole question: a small pool is a fingerprint, not a reputation.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone without a devops person, and anyone whose data has no residency constraint. Use Smartlead or Instantly, which cost less than one day of engineering time a month.

also_considered.name: Saleshandy
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely cheap for what it includes ($34-$149/mo on annual billing, unlimited mailboxes and warm-up), but its own pricing page rendered the Scale send cap two different ways on the same day, and the mailbox infrastructure add-on is $3.49 per mailbox/mo with a 25-mailbox minimum plus $14/yr per domain.

also_considered.name: QuickMail
also_considered.why_not: Solid and honest ($49/$99/$299 per month, unlimited senders, MailFlow warm-up free), but no annual pricing is shown on the page and the lead data and AI tooling are thinner than the top three.

also_considered.name: Apollo.io
also_considered.why_not: Data and sending in one account with a free-forever Starter plan, but its pricing table would not render for us on 2026-08-29, so we will not quote a number. Note the free plan only connects Gmail mailboxes; Microsoft and other providers need a paid plan.

also_considered.name: GMass
also_considered.why_not: The cheapest way to send from inside Gmail ($20-$49/mo on annual billing), but the free plan is a 7-day trial capped at 50 emails per rolling 24 hours, and you are hard-capped by Gmail itself at 500/day (personal) or 2,000/day (Workspace).

also_considered.name: Woodpecker
also_considered.why_not: Usage-based at $7 per 100 contacted prospects is fair and legible, but every piece of infrastructure is a separate line: Google/Microsoft mailboxes $6/mo each, third-party $4/mo, extra warm-ups $5/mo each, LinkedIn $29/mo, API and webhooks $20/mo, agency panel $27/mo per client.

also_considered.name: Amplemarket
also_considered.why_not: Sales-led pricing with no public numbers on the vendor page, which fails the basic test for this list. Its blog also ranks itself in its own best-of comparisons.

watch_list: Microsoft tightening tenant outbound limits. The Tenant External Recipient Rate Limit (TERRL), which rolled out to all Exchange Online tenants through April and May 2025, caps external recipients per tenant on a 24-hour sliding window using 500 x (licences^0.7) + 9,500, with trial tenants capped at 5,000, and a separate per-mailbox external recipient limit followed. Any further tightening makes the buy-lots-of-M365-mailboxes strategy that these tools assume much more expensive.

The Exchange Online basic-auth SMTP retirement. Cold email tools that connect M365 mailboxes over SMTP with a password are on borrowed time; the timeline has already slipped more than once. Check whether your tool supports OAuth for M365 before you buy 200 licences.

Whether Google and Microsoft start pattern-matching warm-up pool traffic as artificial engagement. Every tool here sells warm-up and none publishes independent evidence it improves inbox placement. If either provider starts treating pool mail as a negative signal, the whole category reprices overnight.

Clay Sequencer maturing into a real sender. If Clay makes sending as reliable as Smartlead, the research plus sender split that most teams pay for twice collapses into one bill, and Clay moves up this list.
Warmbly reaching a tagged 1.0 or launching its cloud. A maintained open-source sender with a real community would be the first genuine answer for regulated buyers, and would push it above lemlist.

Enforcement against B2B cold email in the EU. Germany treats unsolicited commercial email, including business-to-business, as unlawful without prior consent under UWG section 7, and GDPR still requires a lawful basis, a privacy notice and honouring objections. A serious regulator action against a cold email sender would change what these tools can safely be used for in Europe.
