sales.lead-search.question: I know exactly who my ideal customer is. Which tool actually finds them, exports them, and does not bankrupt me on credits?

method.how: Four things drove the order, in this sequence. First, can you read the price at source without a sales call — three of the best-known products in this category cannot be priced without talking to someone, and that is a ranking penalty, not a neutral fact. Second, what a credit actually buys, because 'credit' is not a unit: Apollo's own API docs charge 1 credit for an email and 8 for a mobile; Lusha charges 1 and 10; Ocean.io charges 0.2 credits just to look at a search result. Third, can the list leave the building — Clay bills exporting as an action, Sales Navigator has no bulk export at all. Fourth, provenance, because the CNIL fined Kaspr EUR 240,000 in December 2024 for collecting LinkedIn contact details, and you are the one sending the emails. Nobody wins on data accuracy here, because no accuracy claim in this category is independently verifiable — every figure below is the vendor's own.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No searches were run inside any platform, no exported list was checked against reality, and no accuracy claim was verified. Prices, credit costs and plan limits were read from each vendor's own pages on 2026-08-29. Apollo's pricing page renders its plan table in JavaScript that did not extract, so Apollo's prices are quoted from Apollo's own comparison pages on apollo.io instead. LinkedIn's help page on exporting from Sales Navigator blocks automated fetching, so nothing about its export rules is quoted from source here.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark of B2B contact-data accuracy. Nobody has published a reproducible test that buys the same 1,000 ICP-matched contacts from Apollo, Cognism, ZoomInfo and Lusha and checks the bounce and connect rates. Every number you will read — Apollo's '98% email accuracy', Cognism's '45% correct person picked up' — is vendor-published or vendor-commissioned, and the tests behind them are not open. Search is actively hostile here: queries for 'Apollo pricing 2026' and 'Clay pricing 2026' returned pages one and two composed almost entirely of competing data vendors publishing pricing critiques of each other, each ending in their own signup. Treat any comparison blog in this category as an advert until proven otherwise.

ranked.name: Apollo.io
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest readable price on a big database; phones cost dearly
ranked.use_it_when: You want a self-serve list of ICP-matched contacts this afternoon, on a published per-seat price, with a free tier to sanity-check the data before paying anything.
ranked.cost: Free plan. Paid $49-$119/user/mo, annual billing. Organization needs 3 seats.
ranked.pricing_detail: From Apollo's own comparison pages: Free $0 with 900 credits/year; Basic $49/user/month with 30,000 credits/year; Professional $79/user/month with 48,000 credits/year; Organization $119/user/month with a 3-user minimum and 72,000 credits/year. Those are annual-billing figures. Apollo's credits page states credits expire at the end of each billing cycle and do not roll over; annual plans unlock the year's credits up front. Trials come with 50 credits and 5 mobile credits. Apollo's pricing FAQ describes 'unlimited' plans as governed by a fair-use policy and mentions a 10,000-credits-per-account-per-month limit for non-paying accounts.
ranked.good_at: Being the only large database in this category with prices you can read and a free tier you can test before committing. Filters, sequences, a browser extension and a CRM sit in one product, so a solo founder can go from ICP definition to first send without buying three tools. Apollo claims 240M+ people and 30M+ companies, and 98% email accuracy via its 'Living Data Network' — both are Apollo's own figures with no independent check.
ranked.the_catch: Mobile numbers are the trap. Apollo's own API documentation prices people enrichment at '1-9 credits per person... 1 credit for demographics/email; +8 credits if mobile phone is returned', and its waterfall phone enrichment at 'typically 8-25 credits' reaching '45+'. So a 5,000-strong list with mobiles can consume 40,000-125,000 credits — more than the entire annual allowance of the $49 Basic plan, and any credits you do not burn die at the end of the cycle. Budget on phone credits, not on the seat price.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose targets are UK or EU and who needs mobile numbers that connect — use Cognism, which screens against DNC registries. Anyone whose ICP is a behaviour rather than a firmographic ('hiring two SDRs', 'just switched CRM') — use Clay.

ranked.name: Clay
ranked.one_liner: Build any ICP filter you can describe; billing is two currencies
ranked.use_it_when: Your ideal customer is defined by a signal no database has a checkbox for, and you would rather assemble a list from 150-odd providers plus scraped and AI-derived columns than accept someone else's filters.
ranked.cost: Free plan. Launch $167/mo monthly, from $54/mo annual. Growth $446/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 500 actions/mo, 100 data credits/mo, 200 rows per table. Launch: $167/mo billed monthly or 'starts at $54/mo' billed annually, from 15,000 actions/mo and 3,000 data credits/mo, up to 50,000 rows per table. Growth: $446/mo monthly or 'starts at $185/mo' annually, from 40,000 actions/mo and 6,000 data credits/mo, unlimited rows. Enterprise is custom, annual commitment. All plans state unlimited seats. Actions reset monthly and do not roll over; data credits roll over up to twice the monthly amount on Launch and Growth. Data credits start at $0.05 each and fall with volume.
ranked.good_at: Expressing an ICP that does not fit a dropdown. Waterfall enrichment runs several providers in sequence so you pay for a mobile once rather than four times, and AI columns let you qualify on things like 'does this company's careers page list a RevOps role'. Nothing else here gets close on the flexibility of the definition itself.
ranked.the_catch: Two meters run at once and the cheap headline is the annual minimum, not the plan. Clay counts an action for 'enriching data, running a table, calling an AI model, sending data to a third-party system, or exporting data' — so re-running a table after fixing a formula, and exporting the result, both cost you, and actions never roll over. Data credits are a separate pot bought from the marketplace. The $54/mo figure is the bottom of a slider on annual billing; the same volume billed monthly is $167. First-month bill shock in this product is normal, not exceptional.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants a list rather than a system. If your ICP is 'US SaaS companies, 50-200 staff, VP Sales', Clay is a spreadsheet-shaped tax on a query Apollo answers for $49. Non-technical teams with no time to learn it should not start here.

ranked.name: Cognism
ranked.one_liner: The compliance-first pick for UK and EU calling; price is a phone call
ranked.use_it_when: You are dialling European mobiles, your legal team asks where the data came from, and you need an answer better than 'publicly available sources'.
ranked.cost: No public price. Quote only. Packages bundle 5 seats.
ranked.pricing_detail: Cognism's pricing page states no monetary figures. Two prospecting packages, Standard and Pro, each 'with 5 seats included', plus optional CRM Enrichment and Data-as-a-Service add-ons via API or bulk delivery. The credit rule is stated plainly: '1 credit = 1 revealed contact' with 'no charge for viewing previously revealed contacts'. Credits are allocated per seat subscription with more available to buy. Pricing is 'tailored based on the product you need, your team setup and how you plan to use the platform' — that means a sales call.
ranked.good_at: Provenance and phone hygiene, which is the part of this category that gets people fined. Cognism states it scrubs against DNC registries in the US, Australia, UK (TPS/CTPS), France, Germany and other European countries, covering 15 territories, and markets a 'GDPR & CCPA-compliant-first contact list'. Its phone-verified 'Diamond Data' is claimed to produce a 45% correct-person-picked-up rate against 18% for standard numbers, attributed by Cognism to an independent study it does not name on that page. Re-viewing a contact you already revealed costs nothing, which is rarer than it sounds.
ranked.the_catch: You cannot buy one seat and you cannot find out what it costs without a meeting. The entry package is five seats, so the real cheque is a team's worth of licence even if two people will use it, and the quote-only model means the price you are offered depends on how you negotiate rather than on a published rate. Compliance posture is also a claim, not a certificate: Cognism owns Kaspr, the company the CNIL fined EUR 240,000 in December 2024 over LinkedIn-sourced contact details, so ask specifically which product's data you are buying and where it came from.
ranked.wrong_for: Solo founders and small teams testing an ICP — five seats and an annual conversation is the wrong shape; use Apollo or Hunter. US-only email prospecting where you do not need phones — you are paying for the expensive half of the product.

ranked.name: LinkedIn Sales Navigator
ranked.one_liner: Freshest ICP data anywhere; deliberately hard to get out
ranked.use_it_when: You need to define and sanity-check the ICP itself — the job titles, the headcount bands, the companies that actually exist — against data the people maintain themselves.
ranked.cost: Core $99.99/mo or $959.88/yr. Advanced $179.99/mo or $1,679.88/yr. Advanced Plus: quote.
ranked.pricing_detail: From LinkedIn's own compare-plans page: Core USD $99.99/mo, $959.88/yr; Advanced USD $179.99/mo, $1,679.88/yr; Advanced Plus listed with no price. All three tiers show 50 InMail credits per month. Prices are also shown in AUD, CAD, EUR, GBP and INR. Per seat.
ranked.good_at: Currency of data. Job changes, headcount and titles are updated by the humans they describe, not inferred by a scraper, so it is the best place to discover which segments exist and who sits in them before you pay a database vendor to sell you a stale version of the same thing. The filter set for company-level targeting is the deepest available.
ranked.the_catch: It is a reading room, not a data source. There is no email address, no phone number, and no straightforward bulk export — getting lists out is what every browser extension in this category exists to do, and doing it is squarely against LinkedIn's user agreement, which is why those extensions keep dying. LinkedIn's own help page on exporting blocks automated fetching, so nothing here is quoted from it: verify the export rules with LinkedIn before you build a workflow on top of them. Budget for a second tool regardless.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs a CSV of contactable people at the end of the hour. Use Apollo for that, or Cognism if the numbers must be callable in Europe.

ranked.name: Apify (with Crawlee)
ranked.one_liner: Build the list yourself when no database has your niche
ranked.use_it_when: Your ICP is local, physical or long-tail — clinics in three counties, independent gyms, marine engineering firms — and the contact databases return either nothing or the same 400 rows everyone else bought.
ranked.cost: Free tier: $5/mo of credits. Paid $19, $199 or $999/mo. Google Maps actor from $1.50/1,000 places.
ranked.pricing_detail: Plans from Apify's pricing page: Free $0 with '$5 to spend in Apify Store or on your own Actors'; Starter $19/mo; Scale $199/mo; Business $999/mo; Enterprise custom. Annual billing takes 10% off. Compute is $0.2/compute unit on Free and Starter, $0.16 on Scale, $0.13 on Business. Actors bill either pay-per-event or pay-per-usage against platform credits. The Google Maps scraper is priced 'from $1.50 / 1,000 scraped places' with per-event add-ons: place details and company contacts $0.0020 each on the FREE tier or $0.0015 on SILVER, social profile enrichment $0.10 on FREE against $0.007 on SILVER. Crawlee, the underlying crawling library, is Apache-2.0 and per its own docs 'runs anywhere' — genuinely self-hostable if the data cannot leave your infrastructure.
ranked.good_at: Reaching the businesses no B2B database bothers to index, at a cost per record nothing else here can match — $1.50 per 1,000 Google Maps places against roughly $0.05 per Clay data credit. And it is the only entry here with a real open-source escape hatch: Crawlee under Apache-2.0, self-hosted, no vendor holding your list.
ranked.the_catch: You become the data controller, and the enrichment add-ons cost more on the free tier than on paid. Social profile enrichment is $0.10 per profile on FREE against $0.007 on SILVER — a 14x gap that turns a cheap experiment into a bill. Scrapers also break silently when a site changes its markup, so a Monday list can be half-empty by Friday with no error. Most importantly, the Kaspr decision is about exactly this activity: if you scrape personal contact details of EU residents, the Article 14 duty to tell those people, the retention limit and the obligation to name your sources on request are yours, not a vendor's.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone selling to standard corporate ICPs where the databases already have good coverage — Apollo is cheaper once you count your own hours. Teams with no engineer to babysit broken actors should not pick this.

also_considered.name: ZoomInfo
also_considered.why_not: Deepest US enterprise coverage, but the pricing page publishes no price at all and states 'credits represent the consumption (export) of a professional or company profile' — one credit per record out, on a quoted annual contract. Priced for teams with procurement, not for you.

also_considered.name: Hunter.io
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely free 50 credits/mo, then $34-$209/mo on annual billing; 1 credit per email found, 0.5 per verification. Excellent at domain-to-email, thin as an ICP search engine — no phones, shallow filters.

also_considered.name: Lusha
also_considered.why_not: Clear credit rules on its own page — 1 credit per email, 10 per phone, 40 free credits a month, monthly rollover to twice your limit — but the paid plan table did not render, so no price could be read at source.

also_considered.name: Ocean.io
also_considered.why_not: Strong lookalike search from $567/yr (9,000 credits at $0.063), free exports, but merely viewing search results costs 0.2 credits each — you pay to browse before you pay to reveal.

also_considered.name: Instantly Lead Finder
also_considered.why_not: $47-$197/mo of credits over a claimed 450M-lead database, but credits are a separate purchase from Instantly's sending plans, so the real bill is two subscriptions.

also_considered.name: Clearbit
also_considered.why_not: Excluded: discontinued. Clearbit's own blog retired the free Clearbit platform, Weekly Visitor Report, TAM Calculator, Connect and the free Slack integration on 30 April 2025, and the Logo API on 1 December 2025, folding into HubSpot Breeze Intelligence.

watch_list: India's DPDP Rules, 2025: Rules 3 and 5-16 — notice standards, security safeguards, breach notification — commence eighteen months after publication. Any vendor selling Indian contact data has a deadline it has not talked to you about.

Further CNIL-style enforcement down the supply chain after Kaspr. The decision penalised collecting details from users who had restricted visibility, five-year retention, and a refusal to name sources on request. If regulators start pursuing buyers rather than scrapers, provenance stops being a nice-to-have and Cognism's posture becomes the ranking.
Clay's slider pricing. If the annual entry point moves off '$54/mo' or actions get repriced, the gap to Apollo changes shape overnight.
Apollo tightening the fair-use policy behind its 'unlimited' plans, or moving phone credits again. The 8-credit mobile is the whole economics of that pick.
LinkedIn restricting third-party extraction further. Every extension-based prospecting tool sits on a permission LinkedIn can revoke, and it periodically does.

Anyone publishing a reproducible accuracy benchmark — same ICP, same 1,000 contacts, bounce and connect rates across vendors. That would reorder this list on evidence rather than on pricing transparency.

social.trends.question: Something is blowing up in my niche this week. Which tool tells me while it still matters?

method.how: Ranked on three things the marketing never mentions: how fresh the data actually is, what the tool physically samples, and whether it flags something rising or something that already peaked. Sampling is where most of them fail - a product watching a fixed set of accounts, feeds or keywords is not watching a platform, and Talkwalker's own tier chart quietly admits its entry plan returns a sampled subset. Refresh rate is the main upsell lever: the entry tier of nearly every paid listener is 12 hours or more behind, which for this job is a day late. The honest summary is that nothing does the full job - platform-native feeds are fast but single-platform, keyword listeners only find trends you already named, and by the time a hashtag charts anywhere it has usually peaked.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No live queries were run through any of these tools and no detection latency was measured. Every price, quota and refresh rate was read from the vendor's own pricing page on 2026-08-29; where a vendor published no number, this entry says quote-only rather than guessing. All coverage claims are the vendors' own.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for trend-detection latency or real platform coverage in this category. None exists. The 'best social listening tools 2026' listicles that fill the first page of search are published by Hootsuite, Meltwater and Onclusive - vendors ranking themselves, usually near the top. Treat every coverage figure quoted here, including the ones repeated above, as marketing until somebody measures it.

ranked.name: Google Trends (Trending Now)
ranked.one_liner: Free, fastest, and only ever sees what people type into Google.
ranked.use_it_when: You want to confirm within a few hours that a spike is real before committing a day's work to it.
ranked.cost: Free. No account needed.
ranked.pricing_detail: No paid tier. The usual paid layer on top is Glimpse, a browser extension that adds absolute search volumes to the same underlying data; its own pricing page published no prices as of 2026-08-29, so check current pricing with the vendor before budgeting for it.
ranked.good_at: Latency and export. Trending Now offers windows down to the past 4 hours, alongside 24 hours, 48 hours and 7 days, with volume ranges, percentage rise, region and roughly 18 category filters, plus CSV, clipboard and RSS output. Nothing paid here is faster.
ranked.the_catch: It samples Google searches, not social conversation. A term with real momentum on Reddit or TikTok can sit below the reporting threshold and show you a flat empty chart, which reads as 'no trend' when it means 'too small to measure'. Trending Now also skews to news, sport and entertainment - the national story, not your corner of it. And Explore gives a relative 0-100 index, not absolute volume, so you cannot compare two niches honestly.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs to read what people are actually saying, or whose niche is too small to register in search volume. Use Octolens for that, or Brand24 if the niche is consumer rather than technical.

ranked.name: Octolens
ranked.one_liner: Hourly cross-platform mention tracking at the only honest published price.
ranked.use_it_when: Your niche lives on Reddit, X, Hacker News, LinkedIn, GitHub or YouTube and you already know which terms are worth watching.
ranked.cost: $159/mo Pro (billed annually). Scale $499/mo. Enterprise custom. 7-day trial.
ranked.pricing_detail: Pro: $159/month billed annually - 10 keywords (extras $10 each), 15,000 mentions (extras $0.013 per mention), unlimited seats, 2 years of history, hourly refresh. Scale: $499/month billed annually - 40 keywords (extras $5 each), 50,000 mentions (extras $0.01 each), unlimited history, real-time refresh, and adds podcasts, news, web and newsletters. Enterprise: custom pricing, unlimited keywords and mentions. Trial is 7 days capped at 5,000 mentions. Both headline prices are annual-billed rates - there is no month-to-month figure published.
ranked.good_at: Coverage per pound. Pro lists Reddit, X, LinkedIn, Bluesky, DEV, TikTok, Hacker News, YouTube, GitHub and Stack Overflow at a price where the enterprise vendors will not even quote you. Hourly refresh at the entry tier beats every other paid tool here.
ranked.the_catch: It is keyword-driven, so it can only find trends you already named - and the thing genuinely rising in your niche this week is by definition a phrase you have not typed yet. Real-time refresh is Scale-only at $499; Pro is hourly. Mentions above 15,000 are priced per mention rather than simply stopping, so confirm how overage is billed before a viral week does it for you. The $159 is annual billing, so it is a $1,908 commitment, not a monthly experiment.
ranked.wrong_for: Discovery from a blank page. Find the term with Google Trends or Exploding Topics first, then point Octolens at it.

ranked.name: Brand24
ranked.one_liner: Widest consumer platform list with its prices actually printed on the page.
ranked.use_it_when: Your niche is consumer-facing and lives on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and Facebook rather than developer forums.
ranked.cost: $199-$599/mo billed annually ($249-$699 monthly). Enterprise from $1,499/mo. 14-day trial, no card.
ranked.pricing_detail: Individual: $249/month, or $199/month billed annually - 3 keywords, 2,000 mentions/month, 1 user, updates every 12 hours. Team: $349, or $299 annually - 7 keywords, 10,000 mentions, unlimited users, hourly updates. Pro: $499, or $399 annually - 12 keywords, 40,000 mentions, real-time updates, events detection, AI insights on 2 projects. Business: $699, or $599 annually - 25 keywords, 100,000 mentions, real-time, AI insights on 5 projects. Enterprise: from $1,499/month, annual billing only.
ranked.good_at: Breadth plus a spike alarm. It lists Facebook, Instagram, X, news, blogs, Reddit, LinkedIn, Medium, Quora, YouTube, TikTok, reviews, Twitch, newsletters and podcasts on every tier, and its AI Anomaly Detector flags, in its own words, 'unusual spikes in the number or reach of mentions' rather than waiting for you to spot them.
ranked.the_catch: Freshness is the upsell, and it is severe. The $199/mo Individual tier updates every 12 hours - for a right-now job that is half a day late, and the trend has moved. Hourly starts at $299, real-time at $399, which is where events detection also appears. Individual's 3 keywords and 2,000 mentions a month will be eaten by one busy hashtag, and mention caps mean a genuinely viral topic is the exact scenario in which your data stops.
ranked.wrong_for: Technical and developer niches - it does not list Hacker News, GitHub or Stack Overflow. Use Octolens. Also wrong if you only need one platform, where the platform's own free trend feed is faster and costs nothing.

ranked.name: Exploding Topics
ranked.one_liner: Finds next year's trend, not this week's. Know which you need.
ranked.use_it_when: You are choosing what to build, sell or write about next quarter and want the topic before it is crowded.
ranked.cost: $39-$249/mo. 7-day trial. No free plan on the pricing page.
ranked.pricing_detail: Entrepreneur $39/month: 100 tracked trends, 10 trend analyses, trends database, trending products, meta trends, channel breakdown. Investor $99/month: 500 tracked trends, 100 analyses, plus trending startups, trend forecasting and CSV export. Business $249/month: 2,000 tracked trends, 500 analyses, plus trend reports. Seven-day free trial on all three. The pricing page showed no monthly/annual toggle and no free plan as of 2026-08-29, so the annual discount, if any, is not published - ask before you commit.
ranked.good_at: Curation. Human-filtered rising topics with a chart and a channel breakdown, which is exactly what raw Google Trends cannot give you in a niche too small to clear the noise floor. Good for spotting a category before your competitors name it.
ranked.the_catch: It is answering a different question from the one you asked. The vendor's own headline claim is 'Discover Trends 12+ Months Before Everyone Else' - a slow signal derived largely from search and mention volume. Something spiking on TikTok this morning has either been in the database for a year or will never appear at all. Buying this to catch live trends is the single most common mistake in this category, and the tracked-trend quotas (100 on the $39 tier) mean you are watching a list you chose weeks ago.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone reacting to a live spike, or anyone who needs to read the actual conversation. Google Trends for speed, Octolens or Brand24 for what people are saying.

ranked.name: Talkwalker
ranked.one_liner: The only one with real volume, and even it samples your entry tier.
ranked.use_it_when: You need defensible numbers across many markets and languages, and someone above you signs the cheque.
ranked.cost: Quote-only. No prices published. Tiers: Core, Analyze, Business.
ranked.pricing_detail: No figures published on the pricing page as of 2026-08-29 - check current pricing with sales. Three named tiers: Core, Analyze (marked most popular) and Business. Analyze is described as 2x non-sampled results volume over Core with 25 additional topics, filters and channels; Business as 6x non-sampled volume over Analyze with 3x more topics and additional historical data. Expect an annual contract.
ranked.good_at: Scale and languages. Vendor claims 30+ social platforms, 150 million data sources, 187 languages and 196 countries. Nothing with a published price is in the same weight class, and multi-market work is where it genuinely earns the money.
ranked.the_catch: Read the tier wording rather than the headline. Selling higher tiers as '2x' and '6x non-sampled results volume' is an admission that the entry tier returns a sample - you get a fraction of the matching conversation and are not told which fraction or how it was chosen. Spotting a trend from an undisclosed sample is guesswork with a good dashboard. Add quote-only pricing, an annual commitment and a demo call before you learn the number, and the evaluation itself costs you a week.
ranked.wrong_for: Solo operators and small teams. If you resent booking a demo to learn a price, you cannot afford this - use Octolens, or Brand24 for consumer platforms.

also_considered.name: GummySearch
also_considered.why_not: Discontinued - its own site states 'GummySearch is closed as of 11/30/2025'. Do not sign up; the Reddit trend-research gap it left is still open.

also_considered.name: TikTok Creative Center
also_considered.why_not: Free and platform-native, the best single source for short-form trends, but TikTok-only and region-filtered, and its pages would not render for verification here - check the filters and time windows yourself before relying on it.

also_considered.name: Determ
also_considered.why_not: Real-time updates on every tier from EUR 99/month, which beats Brand24's entry plan, but 1 topic and 1,000 mentions a month is exhausted in days by exactly the spike you bought it to catch.

also_considered.name: BuzzSumo
also_considered.why_not: The $199/mo headline is the annual-billed rate, and it ranks published articles and engagement rather than live conversation - always a step behind.

also_considered.name: Sprout Social
also_considered.why_not: Listening is a quote-only add-on stacked on plans starting at $199 per seat per month. Two prices to negotiate for one answer.

also_considered.name: Harken
also_considered.why_not: The only self-hostable option found (MIT licence, Docker Compose, Hacker News/Bluesky/Reddit/Mastodon/RSS, data stays on your machine) - and it has 3 GitHub stars and one author. Fine to run if your data cannot leave your infrastructure; do not build a business process on it.

watch_list: X/Twitter data access. Almost every paid listener resells it. One repricing and half this list loses its most reactive source overnight.
Instagram and Facebook remain the biggest blind spot in every tool here. If Meta's Content Library ever opens beyond approved researchers, the ranking changes completely.
Reddit's paid Data API terms. GummySearch's closure is what that risk looks like when it lands.
Whether Octolens holds its price. $159/mo for that platform list is the outlier on this page; watch for a quota cut or a tier reshuffle at renewal.
Anyone publishing a real detection-latency benchmark - hours from first spike to appearing in the tool. Nobody has. It would reorder this list immediately.
A maintained open-source listener. Harken is one person's side project; a serious alternative would go straight into the ranked five.

automation.support-bot.question: I want an AI chatbot answering support questions on my site — which one, and what will a resolution actually cost me?

method.how: Ranked on three things a buyer only cares about after go-live: whether the vendor writes down what a billable resolution is, whether the bot can be pinned to your own documentation, and how cleanly it hands a conversation to a human. Per-resolution billing is now the default and the definitions differ enormously — Intercom charges $0.99 only for a defined outcome and explicitly not for a plain handoff, Help Scout charges $0.75 only when nobody escalates, Tidio bills every conversation the bot replies in whether it helps or not, and Freshworks bills per session. Zendesk lost places purely because it will not publish a number. Cost predictability then broke the ties, which is why a flat-rate builder and a self-hostable option are in the list at all.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No bots were deployed, no resolution rates measured. Every price and definition here was read from the vendor's own pricing or product page on 2026-08-29 and is quoted as the vendor states it. Where a page would not render its pricing table (Gorgias) or the vendor publishes no number (Zendesk, Ada, Sierra), that is said plainly rather than guessed.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for support-bot resolution quality. Every resolution-rate figure in this category — Intercom's 76% average, Tidio's 67% — is self-reported by the vendor, measured against the vendor's own definition of 'resolved', and unauditable from outside. Search results for this category are dominated by vendors publishing comparison pages that rank themselves first, and by affiliate roundups. Treat any league table you find, including this one, as opinion. The only number you can trust is the one from your own two-week pilot on your own ticket mix.

ranked.name: Fin
ranked.one_liner: Best answers, and the only honest billing definition in the category
ranked.use_it_when: Volume is high enough that resolution quality beats subscription cost, and you want the bot bolted onto the helpdesk you already run.
ranked.cost: $0.99 per outcome. 50-outcome monthly minimum on non-Intercom helpdesks. Intercom seats from $29/seat/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Fin is $0.99 per outcome on every plan. Intercom's own pricing page lists seats at Essential $29, Advanced $85 and Expert $132 per seat/mo, with Fin included on all three; Advanced adds 20 free Lite seats, Expert 50. Fin can also run standalone on another helpdesk with no Intercom seats, in which case a 50-outcome monthly minimum applies. Billable outcomes, as fin.ai defines them: a resolution ($0.99, 'no further help is requested after Fin's last answer'), a procedure handoff ($0.99, where Fin completes a configured handoff), a disqualification ($0.99) and a qualification ($9.99, where Fin routes a prospect against your criteria). Crucially the page states you are not charged when a conversation is simply passed to your team without an outcome. Vendor states no setup, integration or platform fees. Add-ons: Pro $99/mo, Copilot $29/agent/mo, Proactive Support Plus $99/mo. Annual and monthly billing both offered.
ranked.good_at: Writing down exactly what it will invoice you for — the four outcome types and the explicit carve-out for plain handoffs are the clearest billing contract any vendor here publishes. Runs on Intercom natively and on Salesforce, Freshdesk and HubSpot. Vendor claims a 76% average resolution rate across 12,000+ customers with many above 85%, and ships a testing suite for simulations and regression tests before you push changes live.
ranked.the_catch: That $9.99 qualification outcome is ten times the resolution price, and it fires on a routing decision, not on a solved problem. Turn on sales-side procedures without watching what you have configured and your per-outcome average quietly stops resembling $0.99. The resolution definition is also passive — 'no further help is requested' means a customer who gives up and closes the tab bills the same as one you actually helped. And Fin's own page lists Salesforce, Freshdesk and HubSpot as supported helpdesks but not Zendesk, so check that before you plan a migration around it.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone doing under a few hundred conversations a month, where the seat cost plus per-outcome fee dwarfs the value — use Help Scout or Tidio. Anyone whose data cannot leave their own servers — use Chatwoot.

ranked.name: AI Answers
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest per-resolution price, and it only bills when nobody escalates
ranked.use_it_when: You want a real helpdesk plus a bot without a Fin-sized bill, and you want a hard ceiling on what the AI can spend.
ranked.cost: AI Answers $0.75/resolution. Helpdesk free up to 5 users, then $25-$75/user/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Help Scout's pricing page lists Free ($0, up to 5 users), Standard $25/user/mo, Plus $45/user/mo and Pro $75/user/mo, with 16% off for annual billing. Billing is per user seat, not per contact. AI Answers, the autonomous chatbot, is separate and usage-based at $0.75 per resolution, and the page states billing occurs only when the customer receives an AI response without escalating to human support. A three-month free trial of AI Answers is offered, and monthly spend caps are available for cost predictability. Lighter AI features — AI Assist, AI Drafts, AI Summarize — are bundled into the paid plans rather than metered.
ranked.good_at: The lowest published per-resolution price of any mainstream vendor, paired with the one cost control everyone else omits: a monthly spend cap. Escalation is free, which aligns the vendor's incentive with yours rather than against it. And the free tier for up to five users means a small team gets a working helpdesk before it pays for anything.
ranked.the_catch: Per-user billing means the helpdesk cost climbs with headcount even as the bot deflects more work, so the two halves of your bill pull in opposite directions. Help Scout is also a lighter product than Intercom or Zendesk — fewer channels, thinner automation, less enterprise governance — and its own site did not surface a published resolution-rate figure to compare against Fin's 76% claim. The vendor's own AI Answers feature pages returned 404 when checked on 2026-08-29, so the $0.75 figure and escalation carve-out are read from the pricing page only.
ranked.wrong_for: Large teams where per-seat costs compound badly, and anyone needing deep multi-system agentic actions — use Fin or Zendesk. Anyone who wants no helpdesk at all, just a widget — use Chatbase.

ranked.name: Chatbase
ranked.one_liner: Flat monthly bill, no helpdesk migration, no resolution roulette
ranked.use_it_when: You want a docs-trained widget live this week, on a fixed monthly number you can put in a budget.
ranked.cost: Free tier (50 credits/mo). Paid $40-$500/mo. Extra agents $25/mo each.
ranked.pricing_detail: From the vendor's pricing page: Free $0 (50 message credits/mo, 1 member), Hobby $40/mo or $384/yr (700 credits, 2 members), Standard $150/mo or $1,440/yr (4,000 credits, 3 members), Pro $500/mo or $4,800/yr (15,000 credits, 5 members), Enterprise custom. Annual saves 20%. Add-ons: each extra AI agent $25/mo, auto-recharge credits $40 per 1,000, removing Chatbase branding $99/mo. Note the unit is message credits, not resolutions — you pay for the bot talking, resolved or not. The pricing page does not state whether unused credits roll over, and the credit-consumption docs could not be reached on 2026-08-29; assume they expire until Chatbase tells you otherwise.
ranked.good_at: Getting a bot trained on your own content onto your site without touching your existing support stack, on a predictable flat fee. Guardrails are configured as plain instructions ('don't handle refunds; direct users to billing support'), and it ships its own built-in helpdesk for human handoff so escalation doesn't need a second product.
ranked.the_catch: The unbundling is where it stings. $99/mo to remove the vendor's branding from your own site is more than the entry plan costs, and each additional agent is another $25/mo — a three-product company on Standard is paying $200/mo before overage. Credits are consumed per message, so a chatty bot burns budget on conversations it never resolves, and the auto-recharge rate of $40/1,000 is a hard cliff to hit unattended. The site says agents are built by connecting your sources and setting guardrails, but does not state that answers are restricted to those sources — if docs-only answering is a compliance requirement, get it in writing before you buy.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants to pay only for outcomes — use Fin or Help Scout. Anyone who needs a mature ticketing system underneath — use Help Scout or Zendesk.

ranked.name: Lyro
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest real entry point; explicitly refuses to answer off-script
ranked.use_it_when: You are a small shop, you want the bot pinned hard to your own help content, and $30-50/mo is the whole budget.
ranked.cost: Free plan (50 Lyro conversations, lifetime). Paid from $24.17/mo. Lyro add-on from $32.50/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Tidio's pricing page: Free $0, Starter $24.17/mo (100 billable conversations, 50 Lyro conversations included), Growth from $49.17/mo, Plus from $300/mo plus usage, Premium custom. Two months free on annual billing. The Lyro AI Agent add-on starts at $32.50/mo for 50 Lyro conversations. Read the billing unit carefully: Tidio bills per Lyro conversation, not per resolution. Its own definition is 'a customer interaction initiated through any channel integrated with Tidio that has at least one reply from our AI Agent' — multiple Lyro replies in one thread count once, even if the customer returns later. Pay-per-resolution billing exists only on the Premium tier. The free plan's 50 Lyro conversations are a one-off lifetime allowance, not monthly.
ranked.good_at: Grounding. The vendor states plainly that 'Lyro works only with the content and guidance you provide' and that when the answer isn't in your material it forwards to a human and learns from the reply — the most explicit docs-only commitment of anything here. Handoff rules are configurable per topic or customer value, and you can watch conversations live and jump in. Vendor claims a 67% average resolution rate, while conceding that figure counts automated conversations rather than problems genuinely solved.
ranked.the_catch: You are billed for the bot opening its mouth, not for it helping. Every conversation where Lyro replies once and then hands off to a human bills as a Lyro conversation and you pay the human's time too — the exact double-charge Fin and Help Scout explicitly avoid. Pay-per-resolution is dangled only at the Premium tier, which is custom-priced and out of reach of the audience the cheap plans are aimed at. The free plan's 50 conversations are lifetime, so it is a demo, not a free tier. And Tidio meters two separate things — billable conversations and Lyro conversations — so it is easy to exhaust one while the other looks healthy.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone with volume, where per-conversation billing on unresolved chats compounds fast — use Help Scout or Fin. Anyone needing complex agentic actions across back-end systems — use Fin.

ranked.name: Chatwoot + Captain AI
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed, self-hostable, the only pick where data never leaves
ranked.use_it_when: Regulatory or contractual reasons mean customer conversations cannot sit on a vendor's servers.
ranked.cost: Self-host free (MIT). Cloud $0-$99/agent/mo. Captain AI credits $20/1,000.
ranked.pricing_detail: Cloud plans from the vendor's pricing page: Hacker $0 (up to 2 agents), Startups $19/agent/mo billed annually (300 Captain credits/mo), Business $39/agent/mo (500 credits), Enterprise $99/agent/mo (800 credits). Extra Captain AI usage is $20 per 1,000 credits. Credits, not resolutions — they are spent on reply suggestions, summarisation, knowledge-base answers, copilot suggestions and auto-generated customer memories, so internal agent-assist features drain the same pool as customer-facing answers. The source is MIT-licensed (chatwoot/chatwoot on GitHub, latest release 4.15.1 on 17 June 2026), which permits commercial use without restriction, but the repository also carries a separate /enterprise directory — check its licence before assuming everything in the repo is MIT. Self-hosted deployment docs are at developers.chatwoot.com; those docs did not confirm whether Captain AI runs on self-hosted installs or what it costs there, so verify that before committing.
ranked.good_at: Being genuinely yours. MIT on the core means you can run it, modify it and use it commercially with no licence fee and no per-seat meter, on your own infrastructure, with the conversation data never crossing a vendor boundary. The cloud tier is also the cheapest per-agent helpdesk here if you want someone else to run it.
ranked.the_catch: You are buying a helpdesk with AI attached, not an AI product — Captain AI is a newer, thinner layer than Fin or Lyro, and the credit pool is shared with internal copilot features, so agents idly using reply suggestions burn the same budget as customer answers. The self-hosted route means you own upgrades, scaling, embeddings and the LLM bill, none of which are in the $0. And the crucial question for this job — whether Captain AI works at all on a self-hosted install, and on what terms — was not answerable from the vendor's own self-hosting docs on 2026-08-29. If self-hosted AI is the reason you are here, confirm it first.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone without an ops team, and anyone who wants the best answers rather than the most control — use Fin. Anyone who just wants a widget on a marketing site — use Chatbase.

also_considered.name: Zendesk AI agents
also_considered.why_not: Will not publish a per-automated-resolution price. Its own page says resolutions are 'priced based on the value delivered' in tiers, with an unspecified plan allowance — you cannot forecast a bill from public information, and Suite seats are already $55-$115/agent/mo annually.

also_considered.name: Crisp
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely cheap and priced per workspace rather than per seat ($0/$45/$95/$295 a month, with $5-$75 of AI credits bundled). Dropped only because the page states no overage rate once bundled credits run out, so the third month is unforecastable.

also_considered.name: Freshdesk / Freddy AI Agent
also_considered.why_not: Bills per session, not per resolution — 500 sessions included on all plans, then $49 per 100. You pay whether the bot helped or not, and the page never defines a session.

also_considered.name: Sierra
also_considered.why_not: Outcome-based pricing with no published figure anywhere on the site. Enterprise sales cycle; you cannot evaluate it against this list without a call.

also_considered.name: Ada
also_considered.why_not: No pricing published at all — the pricing URL redirects to a demo booking form. Same problem as Sierra.

also_considered.name: Gorgias
also_considered.why_not: Strong if you are Shopify-native — priced per ticket volume, never per agent, with AI Agent billed only when it resolves. Excluded because the pricing table would not render for verification on 2026-08-29, so no number here would be trustworthy. Check current pricing.

watch_list: Whether Zendesk starts publishing an actual per-automated-resolution price. Until it does, it cannot be ranked honestly against vendors that do.
Whether Help Scout's $0.75/resolution forces Intercom off $0.99, or whether Intercom instead leans harder on high-value outcome types like the $9.99 qualification.

Outcome-type proliferation generally. Fin already bills four different things at two different prices; if 'resolution' fragments into a dozen billable actions across vendors, per-resolution pricing stops being comparable at all.
Whether Tidio moves pay-per-resolution below the custom-priced Premium tier. That single change would move it up this list.
Whether Captain AI becomes clearly available and documented on self-hosted Chatwoot. That is the only thing keeping the open option at rank 5.
Any independent, third-party benchmark of resolution quality on a common ticket set. None exists today, and its arrival would invalidate every vendor-claimed percentage quoted here.

automation.workflow.question: I need branching, loops and retries, not just app-to-app triggers. Which automation platform copes when a run dies halfway?

method.how: Ranked on control flow and failure behaviour first, price second. I looked for real branching, iteration over collections, per-step retry, a dedicated error path, and what the platform does with a run that dies at step seven of twelve. Per-run pricing beat per-step pricing, because per-step billing punishes exactly the loop-heavy workflows this job is about. Self-hostability and the actual licence text were treated as a hard filter, not a bullet point: two of the best options here are not OSI open source. Nothing on this list was found to be discontinued as of the check.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No load tests, no reliability measurement, no long-running production trial. Prices and licence terms read from vendors' own pricing pages and repository LICENCE files on 2026-08-29. Pipedream's pricing page renders in JavaScript and could not be read at source, so no Pipedream prices are quoted here.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for workflow automation platforms. Nobody publishes comparable throughput, reliability or failure-recovery numbers, and review sites in this category are pay-to-play. Search results are dominated by the vendors ranking themselves: every one of these companies publishes an 'X vs Y' page in which X wins. Treat any comparison table you find, including this one, as an argument rather than a measurement.

ranked.name: n8n
ranked.one_liner: Best control flow per pound, if you can live with the licence
ranked.use_it_when: You want branching, loops over items and per-node retries, and you either want to self-host for free or you want cloud billing that does not punish long workflows.
ranked.cost: Free self-hosted (source-available). Cloud EUR 20-EUR 667/mo billed annually.
ranked.pricing_detail: Cloud, billed annually: Starter EUR 20/mo (2,500 workflow executions), Pro EUR 50/mo (10,000), Business EUR 667/mo (40,000, includes the self-hosted licence), Enterprise on request. Business overage is quoted as EUR 4,000 per extra bucket of 300,000 executions. An execution is one run of the whole workflow with unlimited steps, so step count does not affect the bill. The Community Edition is free to download and run yourself with no execution cap.
ranked.good_at: Pricing per workflow run rather than per step, which is the single biggest cost difference in this category once loops are involved. Per-node 'retry on fail' with a wait between tries, an error output branch per node, and a dedicated error workflow triggered by the Error Trigger node when a production run fails. Free self-hosting means an unmetered dev and staging environment, which none of the pure-SaaS options give you.
ranked.the_catch: The Community Edition is under the Sustainable Use Licence, not an open source licence: internal business use only, and you may not host it for other people or white-label it. If you are an agency planning to run flows for clients on your own box, that is the wrong licence and you need a commercial one. Second, the cloud pricing cliff is brutal: EUR 50/mo to EUR 667/mo with nothing in between, and self-hosting with a licence starts at the top of that cliff. Third, n8n's own docs say error workflows do not fire on manual runs, only on automatic ones, so you cannot test your error handling by clicking execute.
ranked.wrong_for: Agencies reselling hosted automation to clients, and anyone who wants a genuinely OSI-licensed stack. Use Activepieces or Windmill instead. Non-technical teams who will not touch expressions should use Make.

ranked.name: Make
ranked.one_liner: Routers, iterators and error routes, cheap, if you configure them
ranked.use_it_when: You want to draw the branching visually, you are iterating over collections and aggregating results, and you want a real free tier before committing.
ranked.cost: Free 1,000 credits/mo. Paid $12-$38/mo at 10,000 credits.
ranked.pricing_detail: Billed monthly by default: Core $12/mo, Pro $21/mo, Teams $38/mo, all quoted at the smallest volume of 10,000 credits per month; annual billing saves 15% or more. Free plan gets 1,000 credits/mo with no time limit but only 2 active scenarios and a 15-minute minimum schedule interval. One module action equals one credit; code execution costs 2 credits per second. Routers and error handlers consume zero credits. Credits expire at the end of the billing term and do not roll over. Custom variables, priority execution and execution log search start at Pro; teams and roles at Teams.
ranked.good_at: The most expressive visual control flow here. Routers for branching, iterators and aggregators for loops that fan out and collapse back, and error handler routes attached to individual modules with Resume, Ignore, Break, Rollback and Commit directives, so you can decide per-step whether a failure retries, is swallowed, or unwinds. The break handler plus incomplete executions is the closest thing in this list to resuming a half-finished run.
ranked.the_catch: Storing incomplete executions is off by default. Turn it on per scenario or a run that dies at step seven is simply gone, with whatever it already wrote left written and no way to resume. The number you can store is capped by your plan. Second, the per-module credit model is the opposite of n8n's: an iterator over 500 rows calling three modules is roughly 1,500 credits, so the $12 tier evaporates on exactly the loop-heavy work you came for. Third, credits expire at the end of the term, so a quiet month is money burned.
ranked.wrong_for: High-volume loops over large collections, where per-module billing gets expensive fast; use n8n. Data that cannot leave your infrastructure; use Windmill or Activepieces.

ranked.name: Windmill
ranked.one_liner: Genuinely open source, proper retries, not really no-code
ranked.use_it_when: The data cannot leave your infrastructure, you need AGPL rather than a source-available licence, and you want retry policies, error handlers and suspend/resume as first-class flow features.
ranked.cost: Free self-hosted (AGPL-3.0). Enterprise from $120/mo plus seats and workers.
ranked.pricing_detail: The open source edition is AGPL-3.0 and self-hosted with unlimited executions at no cost. Enterprise starts at $120/mo; the configurator shows developer seats at $20/user/mo and operator (execution-only) seats at $10/user/mo, plus compute: $100/mo for 2 compute units at 2GB per worker, i.e. $50 per worker per month, with native subworkers at $50/mo. Audit logs, SAML, external secret backends, autoscaling, distributed dependency cache and the GitHub app are enterprise-only.
ranked.good_at: The only tool here under a licence that lets you do whatever you want commercially, including hosting it for other people, as long as you honour AGPL section 13 and publish modifications to network users. Flows have per-step retry configuration, error handlers, branching, for-loops with parallelism, and approval steps that suspend a run and resume it later, which is the same machinery you need for resuming after a failure.
ranked.the_catch: 'Without code' does not survive contact with it. The flow builder is real, but Windmill is a script runner with a flow layer on top, and within an hour you are writing TypeScript or Python for anything the built-in steps do not cover. There is no large catalogue of pre-built app connectors like Zapier's or Make's, so integrations are yours to write. And the enterprise pricing is infrastructure-shaped, seats plus compute units plus workers, so the bill is harder to predict than a flat SaaS tier.
ranked.wrong_for: Non-developers, and anyone who wanted a connector catalogue rather than a runtime. Use Make or Activepieces. Also wrong if AGPL is banned by your legal team, in which case n8n Business or Activepieces MIT core is the answer.

ranked.name: Activepieces
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed self-host that a non-developer can actually use
ranked.use_it_when: You want an open, self-hostable builder that a non-technical colleague can maintain, and you need a licence that permits commercial hosting.
ranked.cost: Free self-hosted (MIT core). Cloud free, then $16-$166/mo billed yearly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Cloud: Free with 100 credits per day that refresh each morning; Plus $16/mo billed yearly (10,000 credits/mo); Team $166/mo billed yearly (50,000 credits/mo); Ultimate custom; Embed from $36k/yr. Overage is $0.007 per extra credit. One full flow run is 1 credit regardless of step count; AI actions cost more (2 credits fast model, 10 smart, 20 frontier, 1 with your own key). The Community Edition self-hosts free with no cap on runs, users or flows, but excludes Agents, Chat, Projects, API access, team and admin features, SSO, roles, audit logs and Git Sync.
ranked.good_at: The licence. The core is MIT, so unlike n8n you may host it commercially for other people. Per-run credit billing rather than per-step. Branching, loops and retries in a builder that is deliberately simpler than n8n's, and building a missing connector is a documented TypeScript 'piece' rather than a fight.
ranked.the_catch: packages/ee and the server ee directory are not MIT, they are under a separate commercial licence, and the free self-hosted edition drops exactly what you want on day three: API access, projects, roles, audit logs and Git Sync. Version control for your flows is a paid feature. The free cloud tier's 100 credits reset daily rather than pooling, so a busy Tuesday stops dead at lunchtime. And the piece catalogue is much smaller than Zapier's or Make's, so budget for writing your own.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone needing a broad connector catalogue out of the box, or complex multi-branch flows with heavy data reshaping; use Make or n8n.

ranked.name: Zapier
ranked.one_liner: Most connectors, weakest control flow, priced per step
ranked.use_it_when: The workflow is mostly linear, the value is in reaching an obscure SaaS app nobody else integrates, and volume is low enough that per-task billing does not matter.
ranked.cost: Free 100 tasks/mo, two-step only. Professional from $19.99/mo, Team from $69/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 100 tasks/mo, unlimited Zaps but two-step only, no webhooks, no premium apps. Professional from $19.99/mo with multi-step Zaps, webhooks and unlimited premium apps; Team from $69/mo for 25 users and shared folders; Enterprise custom. Annual billing saves 33%. Task allowances scale with price. A task is each action step and each external connector call; built-in tools like Filters, Formatter, Paths, Delay, Looping and Digest do not consume tasks, and triggers and polling checks do not either. Exceeding your limit switches you to pay-as-you-go per-task billing unless you turn that off, and once you hit your maximum the Zaps pause until the next period.
ranked.good_at: Reach. The connector catalogue is the widest of anything here, and the long tail of niche business apps is the reason to pay. Setup is fastest, filters and Paths cover simple branching, and the free tier is a genuine, if crippled, place to start.
ranked.the_catch: It is priced per step, which is the wrong shape for this job: a twelve-action Zap run 100 times is roughly 1,200 tasks. Control flow is bolted on, Paths plus a separate Looping step, so anything with nested iteration or conditional retry gets unwieldy quickly compared with Make's routers or n8n's loop nodes. The free plan's two-step limit means it demos rather than works. And the pay-as-you-go rollover is opt-out, not opt-in, so a runaway loop bills you rather than stopping you.
ranked.wrong_for: Anything loop-heavy, branch-heavy or high-volume, and anything with a data residency requirement. Use n8n or Make for the former, Windmill or Activepieces for the latter.

also_considered.name: Workato
also_considered.why_not: Enterprise-grade orchestration, but no price is published anywhere on its pricing page; you cannot evaluate it without a sales call.

also_considered.name: Tray.ai
also_considered.why_not: Same problem as Workato: capable, sales-gated, and priced for organisations with a procurement department.

also_considered.name: Pipedream
also_considered.why_not: Powerful, but code-first and billed by compute (docs state 1 credit per 30 seconds at 256MB); its pricing page renders in JavaScript and no tier prices could be read at source.

also_considered.name: Microsoft Power Automate
also_considered.why_not: The right answer inside a Microsoft estate at $15/user/mo Premium, $150/bot/mo Process, $215/bot/mo Hosted Process, but the licensing and Dataverse entitlements are their own project.

also_considered.name: Node-RED
also_considered.why_not: Apache-2.0, genuinely free, unbeatable for hardware and event wiring, but you write JavaScript function nodes and there is no managed cloud or connector marketplace.

also_considered.name: Automatisch
also_considered.why_not: AGPL-3.0 with a commercial carve-out for files containing '.ee.', and a far smaller integration set than Activepieces for the same self-hosting effort.

watch_list: n8n tightening or relaxing the Sustainable Use Licence, or moving more of the Community Edition behind the Business tier. That licence is the only reason it is not an unambiguous first pick.
Make changing which modules consume credits. Routers and error handlers are free today; if that changes, the cheap tiers stop being cheap for loop-heavy work.
Activepieces moving more features from the MIT core into packages/ee. Git Sync and API access are already outside the free self-hosted edition.
Any of these shipping true resume-from-failed-step, replaying from the failing node with prior state intact rather than re-running the whole workflow. That would reorder the top three immediately.
Zapier switching from per-task to per-run billing, or adding real nested loops. Either would move it up several places.
AGPL or MIT projects in this space relicensing to BSL or 'fair source'. It has happened repeatedly in adjacent categories and would change the self-hosting recommendation overnight.

code.deploy.question: I built a side project. Where do I host it so a traffic spike can't hand me a four-figure bill?

method.how: Ranked on one question first: what does a sudden 100x traffic day actually cost you? Platforms that cannot bill you at all on their free tier, or that charge nothing for egress, rank above platforms that meter bandwidth per GB. Second tie-breaker: does a spend cap exist, and does it stop the meter or just stop the site? Third: how much of a real app you can deploy without leaving the free tier. Ease of setup was deliberately weighted last, because the platforms with the smoothest onboarding are the ones with the sharpest overage rates.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No load tests, no synthetic spikes, no billing experiments. Every limit, price and overage rate here was read from the vendor's own pricing or docs page on 2026-08-29 and is quoted as read. Hetzner's cloud prices could not be read from their pricing page (JavaScript-rendered), so no Hetzner figure is quoted.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for hosting cost or free-tier generosity. Nobody neutral publishes spike-cost tests. Search results for this category are dominated by the vendors ranking themselves — Vercel publishes its own 'Vercel vs Netlify' and 'Vercel vs Fastly' comparison pages inside its docs, and they rank well. Treat every comparison article you find as marketing until you have opened the pricing page yourself.

ranked.name: Cloudflare Workers (with Static Assets)
ranked.one_liner: The only one where bandwidth is genuinely not a billable line
ranked.use_it_when: You want a static site, an SPA, or a request/response app, and you want the traffic-spike question to simply not apply.
ranked.cost: Free plan. Workers Paid $5/mo minimum. No egress charges on any plan.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: 100,000 requests/day, 10 ms CPU time per invocation, Worker script up to 3 MB gzipped, 20,000 static asset files per version, 25 MiB max per asset, 50 subrequests per request. Paid: $5/mo including 10 million requests and 30 million CPU-milliseconds, then +$0.30 per additional million requests and +$0.02 per additional million CPU-ms. Docs state plainly: 'There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth)' and 'Requests to static assets are free and unlimited.' Bundled free storage is thin: Workers KV free is 100,000 reads/day but only 1,000 writes/day and 1 GB stored; D1 free is 5 million rows read/day, 100,000 rows written/day, 5 GB total. Cloudflare Pages free allows 500 builds/month, 1 concurrent build, 20,000 files, 25 MiB max file.
ranked.good_at: Removing the entire category of risk this list exists to warn about. Static asset requests are free and uncapped, and there is no per-GB egress rate anywhere in the pricing. On the free plan a spike does not generate a bill — once you pass 100,000 requests in a day, further operations 'fail with an error' until the day rolls over. Your site goes down; your card does not get charged.
ranked.the_catch: There is no spend cap on Workers Paid. Once you are on the $5 plan, request and CPU overage bills automatically with nothing to stop it — the only brake Cloudflare documents is setting a per-invocation CPU limit in your Wrangler config, which caps runaway compute per request but not total volume. The 10 ms CPU ceiling on free is also tighter than it sounds: any real server-rendering work blows through it. And the free storage write limits are brutally low — 1,000 KV writes a day means one bot crawling a form can lock your app for 24 hours.
ranked.wrong_for: Anything that needs a long-running process, a persistent connection, a large native dependency, or a Docker image. Use Railway or a VPS with Coolify for that.

ranked.name: Vercel
ranked.one_liner: Hobby literally cannot bill you. That is the point.
ranked.use_it_when: It's a Next.js app, or any framework front end, and it is a genuine personal project you are not making money from.
ranked.cost: Free Hobby (non-commercial only). Pro $20/seat/mo plus usage.
ranked.pricing_detail: Hobby typical monthly usage guidelines: up to 100 GB Fast Data Transfer, up to 10 GB Fast Origin Transfer, 4 CPU-hrs Active CPU, 360 GB-hrs Provisioned Memory, 1M function invocations, 5K image transformations, 300K image cache reads, 100K image cache writes, 50,000 Web Analytics events. Hobby build machines: 2 vCPU, 8 GB, 32 GB disk; 100 deployments/day; 200 projects; 1 hour of runtime logs. Pro includes the first 1 TB Fast Data Transfer and first 10,000,000 Edge Requests, then Fast Data Transfer is $0.15-$0.35 per GB and Edge Requests $2.00-$3.20 per million, both varying by region. Other Pro on-demand rates: Active CPU from $0.128/hr, Provisioned Memory from $0.0106 per GB-hr, invocations $0.60 per 1M, image transformations $0.05 per 1K, image cache writes $4.00 per 1M. Builds are $0.0035 per CPU-minute.
ranked.good_at: Being the safest free tier on this list for someone who is bad at watching dashboards. Hobby has no billing cycle at all: exceed a limit and, in Vercel's own words, 'you will have to wait until 30 days have passed before you can use the feature again.' There is no card, so there is no bill. Deploy-from-git and preview URLs are still the smoothest here, and Next.js works without you configuring anything.
ranked.the_catch: Hobby is restricted to non-commercial personal use, and Vercel's definition is far wider than people expect: any payment processing, any advertising of a product or service, any ad units including AdSense, affiliate linking as the site's main purpose, and — explicitly — asking for donations. Being paid to build or host the site also counts, so a client project on Hobby is a terms violation. The moment your side project earns anything you are on Pro at $20/seat plus usage, and Pro's protection is Spend Management, which pauses your production deployments when you cross your budget. Raising the budget does not un-pause anything — Vercel documents that paused projects must be resumed manually.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone with ads, donations, Stripe, or a paying client on the site who wants to stay free — that is a terms breach, not a grey area. Use Cloudflare Workers or a VPS instead. Also wrong for containers and background workers.

ranked.name: Railway
ranked.one_liner: Containers and a database, with a kill switch you configure
ranked.use_it_when: Your project is a Dockerfile plus Postgres plus a worker, and you want it deployed today without touching a server.
ranked.cost: No standing free tier. Hobby $5/mo, Pro $20/mo — each is a credit against usage.
ranked.pricing_detail: Trial: a one-time $5 credit on account creation, capped at 2 replicas, 1 GB RAM, 2 vCPU per service. Hobby: $5/month, which includes $5 of resource usage — the fee is a credit, not an allowance on top; caps of 6 replicas, 48 GB RAM, 48 vCPU, 5 GB volume per service. Pro: $20/month including $20 of usage; 42 replicas, 1 TB RAM, 1,000 vCPU, up to 1 TB volume. Usage rates: memory $0.00000386 per GB/sec (about $10 per GB/month), CPU $0.00000772 per vCPU/sec (about $20 per vCPU/month), network egress $0.05 per GB, volume storage $0.15 per GB-month, object storage $0.015 per GB-month.
ranked.good_at: Being the one platform here with a documented hard kill switch. You can set a hard usage limit and Railway states that 'once your resource usage hits the specified hard limit, all your workloads will be taken offline to prevent them from incurring further resource usage,' with warning emails at 75%, 90% and 100%. That is a real spend cap, not a spend alert. It also deploys arbitrary containers and managed databases with roughly the effort of a Vercel deploy.
ranked.the_catch: The $5 is a credit you burn, not headroom on top of the subscription — and always-on compute eats it fast at roughly $10 per GB of RAM per month, so a single 512 MB service plus a small Postgres is already past $5 before any traffic arrives. Egress is $0.05/GB, more than twice Fly's North America rate and infinitely more than Cloudflare's. And the kill switch is genuinely destructive: hitting it takes down your database alongside your app, which Railway's own docs flag as risky for anything you care about.
ranked.wrong_for: A plain static site — you would be paying for a running container to serve files Cloudflare serves free. Use Cloudflare Workers.

ranked.name: Coolify on your own VPS
ranked.one_liner: Fixed monthly cost. A spike breaks the box, not your bank
ranked.use_it_when: You want a Heroku-style git-push deploy but a bill that is the same number every month regardless of traffic, or your data can't sit on someone else's platform.
ranked.cost: Software free, Apache-2.0. Coolify Cloud $5/mo for 2 servers, +$3/mo per extra server. VPS billed separately.
ranked.pricing_detail: Self-hosting Coolify is free with, per its own pricing page, 'full access to all features' and 'no limitation or restrictions'; the repository is Apache-2.0, so commercial use is fine. Coolify Cloud (the hosted control plane that manages your servers for you) is $5/month covering 2 servers, plus $3/month per additional server, with 20% off annually — you still pay for the servers themselves. On the server side, DigitalOcean's cheapest Basic Droplet is $4.00/month for 512 MiB RAM, 1 vCPU, 10 GiB SSD with 500 GiB of included outbound transfer; inbound is always free. Hetzner is generally cheaper again, but its cloud prices are rendered client-side and could not be read at source on 2026-08-29 — check current pricing before you rely on a figure.
ranked.good_at: Cost predictability, which is the entire question here. A fixed VPS does not have an overage rate; a spike degrades the box or drops requests, and the invoice is unchanged. It also runs anything Docker runs, gives you real databases you own, and Apache-2.0 means no licence surprise if the project turns commercial.
ranked.the_catch: You are now the on-call engineer. Coolify does not patch your kernel, rotate your backups, or restore the box when a bad deploy wedges Docker on a 512 MB droplet — and 512 MB is not enough to run Coolify plus an app plus a build, so the $4 tier is a false economy. The default single-server setup has no redundancy, so any maintenance is downtime. And Coolify itself moves fast; upgrades occasionally break things, and there is no support contract when they do.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who does not want to think about servers ever again, or a project with no maintainer for weeks at a time. Use Render or Vercel.

ranked.name: Render
ranked.one_liner: Easiest real backend to stand up. Watch the bandwidth line.
ranked.use_it_when: You want a web service, a cron job and a Postgres in one dashboard, with the least configuration of any full-stack option here.
ranked.cost: Free tier with spin-down. Hobby workspace $0/mo, Pro $25/mo, Scale $499/mo. Compute billed on top.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free instances: 750 free instance hours per workspace per calendar month; free web services spin down after 15 minutes with no inbound traffic and take roughly a minute to wake, showing a loading page. Bandwidth is where it bites: Hobby gets 5 GB included per month, then $0.15 per GB; Pro 25 GB then $0.15 per GB; Scale 1 TB then $0.15 per GB. Build pipeline minutes: Hobby 500/month, Pro 1K/month, Scale 5K/month, then $5 per 1K minutes. Free Postgres databases expire 30 days after creation, with a 14-day grace period before Render deletes the database and all its data. Free Key Value (Redis) instances do not persist to disk, so all data is lost on restart and on upgrade to a paid plan.
ranked.good_at: Getting a working backend, database and background worker live faster than anything else on this list that isn't a PaaS you have to configure. Static sites deploy free. And Render's failure mode without a card on file is the safe one: it 'suspends all of your Free services for the remainder of the month' rather than billing you.
ranked.the_catch: 5 GB of included bandwidth on Hobby is the tightest allowance here by a wide margin, and once you have added a payment method Render bills the overage at $0.15/GB instead of suspending. A single 2 MB hero image on a page that gets 100,000 views is roughly 200 GB — about $30 on top of a plan that advertises itself as free. Add the 30-day expiry on free Postgres (with permanent deletion 14 days later) and the free tier is a demo, not a home.
ranked.wrong_for: A content-heavy or image-heavy site, and anything where 5 GB/month is plausible to exceed. Use Cloudflare Workers, where that traffic costs nothing.

also_considered.name: Netlify
also_considered.why_not: Free is now 300 credits/month and bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB — roughly 15 GB before the site pauses until the next cycle. Safe (it pauses, it doesn't bill; auto-recharge is off by default) but the ceiling is too low to rank.

also_considered.name: Fly.io
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely good for containers close to users, but there is no documented free allowance and no spend cap, and egress is metered at $0.02/GB in North America and Europe, $0.04 in Asia-Pacific and South America, $0.12 in Africa and India. Exactly the shape of bill this list warns about.

also_considered.name: GitHub Pages
also_considered.why_not: Free and fine for a static site — 1 GB published size, a soft 100 GB/month bandwidth limit, a soft 10 builds/hour — but GitHub prohibits running an online business, e-commerce or commercial SaaS on it, and there is no server-side code at all.

also_considered.name: DigitalOcean Droplet with plain Docker
also_considered.why_not: $4.00/month for 512 MiB, 1 vCPU, 10 GiB SSD and 500 GiB of outbound transfer is the cheapest fixed-cost route, but with no control plane you are hand-rolling deploys, TLS and rollbacks. Coolify on the same box gets you that for free.

also_considered.name: Deno Deploy Classic
also_considered.why_not: Excluded — discontinued. Deno shut down Deploy Classic (dash.deno.com) and the subhosting v1 API on 20 July 2026. The successor at console.deno.com is a different product; don't start anything on the old one.

watch_list: Whether Cloudflare ever ships a real spend cap on Workers Paid. It is the only thing keeping the top pick from being unambiguous for people who have added a card.
Netlify's credit conversion rate. At 20 credits per GB, the 300-credit free plan is about 15 GB; if that rate improves, Netlify re-enters the ranking.
Render's 5 GB Hobby bandwidth allowance. If it stays this low while overage is billed at $0.15/GB, Render should drop off the list entirely.
Vercel's non-commercial rule on Hobby, which currently catches ads and donations. Any relaxation would make Hobby the default answer for most side projects.

Cloudflare folding Pages into Workers. Cloudflare already points projects needing scale at Workers Static Assets rather than Pages; if Pages goes into maintenance, existing Pages deploys need a migration plan.
Whether anyone ships a hard spend cap that throttles rather than kills. Today the only real caps — Railway's and Vercel's — take your app offline, which is a different kind of bad day.
