code.pr-review.question: Which AI reviewer catches real bugs in my PRs without burying the team in nitpicks, and does my code leave my network?

method.how: Signal-to-noise decided the order, but nobody can measure it honestly, so it was approached sideways. First: what does the tool post by default, and how hard is it to turn the volume down without turning the tool off — a per-repo config file that ships in the repo beats a settings page nobody can find. Second: how does the bill scale when the bot is noisy? A per-seat price is predictable; a per-review credit is a meter that runs faster the more PRs you open, and a premium-request multiplier is a meter you may not know is running. Third: where does private code go, and is there a self-hosted build for people who can't answer 'a third party's AWS account' to that question. Raw bug-catch rate came last, deliberately, because the only public head-to-head is written by one of the vendors — see blind_note. Be clear-eyed: every tool here will still comment on things you do not care about in week one. The ones ranked highest are the ones that get quieter as you correct them, rather than the ones that claim to be right more often.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No PRs were reviewed, no false-positive rate was measured, no tool was run against a real codebase for a sprint. Every price, credit rule, rate limit, retention statement and platform list below was read from the vendor's own pricing page, docs or repository on 2026-08-29 and is quoted as the vendor states it. Cursor Bugbot is ranked without a price because Cursor does not publish one — that is stated in its entry rather than guessed at.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: There is no independent benchmark for AI pull-request review. The only public head-to-head comparison found is Greptile's own, at greptile.com/benchmarks: 50 real bugs, tools run in hosted cloud plans on default settings, scoring Greptile 82%, Bugbot 58%, Copilot 54%, CodeRabbit 44%, Graphite 6%, and on critical bugs Greptile 100% against Bugbot 64%, Copilot 57%, CodeRabbit 36%, Graphite 0%. Greptile designed, ran and published it, and it finished first in it. Treat it as a vendor claim, not evidence. Cursor's '70%+ of flags get resolved before merge' and Greptile's '43% comment acceptance rate' are likewise self-reported and are not measured the same way. Search results for 'best AI code review tool' in this category are close to worthless: they are dominated by the vendors' own comparison pages and by affiliate roundups, and several of the vendors publish a comparison table in which they win.
method.extra_note: Every entry states its billing unit (per seat, per review, per premium request), whether private repository code leaves your infrastructure, and whether a self-hosted build exists and at what tier — because those three are where buyers in this category get caught.

ranked.name: Greptile
ranked.one_liner: Fewest comments per PR, and unlimited repos per seat
ranked.use_it_when: You have tried an AI reviewer, your team muted it, and you want the one that posts least. Also when you have far more repositories than developers — Greptile charges per seat with unlimited repos, so a two-person team with forty services pays for two seats.
ranked.cost: Free Starter (1 developer, 50 credits/mo). Pro $30/seat/mo. Extra reviews $1 each.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter: free, 50 credits per month, unlimited repositories, 1 active developer. Pro: $30 per seat per month, 50 credits per seat per month, unlimited repositories, unlimited users, custom rules, unlimited external app integrations. Credits pool: 'One standard review uses 1 credit, one TREX review uses 3 credits, and additional credits are $1 each.' Enterprise: custom, and the only tier with self-hosting, SSO/SAML, GitHub Enterprise support and a custom DPA. 14-day free trial on Pro. Free for qualified non-commercial projects under MIT or Apache licences. 50% off for pre-Series A startups under $2M revenue.
ranked.good_at: Restraint. It learns the codebase over time and, per its docs, 'reads other engineers' comments to understand your coding standards' — so the corrections you leave on its comments are the tuning mechanism, rather than a config file you have to maintain. The credit model also makes the noise visible: if it is reviewing things you don't care about you can see it in the credit burn. Self-hosted Enterprise deployments can bring their own LLM via a custom base URL and keys, which is rare — most rivals' self-hosted builds still call the vendor's model endpoint.
ranked.the_catch: 50 credits per seat per month is roughly 50 pull requests, and a team that opens more than that per developer starts paying $1 a review on top of the $30 seat. A deep 'TREX' review costs 3 credits, so heavy use burns the allowance three times faster. Worse for anyone with a compliance question: Greptile's security page says it 'stores customer code on an encrypted filesystem on our servers' and that code 'remains cached on our machines until access is revoked in GitHub or GitLab', and AI training is opt-OUT, not opt-in — 'if you do not wish to permit Greptile to engage in AI training, you may manage preferences and settings related to AI training within your account'. Nobody flips that switch on day one because nobody knows it is there. Self-hosting, which is the only way code never leaves your servers, is Enterprise-only at an unpublished price.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone on Bitbucket or Azure DevOps, or anyone who needs breadth of platform support — use CodeRabbit. Open-source maintainers of commercial-licensed projects who don't qualify for the free non-commercial tier are also better off on CodeRabbit's open-source plan.

ranked.name: CodeRabbit
ranked.one_liner: Loudest by default, but the only one you can genuinely quieten
ranked.use_it_when: You need it on every platform your org actually uses — GitHub.com, GitLab.com, Bitbucket Cloud, Azure DevOps, GitHub Enterprise Server, self-managed GitLab and Bitbucket Data Center are all supported — or you maintain public repositories and want a real reviewer for nothing.
ranked.cost: Free tier (summaries only). Open-source free. Paid $24-$72/dev/mo annual; $30-$90 monthly.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free plan: unlimited public and private repositories, no card, but PR summarisation only — full reviews come through the VS Code extension and CLI, not on the PR. Open Source plan: unlimited public repositories, 'Open-source projects receive Team features with no paid subscription required', with rate limits that vary by project popularity. Essentials $24/developer/month billed annually or $30 monthly, rate-limited to 5 PR reviews per developer per hour under a fair-usage policy. Team $48 annual / $60 monthly. Advanced is quoted as $72/developer/month on the pricing page (billed annually) and $90/developer/month billed monthly in the docs. Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, RBAC, audit logging, API access and self-hosting. 14-day trial on all plans, no card.
ranked.good_at: Noise control that lives in the repo. `.coderabbit.yaml` has a `profile` setting documented as 'quiet for only the most important feedback, chill for balanced feedback, assertive for more feedback (which may feel nitpicky)' — default is chill. On top of that: path filters to exclude lock files and generated code, path-specific instructions by glob, automatic pickup of your existing `AGENTS.md` or `.cursorrules`, and custom pass/fail checks. It is also the clearest of the group on training: 'CodeRabbit never uses customer code for training. This remains true whether data retention is enabled or disabled', and 'Neither CodeRabbit, OpenAI, nor Anthropic uses your code to train our models.'
ranked.the_catch: Out of the box it is the chattiest reviewer here, and the default `chill` profile is still more comments than most teams will tolerate on a large PR — you will spend the first week editing `.coderabbit.yaml` down to `quiet` with aggressive path filters, and if nobody does that work the team mutes it. The free tier is a demo, not a product: it summarises PRs and nothing more. And self-hosting — the answer to 'can our code stay on our infrastructure' — is gated behind 'Enterprise customers with 500+ user seats'. If you are a 30-person company that cannot let code out, this tool has no plan for you, no matter what the Enterprise page implies. Note also that the vendor caches encrypted code and stores vector representations of your codebase by default; only self-hosted lets you opt out of all retention.
ranked.wrong_for: Small teams whose code legally cannot leave their network — the 500-seat self-hosting floor rules you out, so use PR-Agent. Teams that want minimal comments with no config work should start with Greptile instead.

ranked.name: Cursor Bugbot
ranked.one_liner: Bugs, not style. Nobody will tell you what it costs
ranked.use_it_when: Your team already pays for Cursor, and you want a reviewer that only opens its mouth for logic bugs — no style opinions, no summaries you didn't ask for.
ranked.cost: Included with Cursor Pro $20/mo, Pro+, Ultra, Teams $40/user/mo — then usage-based. No per-review price published: check current pricing.
ranked.pricing_detail: Cursor plans: Hobby free, Pro $20/month, Pro+ and Ultra unpriced on the page, Teams Standard $40/user/month, Enterprise custom. The Start plan does not include Bugbot. Cursor's docs say only 'Bugbot uses usage-based billing', 'Bugbot Teams bills from on-demand spend' and 'When you use all included Bugbot usage, additional Bugbot reviews bill from on-demand spend'. What the included usage is, and what a review costs beyond it, is not published anywhere readable. Autofix is billed separately: 'Autofix uses Cloud Agent credits and is billed at your plan rates.' 14-day free trial on all plans.
ranked.good_at: Precision as a design goal rather than a marketing line. Cursor states 'Bugbot detects the hardest logic bugs with a low false positive rate' and, as its own metric, '70%+ of flags get resolved before merge' and 'more than half of the bugs that we find are ultimately fixed by engineers' — both vendor-reported. Practically, it does two things that cut noise: incremental review is on by default so it only looks at changes since the last pass, and it reads both top-level and inline PR comments to 'avoid duplicate suggestions and build on prior feedback', so it stops re-litigating threads a human already closed. Platform coverage is broad: GitHub and GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab and GitLab Self-Hosted, Bitbucket and Bitbucket Data Center, Azure DevOps in limited availability.
ranked.the_catch: You cannot forecast the bill. There is no published per-review rate, no published included allowance, and reviews that exceed the invisible allowance silently draw from on-demand spend — which is exactly the shape of bill that arrives larger than expected in month two. The lever that would let you manage it works against you: 'effort levels are available only for usage-based Bugbot plans', and the High level is explicitly described as 'more expensive'. Rules are also capped — 30,000 characters per rule, 100,000 combined — so a large monorepo's conventions will not all fit. And there is no self-hosted build: your code is processed by Cursor.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who has to approve a budget before turning a tool on — you cannot, so use Greptile or CodeRabbit where the price is on the page. Also wrong for teams who want summaries, docstrings and style feedback; Bugbot deliberately does not do that.

ranked.name: PR-Agent
ranked.one_liner: MIT-licensed, self-hosted, your keys — code never leaves
ranked.use_it_when: Your code genuinely cannot leave your infrastructure and you are not a 500-seat enterprise, so none of the paid self-hosted tiers are open to you. Run it in your own CI with your own model key and nothing touches a vendor.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT licence, commercial use permitted. You pay LLM API tokens and hosting.
ranked.pricing_detail: No licence cost. Real cost is model tokens on whichever provider you point it at, plus the CI minutes or container you run it in. The README is blunt about the boundary: 'If you host PR-Agent with your OpenAI API key, it is between you and OpenAI.' Recent releases track current models — v0.41.0 added Claude Opus 5 support, v0.40.0 made GPT-5.6 the default and added Gemini 3.6.
ranked.good_at: Being the only entry where the answer to 'does private repo code leave our infrastructure' is a flat no without an enterprise contract. MIT means you can read the prompts, change them, and cut the checks you do not want — which is a more direct noise control than any config file, because you are editing the reviewer itself. Command-driven rather than automatic, so it comments when asked rather than on every push.
ranked.the_catch: Qodo has walked away from it. The README says 'Qodo has donated PR-Agent to the open-source community', that it is now 'fully community-owned' with one named external maintainer, and — the phrase that matters — describes it as a 'community-maintained legacy project' while Qodo's commercial product moved on. Volunteer maintenance means no SLA, no security response commitment, and a real chance the project drifts behind the commercial tools. It is also the weakest reviewer of the five in practice: it works from the diff with far less whole-repository context than Greptile or CodeRabbit, has no memory across PRs, so it will not learn from your corrections, and setting it up in CI is a day of work rather than a GitHub App install.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who wants a reviewer that improves as the team corrects it, or who does not want to own a CI integration — use Greptile or CodeRabbit. Also wrong if 'free' was the only reason: CodeRabbit's open-source plan gives public repos a better reviewer for nothing.

ranked.name: GitHub Copilot code review
ranked.one_liner: Already paid for, but each review now costs thirteen requests
ranked.use_it_when: Your org already pays for Copilot Business or Enterprise and you want a reviewer switched on this afternoon with zero procurement, zero new vendor, and no new place your code goes.
ranked.cost: Copilot Pro $10/mo, Pro+ $39/mo, Max $100/mo; Business $19/seat, Enterprise $39/seat. Each review burns 13 premium requests.
ranked.pricing_detail: Copilot Free does not include PR review — only 'Review selection' in VS Code. Pro $10/month with 300 premium requests per month; Pro+ $39/month with 1,500; Max $100/month; Business $19 per seat/month; Enterprise $39 per seat/month. The number that decides this: 'Each time Copilot reviews a pull request (when assigned as a reviewer) or reviews code in your IDE, 13 premium requests are consumed', and 'Starting June 1, 2026, Copilot code review will have a model multiplier of 13.' Overage is $0.04 per premium request, so a review beyond your allowance is about $0.52. GitHub's docs do not publish premium-request allowances for Business or Enterprise on that page.
ranked.good_at: Zero marginal trust. There is no new vendor, no new data processor, no new security review — the code is already going to GitHub. Nothing else here can be switched on by an org admin without a procurement conversation. It sits natively in the PR as an assigned reviewer, so there is no bot account to explain to the team.
ranked.the_catch: The 13x multiplier, applied 1 June 2026, quietly turned this from the cheap option into the metered one. On Copilot Pro's 300 premium requests a month, that is about 23 pull request reviews — and those same 300 requests are what your agent and chat usage draws from, so a developer who uses Copilot normally will run out mid-month and either stop getting reviews or start paying $0.04 a request. Nobody notices until the allowance is gone. Signal quality is the other problem: it has the least project-specific tuning of the five — no repo-level assertiveness dial comparable to CodeRabbit's `profile`, and no cross-PR learning comparable to Greptile's — so what it says in month three is much the same as month one.
ranked.wrong_for: Any team opening more than a couple of dozen PRs a month per developer — the premium-request maths makes it the expensive choice, not the cheap one, so use Greptile's flat seat or CodeRabbit's. Also wrong for anyone not already on GitHub.

also_considered.name: Graphite (Diamond)
also_considered.why_not: Unlimited AI reviews only from the $40/user/month Team tier; the free and $20 Starter tiers have 'limited AI Reviews'. It also comes bundled with a stacked-PR workflow you have to adopt to get value, and it finished last by a wide margin in the only published head-to-head — which was written by Greptile, so weigh it accordingly.

also_considered.name: Qodo (formerly Qodo Merge)
also_considered.why_not: Priced in credits at $.012/credit with packages quoted as '2,500 credits (~18 reviews/month)' — roughly $1.67 a review, which is opaque compared with a seat price, and the per-review credit cost is not published directly. On-prem and single-tenant SaaS exist but only on Enterprise, custom-priced, 30+ users. Free for open source.

also_considered.name: Gemini Code Assist for GitHub
also_considered.why_not: No longer a free way to get PR review. The feature comparison puts 'Gemini Code Assist for GitHub' on Standard ($19/user/month annual, $22.80 without) and Enterprise ($45/$54) only — the free individual tier does not include it. Also skips any file under .github/workflows, which is where a fair share of the risky changes live.

also_considered.name: Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer
also_considered.why_not: Excluded — being wound down. AWS's own docs state 'As of November 7, 2025, you can't create new repository associations in Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer.' Do not start here; the capability moved into Amazon Q Developer.

also_considered.name: Sourcery
also_considered.why_not: Still operating and does GitHub and GitLab PR review, but no price is shown on the product pages read, so it could not be compared honestly against the others on cost.

watch_list: Anyone publishing a genuinely independent, reproducible false-positive benchmark. Right now the only public head-to-head is written by a vendor that wins it, and the moment a neutral one exists this ranking should be rebuilt around it.
Whether GitHub reverses or reduces the 13x premium-request multiplier on Copilot code review. At 1x it is the obvious default for anyone already paying for Copilot; at 13x it is the fifth choice.
Greptile's 50-credit-per-seat allowance. If it rises, or if overage drops below $1 a review, the credit meter stops being the main reason to hesitate.
CodeRabbit's 500-seat floor on self-hosting. If a self-hosted build appears for teams under 100 people, it becomes the answer for regulated shops and PR-Agent's main reason to exist goes away.
Whether Cursor publishes an actual Bugbot price. Until it does, Bugbot cannot be recommended to anyone who has to justify a budget line.
Whether PR-Agent completes its move to an open-source foundation and picks up active maintainers, or whether 'legacy project' becomes 'unmaintained'.

docs.contract-review.question: Which AI actually flags the risky clauses in a contract — and can I upload a client's agreement without breaching confidentiality?

method.how: Nothing here replaces a lawyer, and the honest framing matters more in this category than any other on this site: a clause these tools miss can cost more than a decade of the subscription you saved. So the ranking is built on three things, in order. First, does the tool review against a stated standard — a playbook, a market benchmark, a checklist — or does it just summarise the document back to you? Summarising is not reviewing, and most 'AI contract review' marketing conflates the two. Second, does the vendor say plainly which governing law its standards assume? A tool trained on US commercial norms will read an England-and-Wales contract fluently and still miss the point. Third, what happens to the document: whether the vendor trains on it, whether it has a zero-data-retention agreement with the underlying model provider, and where the file is stored. That last test reordered the list twice.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No contracts were run through any of these tools, no clause-recall was measured, no output was checked by a lawyer. Prices, security claims, licences and jurisdiction coverage were read from the vendors' own pages and documentation on 2026-08-29. Four of the five picks do not publish a price at all; where that is the case this entry says so rather than repeating a number from a third-party listicle.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: One genuinely independent benchmark exists and it is thin. The Vals Legal AI Report (vals.ai, published 27 February 2025) tested legal AI against lawyer-produced baselines across seven tasks including redlining and document Q&A. Its own limitations are severe: vendors could opt out of individual tasks and several did (LexisNexis withdrew from most sections), the dataset came from a small law-firm consortium, and grading used an LLM-as-judge rather than full human review. It is also now eighteen months old and it covered enterprise research platforms — Harvey, CoCounsel, vLex, Vecflow — not one of the Word add-ins most small teams actually buy. None of Spellbook, LegalOn or Genie AI has been independently benchmarked on clause recall by anyone. Treat search results in this category with real suspicion: nearly every 'best AI contract review tool' page ranks its own publisher, and vendor accuracy claims below are attributed to whoever made them.
method.not_legal_advice: None of these tools give legal advice, and neither does this page. Every one of them will miss things. Use them to arrive at a lawyer's desk with better questions and a shorter list, not to skip the lawyer.

ranked.name: LegalOn
ranked.one_liner: Reviews against lawyer-written playbooks, and says which law they assume.
ranked.use_it_when: You are reviewing the same handful of agreement types repeatedly — NDAs, MSAs, DPAs, vendor terms — under US or England-and-Wales law, and you want the tool to flag deviations from a standard someone qualified actually wrote down.
ranked.cost: No published price. Quote-only, per seat. Free trial offered.
ranked.pricing_detail: Three plans on the pricing page — Core Review (solo attorneys and fractional GCs), Contracting Suite (in-house teams) and Productivity Suite — with no numbers against any of them. The page says pricing is 'priced around your team size and the capabilities you need', confirms a per-seat model, claims zero implementation fees, and states unlimited AI review, redlining and repository storage on all plans. To get a figure you book a demo. Read that as the usual consequence: you cannot compare cost against the alternatives here without sitting through a sales call.
ranked.good_at: Jurisdiction honesty, which almost nobody else in this category offers. The pricing page states coverage for US agreements and England-and-Wales governed contracts, with international playbooks for 23+ countries — a specific claim you can hold them to, rather than 'works in 80+ countries', which usually means the software is sold there, not that the legal standards are localised. On the data side it is the strongest of the five: LegalOn's security page states its LLM providers are contractually bound so that no customer data is used to train, retrain or improve their models and no customer data is stored for any period, even for abuse monitoring — plus SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001:2022 and ISO 27017:2015.
ranked.the_catch: You will not know what it costs until you have given a salesperson your details, and per-seat pricing on a quote basis is where small teams quietly get charged more per head than large ones. Second catch, and the one that bites later: LegalOn's security page states its infrastructure runs on AWS and GCP in the US. If you act for EU or UK clients whose engagement terms or DPAs require data residency in-region, that is a blocker you find at procurement, not at trial. Third: '23+ countries' of international playbooks is not the same depth as the US and England-and-Wales coverage — assume the flagship jurisdictions are deep and the rest are thinner until you have tested your own.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone reviewing one contract a quarter — the seat licence will not pay back. Use Claude Pro with a written checklist instead. Also wrong if your data must stay in the EU or UK; Genie AI hosts in UK and EU data centres.

ranked.name: Spellbook
ranked.one_liner: Redlines inside Word against your standards, then benchmarks the terms.
ranked.use_it_when: You negotiate in Microsoft Word all day, you have house positions you can encode as a playbook, and you want to know whether the indemnity cap you have been offered is normal for this kind of deal.
ranked.cost: No published price. Per-seat licence, quote-only. 7-day free trial.
ranked.pricing_detail: The pricing page publishes no tiers and no numbers. It states only that 'pricing is determined by the number of team members on a license' and directs you to book a demo. The free trial is 7 days, with extended trials said to be available to larger organisations — which tells you where the commercial attention goes. The suite is described as Review, Draft, Ask, Benchmarks and Playbooks, with 'Associate' (a multi-document agent) presented as a premium capability; the page does not say which tier it sits in, so confirm before you buy on the strength of a demo that used it.
ranked.good_at: Two things the others do not do as well. It lives in Word, so the redline arrives where the negotiation already is rather than in a separate web app you have to copy out of. And Benchmarks compares your terms against thousands of similar agreements, which answers a different and more useful question than 'is this clause risky' — namely 'is this clause unusual', which is what you actually argue with on a call. Security posture is solid and specific: the security page states zero-data-retention agreements with both OpenAI and Anthropic, with customer data in requests and responses 'not persisted' and existing only in memory, plus SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA with BAA available, GDPR, and a low-risk EU AI Act assessment.
ranked.the_catch: Spellbook does not publish which legal systems its standards assume. The homepage says 4,500 teams in 80+ countries and lists privacy-regulation compliance — that is a distribution claim, not a jurisdictional one, and this entry could not find a supported-governing-law list at source. For a tool whose whole job is flagging non-market terms, the market it is comparing against matters enormously, and you cannot check it before you buy. The other catch is timing: 7 days is not enough to test a playbook properly on real deals, and when it runs out you are back to a sales call with no price to anchor against. Storage is Canada and US, per the security page.
ranked.wrong_for: Teams who do not work in Word, or who need documented coverage of a specific non-US governing law before signing anything — LegalOn states its jurisdictions, Spellbook does not. Skip it entirely if you need a published price to get budget approved.

ranked.name: Genie AI
ranked.one_liner: The only one here that publishes a price and hosts in the UK.
ranked.use_it_when: You are a UK or EU business, you need the file to stay in-region, and you want to try a legal-specific reviewer today without booking a call with anyone.
ranked.cost: Free tier (exports locked). Pro $75/mo, $59/mo annual. Business $320/mo, $259/mo annual.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0, no card, full AI toolkit, 500+ templates, DOCX editor and PDF import — but exports are locked until you upgrade and AI tokens are limited, so it demos rather than works. Pro: $75/month, or $59/month billed annually ($708/year), one user, unlimited exports, review/redline/negotiate, insights from 50 documents, and a token allowance the pricing page describes as 10x Free — 'approximately 5 documents per month'. Business: $320/month, or $259/month annually ($3,108/year), 5 users, playbooks and negotiation rules, insights from 250 documents, 5x Pro tokens shared across the whole team. Enterprise: custom, stated as starting from $600/month, billed annually.
ranked.good_at: Transparency and data residency. It is the only pick here where you can read the actual number before talking to anyone. Its security page states customer contracts are never used to train shared or internal AI models, that documents are hosted on AWS in UK and EU data centres, and that its LLM providers (OpenAI and Anthropic) operate under zero-data-retention agreements. It holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification (certificate #310012019, current to February 2029, most recent external audit April 2026). For a UK-based founder who cannot send client documents to US infrastructure, that combination is genuinely hard to find at this price.
ranked.the_catch: Two traps, both one tier above where you will look. First, the jurisdiction coverage — '150+ international jurisdictions and 10+ languages' — is an Enterprise feature, from $600/month billed annually. Pro and Business do not list it. If you bought Pro expecting localised review of a German or Australian contract, you bought the wrong tier. Second, the token cap: Pro's allowance is described on the vendor's own page as roughly five documents a month, for $75. That is $15 a contract, against Claude Pro at $17/month for as many as your usage limits allow. Also note it holds ISO 27001 but its security page explicitly states it does not hold SOC 2 — some enterprise procurement teams will stop there. And the pricing page's claim that its 'Eidetic Intelligence' outperforms Claude and ChatGPT is the vendor's, unbenchmarked by anyone independent.
ranked.wrong_for: High-volume reviewers — the token maths falls apart fast; LegalOn and Spellbook sell unlimited-review seats instead. Anyone who needs non-UK/US jurisdiction packs on a small budget, since those sit behind Enterprise.

ranked.name: Claude Pro
ranked.one_liner: No legal playbook, but it reads long contracts and costs nothing much.
ranked.use_it_when: You are a founder or ops lead checking your own SaaS terms, a lease or a supplier agreement a few times a year, you have written down the ten things you care about, and you want a fast first pass before deciding whether it is worth a lawyer's time.
ranked.cost: Free tier. Pro $20/mo, $17/mo annual. Max from $100/mo. Team $25/seat/mo, $20 annual.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free: $0. Pro: $20/month, or $17/month billed annually, including projects. Max: from $100/month, offered at 5x or 20x Pro usage. Team: $20/seat/month annual or $25 monthly for a standard seat, $100/$125 for a premium seat, minimum 2 and maximum 150 people, and the pricing page states no model training on Team content. Enterprise: $20/seat/month plus usage at API rates, annual billing only.
ranked.good_at: Cost and reach. It will read a 90-page agreement in one pass, answer follow-up questions about a specific sub-clause, and explain in plain English why a limitation-of-liability carve-out matters — for roughly a fifth of the cheapest legal-specific tool here. On the confidentiality question it is also the better of the two big consumer chatbots: Anthropic's help centre states consumer chats are used to improve models only if you choose to allow it, with Incognito chats excluded even then. OpenAI's equivalent page states that ChatGPT Free, Plus and Pro content is used to train models by default, with opt-out available — which is the wrong default for someone else's contract.
ranked.the_catch: It has no playbook and no market benchmark, so it finds what you ask it to find and stays quiet about the rest. That is the exact failure mode that costs money: the missing clause, the one you did not know to ask about, the assignment-on-change-of-control that nobody flagged because nobody mentioned it. It also has no jurisdiction awareness unless you supply it — ask about a contract governed by Scots or NSW law and you may get confident US-shaped reasoning back. And a consumer subscription is not a confidentiality wrapper: if the document belongs to a client, check your engagement terms, their NDA and, if you are regulated, your professional conduct rules before it leaves your machine. Consumer tiers carry no zero-data-retention commitment of the kind Spellbook, LegalOn and Genie AI have with their providers.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone reviewing client contracts under a duty of confidentiality, or reviewing at volume against house positions. Use LegalOn or Spellbook, whose vendors have contractual zero-retention terms and a written playbook. Also wrong if you want a redline back in Word — this gives you prose.

ranked.name: OpenContracts
ranked.one_liner: Self-hosted and MIT-licensed, for documents that cannot leave.
ranked.use_it_when: The contracts legally cannot go to a third-party SaaS — regulated client work, a government engagement, a data agreement that forbids it — and you have someone who can run Docker and wire up your own model endpoint.
ranked.cost: Free. MIT licence, commercial use permitted. Your infrastructure and model costs.
ranked.pricing_detail: No licence fee. MIT is a permissive licence — use, modify, distribute and commercialise with minimal restriction, so unlike some 'open' legal tooling there is no non-commercial clause waiting for you. Real cost is hosting, whatever model you point it at (self-hosted weights, or an API key with its own per-token bill and its own data terms), and the engineering time to keep it running.
ranked.good_at: It is the only option here where the document never leaves your infrastructure at all — Docker Compose deployment is documented for both development and production. The architecture is also the right shape for legal work: it builds a citation graph from human annotations on the actual document, and its agents are designed to ground answers in that structured data rather than free-generate. If your objection to the SaaS tools is 'I cannot verify what it read', this is the one that answers it.
ranked.the_catch: It is a document intelligence and annotation platform, not a contract-risk reviewer. Nothing in it knows what a bad indemnity looks like. There is no playbook, no market benchmark, no jurisdiction knowledge and no clause library of legal standards — you supply the model, the prompts and, critically, the legal judgement about what to look for. Which means the thing you were hoping to buy, you still have to build. Budget for a competent engineer and a lawyer defining the checklist together, and be honest that the total cost may exceed a LegalOn seat. Maintenance looks active (12,725 commits on main, open PRs and issues), but it is a small open-source project — assume no support SLA.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone without engineering support, and anyone who wanted risk-flagging out of the box. If the driver is data residency rather than absolute control, Genie AI's UK/EU hosting solves it with no ops burden.

also_considered.name: Harvey
also_considered.why_not: Enterprise-only and demo-gated — no published price, no self-serve signup, sold to law firms and large in-house teams. It did top five of seven tasks in the Vals report, so if you are that buyer it belongs on your list; if you are reading this, you are probably not.

also_considered.name: Luminance
also_considered.why_not: No pricing and no free trial published on its site; the homepage lists six capability areas and a 'request a demo' button. Nothing to evaluate at source, and this entry will not quote a price it could not read.

also_considered.name: Robin AI
also_considered.why_not: The homepage advertises a free Microsoft Word add-in, which is genuinely interesting, but the pricing URL returns 404 and the domain blocks automated fetching of its product pages, so the add-in's limits and data terms could not be verified at source. 'Trained on millions of clauses' is the vendor's claim; the page does not say whose clauses.

also_considered.name: ChatGPT
also_considered.why_not: Capable enough, but the default is wrong for this job: OpenAI's help centre states Free, Plus and Pro content is used to train models by default with opt-out available, while business and API tiers are not trained on by default. Claude's consumer default is opt-in, which is why it took the slot.

also_considered.name: Lexion
also_considered.why_not: Acquired by Docusign — its own site leads with 'Lexion joins forces with Docusign!' The page still sells the product but says nothing about standalone availability, migration or sunset timeline. Do not start a new procurement on a product whose future the vendor will not state.

also_considered.name: Evisort
also_considered.why_not: Effectively gone as a standalone brand: evisort.com now 302-redirects to workday.com. Whatever the capability became inside Workday, you can no longer buy it as Evisort.

watch_list: A follow-up to the Vals Legal AI Report that tests the Word add-ins — Spellbook, LegalOn, Definely — on clause recall rather than testing enterprise research platforms. That single publication would reorder this list, because right now nobody has independently measured what these tools miss.

Spellbook or LegalOn publishing a per-seat number. Both are quote-only today; a public price would let small teams compare them against Genie AI's $59-$75 without a sales call, and would move whichever publishes first.
EU or UK data residency from LegalOn or Spellbook. Both host in North America; either adding in-region storage removes Genie AI's clearest structural advantage.
Genie AI unbundling jurisdiction packs from Enterprise, or raising the Pro token allowance above roughly five documents a month. Either change makes it a much stronger mid-list pick.
Any change to consumer chatbot training defaults, in either direction. Anthropic's consumer opt-in posture is the reason Claude ranks where it does; if that flips, the pick flips.

An open-source project that ships an actual clause-risk playbook on top of a local model — OpenContracts plus a maintained, jurisdiction-tagged risk library would be the first genuinely free answer to this job rather than a toolkit for building one.

docs.invoice-extract.question: I need invoice and receipt data as clean JSON. What actually works, what does a page really cost, and who checks the errors?

method.how: Nothing in this category is good enough to run unattended on real supplier mail. Every tool here will get a line item wrong on a creased thermal receipt or a non-English invoice, so the ranking is driven by three things: how much of the field structure you get without writing your own post-processing, whether a correction workflow is included or is something you build, and whether you can read a per-page price on the vendor's own site before you commit. Tools that publish a number per page rank above tools that publish a plan price and a slider that disagrees with it. Data residency and licence terms decided the last slot.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No invoices or receipts were run through any of these. Prices, language lists, deprecation dates and licences were read from the vendors' own pages and GitHub repos on 2026-08-29. Azure's paid per-page rates could not be read at source at all — the pricing table renders placeholders and pushes you to the signed-in calculator, so no Azure paid rate is quoted here.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: The nearest independent benchmark is OmniDocBench (OpenDataLab, accepted at CVPR 2025): 1,651 annotated PDF pages across ten document categories including financial reports and handwritten notes, in English, Simplified Chinese and mixed. It scores document parsing — text, tables, formulas, reading order — not invoice field accuracy, and it does not cover the parser APIs ranked here. There is no independent public benchmark that scores commercial invoice extraction at line-item level across languages. Search results for this category are dominated by vendors running their own leaderboards and ranking themselves first; treat any accuracy percentage you see as a vendor claim.

ranked.name: Azure AI Document Intelligence
ranked.one_liner: Strongest prebuilt invoice and receipt models; pricing hidden behind a calculator.
ranked.use_it_when: You have mixed supplier invoices and thermal receipts, you need line items and tax totals as typed fields with confidence scores, and you want either a free tier to prototype on or a container you can run inside your own network for data residency.
ranked.cost: Free tier 500 pages/month. Paid: check current pricing.
ranked.pricing_detail: The free (F0) tier is listed on Microsoft's pricing page as 0-500 pages free per month. The S0 pay-as-you-go table lists Read, Prebuilt Models (invoice, receipt, layout, ID, tax forms), Custom Classification and Custom Extraction as separate per-1,000-page meters, but every figure renders as a placeholder and the page directs you to the signed-in Azure pricing calculator or a sales specialist — so no paid rate is quoted here. Monthly commitment tiers exist at 20,000, 100,000 and 500,000+ pages, separately for cloud and connected containers. Human review is not part of the service at any tier: you build the review UI yourself.
ranked.good_at: The prebuilt invoice model returns supplier, totals, tax and line items as typed fields with per-field confidence, rather than a wall of text you have to regex. prebuilt-receipt handles thermal and hotel receipts, and Microsoft's OCR language list covers 160-plus languages for printed text and 135-plus for handwriting. It is also the only major cloud parser you can deploy as a container, including disconnected, for documents that cannot leave your infrastructure.
ranked.the_catch: You cannot read a paid price on the pricing page. The numbers only populate in the signed-in calculator, so budgeting means a detour before you write a line of code, and rule one of this site is not quoting numbers we cannot read. Worse for anyone outside Western Europe: Microsoft's language-support page lists the current v4.0 invoice model as covering seven languages — English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch — while the 30-plus language list sits on the older v3.1 model. Check your locale before you assume it is covered. And the 135-language handwriting support belongs to the Read model, not the invoice model: handwritten amendments on a receipt often come back as recognised text that never lands in the right field.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs an approver queue out of the box — that is Rossum. Anyone who needs a published per-page price to model cost before starting — Google Document AI publishes one. Anyone whose invoices are mostly Japanese, Polish or Turkish should verify the v4.0 language list first and consider Google.

ranked.name: Document AI Invoice Parser
ranked.one_liner: Public $10 per 1,000 pages; Google keeps switching parts off.
ranked.use_it_when: You want a per-page price you can read and model today, you are already on GCP, and you are prepared to pin processor versions and re-test when Google retires them.
ranked.cost: $10 per 1,000 pages (invoice/expense parser). No free monthly quota.
ranked.pricing_detail: Invoice Parser and Expense Parser bill at $0.10 per every 10 pages in a document, i.e. $10 per 1,000 pages — a 91-100 page document costs $1.00. Enterprise Document OCR is $1.50 per 1,000 pages to 5M pages/month, then $0.60. Custom Extractor is $30 per 1,000 pages to 1M, then $20, plus $0.05 per hour per deployed processor version — that hosting charge runs whether or not you send traffic. Some document types bill per classified document instead of per page: bank statement $0.75, pay slip $0.30, W2 $0.30. Failed 4xx/5xx requests are not billed. No free monthly quota is documented on the pricing page. Human review costs nothing because it no longer exists (see the catch).
ranked.good_at: Transparent per-page pricing published on a page you can read without signing in, a separate Expense Parser tuned for receipts, and a Custom Extractor for when the prebuilt schema misses fields your suppliers use. Broad printed-language coverage on the underlying OCR.
ranked.the_catch: Human-in-the-Loop was deprecated on 16 January 2024, along with Document AI Warehouse. There is no built-in review queue and there will not be one — you build the correction UI and the audit trail. Google also retires processor versions on a published schedule: the deprecation page lists Custom Extractor foundation model versions shut down in April 2025, September 2025 and March 2026, Expense Parser v1.2-v1.4 shut down April 2025, and a further batch of parsers going dark on 30 June 2026. Pinning a version buys you months, not years, and each forced migration means re-testing extraction accuracy against your own documents.
ranked.wrong_for: Teams that need a validation and approval workflow rather than raw JSON — use Rossum. Teams whose documents cannot go to a US or EU public cloud — use Unstract self-hosted or an Azure container.

ranked.name: Mindee
ranked.one_liner: Cleanest developer experience; the plan price and credit slider disagree.
ranked.use_it_when: You want a usable invoice JSON out of a single API call today, you are not on a hyperscaler and do not want to be, and your volume is steady enough to justify a subscription.
ranked.cost: No free tier — 14-day trial. Starter from $44/mo; credits about $0.044 per page.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter is listed at $44/month with an annual option at $529/year; Pro at $116/month or $1,393/year, which adds unlimited seats, live chat support and data processing localisation. Both plans price credits at roughly $0.044 per credit with volume options from 6,000 to 300,000 credits per month. One credit equals one physical page submitted, regardless of document type or file format, with no complexity surcharge — a clean model. Enterprise requires 500,000+ credits committed annually. Caveat: the headline plan price and the credit slider on the same page do not reconcile (6,000 credits at $0.044 is far more than $44), so get the volume included at your quoted price in writing before you sign. Human review is not offered.
ranked.good_at: Time from signup to a parsed invoice. Flat per-page billing with no per-field or per-complexity upcharge, polygons and confidence scores on every field, and model chaining if you need to route document types. Not tied to any cloud account.
ranked.the_catch: There is no permanent free tier — after 14 days you are on a paid plan, so there is no way to run 50 invoices a month for nothing. You pay a platform fee before the first page, which makes low volumes expensive per document. And the pricing page's plan price and credit slider genuinely do not add up, which is exactly the kind of ambiguity that becomes an unpleasant invoice in month two. Like the hyperscalers, it hands you JSON and no correction workflow.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone doing a few hundred documents a month — Azure's 500 free pages or Dext at $25.21/month will be cheaper. Anyone who needs humans in the loop — Rossum.

ranked.name: Rossum
ranked.one_liner: Human review is the product, not an add-on. Enterprise money.
ranked.use_it_when: You run accounts payable at volume, exceptions must be handled by named people with an audit trail, and you are integrating with SAP, NetSuite, Coupa or Dynamics rather than writing code against an API.
ranked.cost: Starter from $18,000/year. Business, Enterprise and Ultimate are quoted.
ranked.pricing_detail: Starter is published as 'starting at $18,000 per year' and includes unlimited seats, document ingestion, Aurora Document AI, the validation screen for exception handling, a 12-month archive and API access. Business adds custom business logic, master-data matching, duplicate detection, an intelligent mailbox, custom functions and webhooks. Enterprise adds SSO, a sandbox, document translation, preferred cloud location and custom branding. Ultimate adds multi-document transactions, a custom email domain, an embeddable UI and a 3-year archive. Pricing is by volume of pages or documents; no per-document rate is published for any tier.
ranked.good_at: This is the only one of the five where human-in-the-loop is included rather than something you build or buy separately: an ergonomic validation screen for exceptions, duplicate detection and master-data matching against your supplier records. Pre-built integrations with SAP (certified), Coupa, NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics, Workday, plus UiPath, Blue Prism, Automation Anywhere, Celonis and Zapier.
ranked.the_catch: $18,000 a year is the floor and everything above it is a sales call — no per-document rate appears anywhere, so you cannot model cost against your volume before talking to someone. The integration list is ERP-shaped: SAP, NetSuite, Dynamics, Coupa, Workday. Xero and QuickBooks are not on it, which rules it out for most of the small businesses that most need automated AP. And the validation screen only pays for itself if you actually staff it; buying Rossum and then not reviewing is buying an expensive parser.
ranked.wrong_for: Small businesses on Xero, QuickBooks or Sage — use Dext. Builders who want an API and nothing else — Mindee or Google Document AI at a fraction of the cost.

ranked.name: Unstract
ranked.one_liner: AGPL self-host for documents that legally cannot leave your network.
ranked.use_it_when: Your invoices contain data that cannot go to a third-party cloud, you can run Docker and supply your own LLM endpoint, and you would rather define the extraction schema in plain English than train a model.
ranked.cost: Self-host free under AGPL-3.0. Cloud from $499/mo (5,000 pages).
ranked.pricing_detail: The community edition is AGPL-3.0 and self-hosts via Docker; the software costs nothing, but you supply your own LLM API keys, so your real per-page cost is whatever your model provider charges plus your compute. Cloud Starter is $499/month, or $416/month billed annually, for 5,000 pages with $0.10/page overage. Growth is $2,249/month, or $1,874/month annually, for 25,000 pages with $0.09/page overage. Enterprise is custom and can be cloud or self-hosted. Human-in-the-loop review is a paid-tier feature, as are LLMChallenge dual-LLM verification, SSO/SAML, audit logs and the SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / HIPAA / GDPR compliance posture.
ranked.good_at: The only option on this list where the documents never leave your infrastructure and the licence is genuinely open. You define what to extract as natural-language prompts in Prompt Studio and deploy it as an API or an ETL pipeline, which beats training a custom extractor when your supplier formats keep changing.
ranked.the_catch: AGPL-3.0 is the trap most people miss. Running it internally is fine. Exposing it as a network service to anyone outside your organisation triggers the source-disclosure obligation on your modifications — check with legal before you wrap it in a customer-facing product. 'Free' is only the licence: you still pay a model provider for every page, so per-document cost is real and variable, and it is on you to cap it. And the human review queue that invoice work actually needs is a paid-edition feature, so the community edition gives you extraction with no correction workflow at all. Accuracy is whatever your chosen LLM manages on your documents — there is no vendor model being tuned on invoices for you.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose data can go to a public cloud — Google Document AI is cheaper per page and needs no ops team. Anyone who wants a supported review queue without an AGPL conversation with legal — Rossum, or Unstract's own paid tiers.

also_considered.name: AWS Textract (AnalyzeExpense)
also_considered.why_not: $10 per 1,000 pages, same as Google, but the free tier is only 100 expense pages a month for three months, and human review means wiring up and separately paying for Amazon A2I.

also_considered.name: Veryfi
also_considered.why_not: Verified per-document pricing ($0.08 a receipt, $0.16 an invoice, $0.25 a bank statement) and a free 100 documents/month tier — but the Starter plan carries a $500/month minimum commitment, which is steep unless receipts are your core product.

also_considered.name: Dext
also_considered.why_not: $25.21/month, or $302.50 billed annually, for 250 documents and 5 users, with 30-plus accounting integrations including Xero, QuickBooks Online and Sage. The right answer if you want bookkeeping rather than an API — which is why it is not ranked on a builder's list.

also_considered.name: Nanonets
also_considered.why_not: Repriced to per-block workflow credits — roughly $0.02 to $0.30 per block run, with a typical invoice workflow running four to six blocks. You cannot forecast a per-document cost until you have built the workflow, which is the wrong order.

also_considered.name: Google Document AI Human-in-the-Loop and Document AI Warehouse
also_considered.why_not: Both deprecated on 16 January 2024. Excluded outright — do not build a review workflow or a document store on either.

also_considered.name: Docling (IBM)
also_considered.why_not: MIT-licensed, genuinely good at turning a PDF into structured layout, tables and reading order, and no commercial restrictions. But it does not extract invoice fields — you would still bolt an LLM on top, which is what Unstract already is.

watch_list: Whether Microsoft extends the v4.0 invoice model beyond its seven listed languages. That alone would reorder the top two for anyone outside Western Europe.
Google's next deprecation batch. Another turndown of Invoice or Expense Parser versions, like the 30 June 2026 group, pushes Document AI down the list.

Frontier vision models called directly. If a general-purpose model gets cheap and reliable enough on line-item tables, the per-page parser APIs lose their reason to exist and this list becomes a list of review workflows.
Anyone publishing an independent, line-item-level invoice benchmark across languages and handwriting. Today there is none, and the whole category grades its own homework.
Unstract moving human-in-the-loop review into the community edition, or relicensing away from AGPL-3.0.
Rossum publishing a per-document rate, or adding Xero and QuickBooks — either would make it viable well below the $18,000 floor.

marketing.campaign-audit.question: My campaign's numbers fell off a cliff. Which tool actually diagnoses why, rather than redrawing Ads Manager in nicer colours?

method.how: Ranked on one test: does the tool reach a conclusion you couldn't reach yourself in Ads Manager? Most of this category fails it — they re-plot the same API data and call the chart an insight, so anything that is only a dashboard was pushed to also_considered. After that, the order is set by platform coverage (search and social both, or just one), by whether the recommendations are threshold rules you could write yourself versus something genuinely computed (statistical significance testing, modelled attribution), and by how honestly the price is published. Pricing here is almost universally banded by your monthly ad spend, which means the tool gets more expensive precisely as the account gets harder to fix — treat any spend-linked price as a tax on scaling and check the band above yours before you sign. Be warned that nothing in this category diagnoses creative, targeting, tracking and measurement all at once; you will end up owning two tools or accepting a blind spot.
method.tested_on: Not independently tested. No accounts were connected, no audits were run. Prices were read from each vendor's own pricing page on 2026-08-29; where a page hides its numbers behind a spend slider or a sales form, that is stated rather than guessed.
method.conflicts: None. No affiliate links, no paid placements, no relationship with any tool listed.
method.blind_note: No independent benchmark exists for PPC audit tools — nobody runs the same broken account through all of them and scores the findings. G2 and Capterra scores are vendor-solicited. Search results for this job are dominated by the vendors ranking themselves and by affiliate roundups that reorder the list by commission, so treat any 'best PPC audit tool' article, including comparisons published by the tools above, as advertising.

ranked.name: Adalysis
ranked.one_liner: Deepest search-side audit; finds waste, tests ads properly
ranked.use_it_when: The money is going out through Google or Microsoft search and you need to know which keywords, ad variants and settings are burning it — with statistical significance behind the ad-testing verdicts rather than a hunch about last week's numbers.
ranked.cost: 30-day free trial. Vendor's pricing page says from $149/mo; check current pricing.
ranked.pricing_detail: One plan in three tiers, priced by maximum monthly ad spend on a slider. All tiers include unlimited Google Ads accounts, unlimited Microsoft Ads accounts and unlimited users. Monthly, six-month (10% off) or annual (15% off) billing; USD or EUR. Trial length rises with tier: 30 days at tier 1, extendable 45 days at tier 2, extendable 60 days at tier 3. The actual tier prices are rendered by the slider and are not in the page source — the $149 figure comes from the pricing page's own description text and is a floor, not your quote.
ranked.good_at: Genuine analysis rather than a rules list: it runs statistical significance testing across ad and RSA variants, so 'this ad is worse' is a computed result, not a threshold someone picked. Unlimited accounts and unlimited users at every tier is unusually generous for an agency — most rivals charge per account. 40+ audit checks across budgets, bidding, ad management and account structure.
ranked.the_catch: Google Ads and Microsoft Ads only. If the failing campaign is Meta, TikTok or Amazon, this tool is blind to it and you have bought nothing. Because the price is set by an ad-spend slider you cannot read without configuring it, you can be quoted well above the advertised floor — and the spend band is a ceiling, so a good month can push you into the next tier. Day three is spent muting alerts: 40+ tools means 40+ things it wants to tell you about, and the signal only appears once you have turned most of them off.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone whose problem is on Meta or TikTok — Adalysis does not connect there at all; use Optmyzr for cross-platform or Motion for creative. Also wrong for a single small account spending a few thousand a month, where Opteo at a published $129 or Adzooma's free plan gets you most of the same findings.

ranked.name: Optmyzr
ranked.one_liner: Broadest platform coverage; audits, alerts and a rule engine
ranked.use_it_when: You run spend across several platforms and need one place that will audit all of them — Google, Microsoft, Meta, LinkedIn, Amazon, Shopping and Performance Max — instead of logging into five interfaces and eyeballing five sets of charts.
ranked.cost: No public prices. Priced by monthly ad spend band; add-ons on top. Check current pricing.
ranked.pricing_detail: Essentials, Premium and Enterprise. Prices are rendered dynamically against monthly ad-spend brackets running from $25K to $500K+ and do not appear in the page source; annual billing is advertised at 30% off. Enterprise is quote-only with unlimited ad accounts under a fair-usage policy. Two things sit outside the plan price: Campaign Automator from $249/mo and Optmyzr for Amazon Ads from $66/mo. Setup service is $199/hour on Essentials; Premium includes one hour, Enterprise four. Essentials gets one onboarding Q&A session and 24-hour email support; the competitor benchmarks, smart placement exclusions and the full Shopping/PMax toolset are Premium-only.
ranked.good_at: Coverage no one else on this list matches — search, social, retail media and PMax audited from one account, which matters when the honest answer to 'why is this underperforming' is 'you moved budget to PMax and lost visibility'. The rule engine lets you encode your own diagnostic checks instead of accepting the vendor's thresholds.
ranked.the_catch: You cannot find out what it costs without engaging sales, and the features you'd assume were included are separate line items: Campaign Automator is $249/mo on top and Amazon Ads is another $66/mo. The 'AI-powered account insights' are the vendor's own description, not a verified capability — much of what arrives is threshold-based, and the thresholds are yours to configure. On Essentials you get one onboarding session and are then billed $199/hour for setup help, which is a real cost for a tool this large.
ranked.wrong_for: A solo advertiser on one Google account — the breadth is dead weight and the quote will reflect it; use Opteo. Also wrong if you need a price before a sales call, in which case Opteo or Adzooma publish theirs.

ranked.name: Opteo
ranked.one_liner: Cheapest real Google Ads engine with prices actually published
ranked.use_it_when: You manage Google Ads, you want a continuous stream of concrete 'change this bid, add this negative, pause this keyword' improvements, and you want to know the bill before you talk to anyone.
ranked.cost: Free trial. $129, $249 or $499/mo by accounts and spend.
ranked.pricing_detail: Basic $129/mo — 10 accounts, $25,000 total monthly spend, 24-hour data refresh. Professional $249/mo — 25 accounts, $100,000 spend, 12-hour refresh. Agency $499/mo — 75 accounts, $250,000 spend, 12-hour refresh. Enterprise is custom with a 6-hour refresh, for spend above $250,000/mo. Two months free on annual billing. No-questions-asked refund on the most recent invoice. Trial length is not stated on the pricing page.
ranked.good_at: Transparency and price. It is the only genuinely capable option here that publishes exact numbers against exact limits, so you can work out your cost in thirty seconds. The improvement queue is well-built for actually working through — each suggestion carries the data behind it and applies in one click.
ranked.the_catch: Google Ads only, and the caps bite in two directions at once: cross $25,000 in total monthly spend or an eleventh account and Basic becomes $249. The suggestions are templated — by week three you will have seen every category of improvement it can generate and will be dismissing the same handful repeatedly, because it is pattern-matching on thresholds, not reasoning about your account. It also will not tell you your tracking is broken, which is the actual cause more often than anyone admits.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone diagnosing Meta, or an agency needing Microsoft Ads too — Adalysis covers both search platforms with unlimited accounts. Skip it if you want a one-off diagnosis rather than an ongoing subscription; the free WordStream grader will give you the headline for nothing.

ranked.name: Adzooma
ranked.one_liner: Free tier across all three platforms; shallow but genuinely free
ranked.use_it_when: You want a no-cost second opinion across Google, Microsoft and Meta before deciding whether the problem justifies a paid tool at all — or you're auditing someone else's account and need a starting list.
ranked.cost: Free forever plan. Silver $69/mo. Gold $179/mo.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free — $0, monthly PPC performance reports, monthly opportunity analysis, a limited number of opportunities shown, 1 SEO profile, 1 web metrics profile, unlimited ad accounts connected, 3 PPC alerts from free templates only, budget tracking, 1 user seat. Silver — $69/mo or $700/yr (20% off): weekly reports and analysis, all opportunities visible, 5 SEO and 5 web metrics profiles, 10 custom PPC alerts, unlimited seats, report branding, priority support. Gold — $179/mo or $1,800/yr: daily reports and analysis, unlimited profiles and alerts, all alert templates. Enterprise on request. Connects to Google Ads, Microsoft Advertising, Meta Ads and GA4.
ranked.good_at: Being free and still touching all three major platforms — nothing else here does that. Connecting unlimited ad accounts on the $0 plan makes it a reasonable triage layer across a portfolio, and the budget tracking catches the dull, common failure of a campaign quietly capped.
ranked.the_catch: The free plan is a demo with a long expiry date: it analyses once a month and deliberately withholds most of the opportunities it found, so you learn that a number exists without learning what it is. One seat, and alerts limited to three from stock templates. The opportunities themselves are rule-based nudges that overlap heavily with Google's own Recommendations tab, which you already have for nothing — so a share of what you're paying $69 for is a prettier version of a free Google screen.
ranked.wrong_for: Anyone who needs to know why an ad variant lost rather than that it lost — the analysis is shallow. Move to Adalysis for search or Motion for social creative. Also wrong for agencies: the single seat on free and the profile caps on Silver are built to push you to Gold.

ranked.name: Triple Whale
ranked.one_liner: For when the campaign is fine and the number is lying
ranked.use_it_when: You run e-commerce, Meta reports a healthy ROAS that your bank balance does not, and the real question is whether the campaign is underperforming or whether platform-reported attribution is double-counting the same order.
ranked.cost: Free plan. Paid $179-$539+/mo, scaling with GMV.
ranked.pricing_detail: Free — $0/mo, no GMV requirement: basic tracking, blended ROAS. Starter — $179/mo or $1,790/yr (two months free): multi-touch attribution, Moby AI chat. Advanced — $259/mo or $2,590/yr: adds creative analytics, product analytics, cohort analysis, SQL editor. Custom — from $539/mo, aimed at brands above $20M annual GMV. Price is a function of annual GMV plus the package, calculated on a slider. 60+ one-click connections including Meta, Google and Amazon. No credit card needed for the free plan.
ranked.good_at: Answering a question none of the others ask. Every tool above assumes the reported numbers are true and audits the settings; this one audits the numbers. Blended ROAS on the free plan alone will tell you whether your channels sum to your actual revenue, which is the fastest way to catch platform over-reporting. The free tier is a real free tier, not a trial.
ranked.the_catch: Multi-touch attribution is a model and you cannot inspect the model. When Triple Whale and Meta disagree by 40% you now hold three numbers and no adjudicator, and the temptation is to believe whichever one flatters the decision you already made. Price scales with GMV, so a good quarter raises the bill for reasons unrelated to usage. Creative analytics — the part that would actually diagnose a failing ad — is gated on Advanced, one tier above the headline $179.
ranked.wrong_for: B2B and lead generation: it is built around Shopify e-commerce and long, low-volume sales cycles get little from it. Also wrong if your tracking is already trustworthy and the campaign really is the problem — spend the money on Adalysis or Optmyzr instead.

also_considered.name: Motion
also_considered.why_not: Genuinely good at creative-level diagnosis for social, but $750/mo up to $50k monthly spend and $1,200/mo above it — a spend-banded floor that prices out most accounts that need diagnosing.

also_considered.name: Madgicx
also_considered.why_not: Meta-focused audit and automation, but the price for the main plan is only visible after signup and is set by your monthly ad-spend band ($1K to $30K+) — you cannot compare it before committing.

also_considered.name: Northbeam
also_considered.why_not: Serious attribution, priced for enterprise: $1,500/mo Starter and $3,500/mo Professional, banded by monthly ad spend. Overkill unless you are past $200k/mo.

also_considered.name: Bïrch (formerly Revealbot)
also_considered.why_not: Rebranded from Revealbot; revealbot.com now redirects to bir.ch. It automates rules across Meta, Google, Snapchat and TikTok from $49/mo — but it executes decisions, it does not diagnose, and spend limits carry overage charges.

also_considered.name: LocaliQ / WordStream Google Ads Performance Grader
also_considered.why_not: Free one-off grade on wasted spend, Quality Score and impression share, no card needed — but it wants Google sign-in and an email, and a poor grade routes you to WordStream's paid services. Fine as a first look, not a tool.

also_considered.name: Matomo On-Premise
also_considered.why_not: The closest thing to a self-hostable answer: free to download and run on your own servers, with a free Marketing Campaigns Reporting plugin that tracks campaign source, medium and content. But it is web analytics, not a PPC auditor — it can prove your conversions are real, not tell you which keyword is wasting money. There is no open-source ad-account auditor; this category is entirely proprietary SaaS.

watch_list: Adalysis or Optmyzr publishing real numbers instead of a spend slider — both currently make you configure or call before you can compare, and either one going transparent would move it up.

Meta and Google exposing account diagnostics through their MCP/agent APIs. If a general-purpose AI agent can pull insights, benchmarks and anomaly signals directly, the rule-engine layer these tools sell becomes very hard to charge $150+/mo for.
Adzooma's free tier shrinking. It is currently the only free multi-platform option here, and free plans this generous rarely survive a funding round.

Any of these moving off ad-spend-banded pricing to flat or per-seat. Spend banding means your bill rises exactly when performance is worst, and a rival breaking that pattern would be a genuine reason to switch.
Motion or another creative-analytics tool launching a tier under $200/mo — creative fatigue is the most common cause of social underperformance and nothing affordable diagnoses it today.
An open-source PPC audit tool appearing. Right now there is nothing to self-host, so anyone whose ad data cannot leave their infrastructure has no option in this category at all.
